Study Notes

empty for now — ready for the lecture material
What this file is
A single self-contained page. Everything lives here — no internet needed once it's open, nothing to install, and you can email it to yourself or print it. Each week becomes its own section in the sidebar on the left.

What goes in as content arrives

The lecture material, rewritten

Every slide's content, reorganised so it reads as an explanation rather than a list of bullets. Definitions kept verbatim where they're the sort of thing an exam asks you to state.

Interactive tools

Working implementations of whatever the week's mechanic is — search algorithms you can step through, tables you can fill in, solvers that show their working. Built so you can check your own hand-worked answers.

Exam takeaways

A numbered list closing each week: the things most likely to be asked, and the exact phrasings worth memorising.

Practice with hidden solutions

Past-exam questions where the answer is folded away until you've had a go, plus a self-test generator that marks you.

Conventions used throughout

A yellow box like this
Something worth learning close to word-for-word — a definition, a rule, or a list an exam expects back.
A green box
A connection, an intuition, or the reason something is defined the way it is. Understanding rather than memorising.
An orange box
A trap. Somewhere the obvious reading is wrong, or a place marks are commonly lost.
📘 A blue box marked with a book
Background I've added that wasn't in the slides. Useful for understanding, but check whether your exam expects it before spending time on it.

Two other things

FeatureWhere
Light / dark toggleTop of the sidebar. It remembers your choice and follows your system setting on first open.
Reset on every toolBottom-right of each tool panel — puts its inputs and output back to how they started.
Print / PDFCtrl/Cmd+P. The sidebar and tools are hidden automatically; the cram sheet is laid out for paper.
To fill this in
Send the lecture slides — PDFs, screenshots or text, one week at a time or several at once. I'll add each week as its own section, build the tools that fit that week's material, and extend the cram sheet as it goes.
★ Start here if a formula blocks you

Reading the Notation

every symbol in the module, said out loud
What this page is for
Most formulas in this module are short sentences written in shorthand. If you cannot read the shorthand, the sentence looks like noise — and no amount of staring fixes that, because the problem is vocabulary, not intelligence.

This page lists every symbol used anywhere in the module, what to say when you see it, and what it does. Then it takes the five worst formulas and decodes them word by word.

Three rules that make any formula readable

Do these in order and most formulas fall apart
  1. Read the left-hand side first. It tells you what is being defined and what it depends on. dist(C₁,C₂) is "a distance between two clusters" — so the answer will be one number, and it depends on two clusters.
  2. Find the little writing under Σ, min or max. That tells you what you are looping over. Under Σ it means "add one of these for every …". Under min it means "try all of these and keep the smallest".
  3. Work from the inside out. Do the innermost bracket first, exactly like arithmetic. The outer symbols just say what to do with the pile of numbers you produced.

A formula is never asking you to do something clever in one step. It is a recipe with the steps stacked up.

Adding things up

symbolsaymeansexample
Σ"sum of" / "add up"Add one term for each thing listed underneath.Σᵢ xᵢ = x₁ + x₂ + x₃ + …
Σi=1n"sum from i equals 1 to n"i counts 1, 2, 3 … up to n. Do the thing n times and add.Σi=13 i² = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14
Σs′"sum over s-prime"One term for every square you could land on.the Bellman equation
Π"product of"Same but multiply instead of add. Rare here.—

The whole trick with Σ: whatever is written under it is the thing that changes from term to term. Everything else stays put.

Sets, membership and size

symbolsaymeansexample
∈"in" / "belongs to"This thing is a member of that collection.p ∈ C₁ — the point p is in cluster 1
{ … }"the set of"A collection, order irrelevant.C = {High, Low, Medium}
|C|"the size of C"How many things are in it.|C| = 4 — four points in the cluster
|x|"the absolute value of x"Drop the minus sign. Same bars, different job — tell them apart by what is inside: a set or a number.|−3| = 3
‖p − q‖"the norm of p minus q"The distance between p and q. Double bars = distance between two points.‖(0,0) − (3,4)‖ = 5
ℝD"R to the D"Points with D coordinates. ℝ² is ordinary (x, y).p ∈ ℝ² — p is a 2D point

The one that catches people: |C| and |x| look identical. If the thing inside is a cluster or a set, it means count. If it is a number, it means make it positive.

Choosing: min, max, arg

symbolsaygives youexample
min"the minimum of"the smallest valuemin of {3, 7, 5} = 3
max"the maximum of"the largest valuemax of {3, 7, 5} = 7
arg min"arg min"the thing that gave the smallest valuearg min = the first item
arg max"arg max"the thing that gave the largest valuearg max = the second item

min/max give a number. arg min/arg max give a name. That is the entire difference, and it is worth marks in Weeks 4, 7 and 8.

If a question says "which action?" or "which feature?", it wants an arg. If it says "what is the value?", it wants the plain min or max.

Probability and averages

symbolsaymeansexample
P(A)"the probability of A"a number from 0 to 1P(heads) = 0.5
P(A | B)"the probability of A given B"A happens, assuming B already did. The bar is not division.P(s′ | s, a) — where you end up, given where you were and what you did
E[X]"the expected value of X" / "the average X"Σ (probability × value), over everything that could happen.E[coin] = 0.5×5 + 0.5×0 = 2.50
N(µ, σ²)"normal with mean mu and variance sigma-squared"a bell curve. The second slot is the variance, not the standard deviation.N(11, 4) ⟹ σ = 2
1predicate"the indicator of …"1 if it is true, 0 if not. Used to count only the cases you want.1Aᵢ=a — 1 on the steps where a was chosen

Hats, stars, primes and subscripts

These are adjectives, not new quantities
marksaymeansexample
ŷ (hat)"y hat"an estimate — what we predicted, not what happenedy = truth, ŷ = prediction
q⋆ (star)"q star"the true or optimal one — usually unknown to the agentq⋆(a) = the real value, Q(a) = our guess
s′ (prime)"s prime"the next one, or another one of the same kinds = now, s′ = where you land
Ui (subscript)"U sub i" / "U at step i"which round we are onU₀, U₁, U₂ — the value map after each sweep
xij (two subs)"x i j"the j-th coordinate of the i-th thingpij — coordinate j of point i
γt (superscript)"gamma to the t"usually a power. Not an index.γ² = γ × γ
Uπ"U under policy pi"the exception: a superscript naming which policyUπ(s)

The Greek letters, and what each one is used for here

lettersayin this module it meanswhere
γgammadiscount factor — how much less a future reward is worthW4, W8
εepsilona small amount: an error tolerance, or the exploration rateW4, W8
δdeltathe biggest change this roundW4
πpia policy — an action for every state. Not 3.14 here.W4
µmua mean — a cluster centre, or a distribution's averageW6, W7
σ, σ²sigmastandard deviation, and varianceW7, W8
β₀, β₁betathe intercept and slope of a fitted lineW7
αalphathe best value MAX can guarantee so farW2
βbetathe best value MIN can guarantee so farW2
εiepsilona residual — one point's errorW7
Σsigma (capital)add up. Different job from lowercase σ.everywhere

Note that β and ε each get used for two different things in different weeks, and σ and Σ are the same letter in different cases. Context tells you which; nobody expects you to guess from the glyph alone.

Everything else

symbolsaymeans
:="is defined as"a definition, not an equation to solve
←"becomes" / "is updated to"overwrite the left with the right, like x = x + 1 in code
⟹"implies" / "therefore"—
≈"is approximately"rounded
∞"infinity"in UCB, a value that always wins
√x"the square root of x"—
ln t"log t" / "natural log of t"base e, not base 10. ln 8 = 2.0794, log₁₀ 8 = 0.9031
f(x)"f of x"a thing that takes x and gives a number back

The five worst formulas, decoded

1 · Single-linkage  (Week 6)
distSL(C₁, C₂) := minp∈C₁, q∈C₂ ‖p − q‖
distSL(C₁,C₂)the single-linkage distance between two clusters — the answer will be one number
:=is defined as
mintake the smallest of everything that follows
p∈C₁, q∈C₂for every point p in cluster 1, paired with every point q in cluster 2
‖p − q‖the distance between that pair

Out loud: "measure every point of C₁ against every point of C₂, and keep the smallest distance."

2 · Within-cluster variance  (Week 6)
V(Ck) = (1 / |Ck|)  Σi,i′ ∈ Ck  d(pi, pi′)²
V(Ck)the variance of cluster k — one number per cluster
|Ck|how many points are in it (not pairs)
Σi,i′one term for every unordered pair of points in the cluster
d(pi, pi′)²the distance between that pair, squared — no square root

Out loud: "take every pair of points in the cluster, square the distance between them, add all of those up, then divide by the number of points."

3 · The Bellman update  (Week 4)
Ui+1(s) = R(s) + γ  maxa  Σs′ P(s′ | s, a) Ui(s′)
Ui+1(s)the new value of square s, after this sweep
R(s)the reward for standing on s — the −0.04 fee
γthe discount factor, 1 on this grid
maxatry every action a, keep the best score
Σs′one term for every square you might land on
P(s′|s,a)the chance of landing on s′ — 0.8, 0.1 or 0.1
Ui(s′)what that square was worth last sweep

Out loud: "for each action, average the old values of the squares it might take you to; keep the best action's number; discount it; add the fee for being here."

4 · Upper Confidence Bound  (Week 8)
At = arg maxa [ Qt(a) + c √( ln t / Nt(a) ) ]
Atthe arm you pull at step t — the answer is an arm, because it is arg max
Qt(a)your current estimate of arm a
cthe exploration parameter you chose in advance
ln tnatural log of the current step number
Nt(a)how many times you have pulled a before now

Out loud: "for each arm, add its estimate to a bonus that grows when you have not tried it much; pull whichever arm scores highest."

5 · Gini-Split  (Week 7)
Gini-Split(Ai) = Σj=1a (nj / n) · Gini(vj)
Aithe feature you are considering splitting on
Σj=1aone term for each value that feature can take — so one per child node
nj / nwhat fraction of the rows land in child j — the weight
Gini(vj)how impure that child is

Out loud: "split the rows by this feature; for each group, work out how mixed it is; average those, weighting each by how big the group is."

If a formula still will not open
Put numbers in it. Take the smallest possible example — two points, two arms, one sweep — and write out every term longhand. A formula that looks impossible in symbols is nearly always three multiplications and an addition once you have actual numbers in front of you.

Every tool in this file exists to do exactly that: they print the longhand version of the formula for whatever numbers you give them.

Come back here whenever a symbol stops you.

Week 01 · Part 1 · Introduction

What is Artificial Intelligence?

definitions, approaches, and the rational agent

Two senses of the phrase

The distinction the lecture opens with
  1. AI is a kind of intelligence — artificial, created by humans.
    • You can use (artificial) intelligence to solve a problem.
    • Some thing or behaviour can be (artificially) intelligent.
    • But there is NO such thing as using "an AI" / "an intelligence".
  2. AI is a science / field of study / field of research — with the goal of creating intelligent systems.
Why the slide bothers making this point
"An AI" treats intelligence as a countable object, like a gadget. The lecture insists it's either a property something has, or a field that studies how to give things that property. Worth using the careful phrasing in written answers — it signals you understood the framing.
The founding definition — John McCarthy, 1956
"AI is the science and engineering of making intelligent machines, especially intelligent computer programs. It is related to the similar task of using computers to understand human intelligence, but AI does not have to confine itself to methods that are biologically observable."

The last clause is the load-bearing one: an intelligent machine does not have to work the way a brain works. That single sentence is what licenses the "rational" column in the table below.

Four approaches to AI

If AI is "the science of making intelligent machines" — what counts as an intelligent machine? There are two independent choices, giving four approaches:

Like humans
cognitive models of how humans think		Rationally
laws from logic, probability
ThinkSystems that think like humansSystems that think rationally
ActSystems that act like humansSystems that act rationally
Reading the two axes
Think vs act — is the machine judged on its internal reasoning, or only on its behaviour?
Humanly vs rationally — is the benchmark what a person would do, or what is provably the best thing to do?

These give very different research programmes. Copying humans means copying our mistakes too; being rational means possibly behaving in ways no person would. This module is almost entirely in the act rationally box.

Systems that act like humans

The criterion
A system is intelligent if a person cannot distinguish its behaviour from a human's.

Turing test

Proposed by Alan Turing in 1950.

  • Let a human ask questions to a system.
  • If the human cannot tell whether the answers came from a human or a machine, it passes the test.

Total Turing test

  • A robot is intelligent if a person cannot distinguish its behaviour from a human's.
  • Includes physical behaviour — not just conversation.

Systems that act rationally: agents

Three definitions to know exactly
  • Agent — a unit that makes an intelligent decision when given the opportunity. It uses the knowledge it has at that point in time to make the decision, and the decision is limited by the range of actions possible at that point in time.
  • Autonomous agent — makes decisions without human input.
  • Rational agent — always takes the best action at a given point.

Examples: a robot, an autonomous vehicle, an enemy monster in a game.

the agent loop, built up over three slides
Perception comes in through sensors; knowledge feeds each stage; the decision goes out through effectors as an action.

Two ways of encoding knowledge

The knowledge box on the left — how the world evolves, effects of my actions, goals — can be filled in two very different ways. This is the split that divides the whole field.

Model-based

explicit knowledge → Symbolic / Classical AI

  • Define an encoding of what the world looks like.
  • Define how we can change that world.
  • Search for good strategies on how to change the world the way we want to.
  • Pretends to think like a human.

Data-driven

tacit knowledge → Machine Learning

  • Reads in coarse data from a specific problem.
  • Is told the problem it's trying to solve.
  • Changes the model such that it gets the correct output.
  • Pretends to learn like a human.
Note the third bullet on the left — that's this whole module
"Search for good strategies on how to change the world the way we want to" is a one-line description of search, which is Part 2. Classical AI encodes the world explicitly and then searches; machine learning fits a model to data instead. Also note the deliberate parallel in the last bullets: one pretends to think like a human, the other pretends to learn like one.

The dimensions a problem can vary along

Each part of the agent diagram comes with a choice. These are the axes you use to characterise a problem before choosing a technique:

Where it sitsThe choiceWhat it means
Knowledgeexplicit vs tacitwritten down in a form we can inspect, vs implicit in a learned model
model-based vs data-driventhe two columns above
Perceptionperfect vs imperfectdo the sensors tell the truth?
Environmentfully vs partially observablecan the agent see the whole state, or only part of it?
static vs dynamicdoes the world change while the agent is deciding?
Actionsinstantaneous vs durativedoes an action take time to complete?
deterministic vs stochasticdoes an action always have the same effect?
Why this table matters more than it looks
Every technique in the module assumes a particular set of answers. The search algorithms in Parts 2 and 3 all assume the easy end of every axis: perfect perception, a fully observable static environment, and instantaneous deterministic actions. If a question describes a problem that breaks one of those assumptions, that's the hint that plain search won't do.

A short history

YearEvent
1950Alan Turing proposes the Turing test
1956John McCarthy's definition of AI
1958Herbert A. Simon: "within 10 years a digital computer will be the world's chess champion"
1967Marvin Minsky: "within a generation, the problem of creating 'artificial intelligence' will substantially be solved"
1997IBM's Deep Blue beats Gary Kasparov
2016DeepMind's AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol
2017DeepMind's AlphaZero becomes one of the strongest chess players of all time
2019DeepMind's AlphaStar achieves grandmaster status in StarCraft II
The point of the two quotes
Simon said chess in ten years; it took 39. Minsky said the whole problem in a generation; the lecture's own summary is that many open challenges still exist and true general intelligence is still a long way off. The pairing is there to show how badly the field has historically mis-estimated difficulty.

The value alignment problem

Definition
  • How to align the values of your system with those of the humans who use, and are impacted by, the system?
  • How to exactly specify what a "good" song recommendation / conversation / game experience is?
Connect it back to the agent diagram
Look at the knowledge box: one of the three things in it is goals. A rational agent "always takes the best action" — but best according to what? The value alignment problem is precisely the difficulty of filling in that one box correctly. The agent will optimise exactly what you specify, which is only useful if what you specified is what you meant.

Human vs artificial intelligence

Human

  • Self-directed goals
  • Common sense
  • Learn from few examples
  • Adapt to similar but different tasks
  • Emotional intelligence
  • Humans ask questions!

Artificial

  • Statistical reasoning
  • Large-scale maths
  • Huge state-space exploration
  • Computational power (at scale)
"Huge state-space exploration"
That's the entry in the right-hand column that Parts 2 and 3 are about. The machine's advantage isn't insight — it's the ability to examine enormous numbers of possibilities systematically. Search is how that advantage gets used.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 1
  1. The two senses of AI — a kind of intelligence (a property, not a countable object — "no such thing as an AI") and a field of research aiming to create intelligent systems.
  2. McCarthy's 1956 definition, especially the closing clause: AI does not have to confine itself to biologically observable methods.
  3. The four approaches — think/act × like humans/rationally. Know that "like humans" means cognitive models and "rationally" means laws from logic and probability.
  4. Turing test (1950, question-and-answer) vs total Turing test (a robot, including physical behaviour).
  5. Agent / autonomous agent / rational agent — be able to give all three definitions, including that an agent's decision is limited by the knowledge and the actions available at that point in time.
  6. Draw the agent loop — sensors → what the world is like now → what it will be like if I do A → what action to do now → effectors, with knowledge (how the world evolves, effects of my actions, goals) feeding in.
  7. Model-based vs data-driven — explicit/symbolic/classical vs tacit/machine learning, four bullets each, and the "pretends to think" / "pretends to learn" contrast.
  8. The seven dimensions — explicit/tacit, model-based/data-driven, perfect/imperfect perception, fully/partially observable, static/dynamic, instantaneous/durative, deterministic/stochastic.
  9. The history dates — 1950 Turing, 1956 McCarthy, 1958 Simon's prediction, 1967 Minsky's prediction, 1997 Deep Blue, 2016 AlphaGo, 2017 AlphaZero, 2019 AlphaStar.
  10. Value alignment — aligning system values with human ones, and the difficulty of exactly specifying what "good" means.
  11. Human vs AI strengths — the two lists, and note humans ask questions.

End of Part 1. Next: search — how a model-based agent actually finds a plan.

Week 01 · Part 2 · Search

Search: BFS, DFS, UCS

turning "what should I do?" into "find me a path"

What search is

Definition — learn this sentence
Search is the process of computing a sequence of actions that form a path to a goal.

Recall the model-based agent from Part 1: it defines an encoding of the world, defines how the world can change, and then searches for good strategies. Search is that third step, made precise.

The five components of a search problem

ComponentWhat it isRomania example
State spacethe set of all states the world can be inthe set of cities
Initial state + goal testwhere we start, and a test telling us whether a state is a goalstart at Arad; is this city Bucharest?
Actionswhat the agent can do in a statedrive along a road leaving this city
Transition modelthe state that results from doing an action in a statedriving Arad→Sibiu leaves you in Sibiu
Action coststhe cost of applying an action in a statethe length of the road
Note what a "goal" is
The goal is a test, not necessarily a single named state. "Any state where all tiles are in order" or "any city with a hospital" are perfectly good goals. That matters later: an algorithm stops when the test passes, whichever state triggered it.
A search problem does not come with the answer
The five components describe a world. They don't say which sequence of actions is good — finding that is the algorithm's job. Different algorithms explore the same problem in different orders and give different answers, and that's the whole content of the rest of this week.

Three example problems

1 · Sliding tiles

State space: every arrangement of the tiles. Initial state: the scrambled board. Goal test: are the tiles in order? Actions: slide a tile adjacent to the gap into the gap. Transition model: the board with that tile and the gap swapped. Costs: 1 per move — so cheapest path = fewest moves.

2 · Navigation (Romania)

The running example for the rest of the week. States = cities, actions = roads, costs = distances. Here the costs are not all equal, which is exactly what separates the algorithms below.

3 · Self-service checkout — giving change

A state is a vector of coin counts, e.g. (3, 3, 0, 1, 3, 0, 3, 1) — how many of each denomination the machine holds. Actions = dispense one coin of some denomination. Goal test = the dispensed amount equals the change owed. Costs = 1 per coin, so the cheapest path uses the fewest coins.

The pattern across all three
None of these look like "navigation", yet all three fit the same five slots. That's the point of the formalism: once you can write a problem as ⟨states, initial, goal test, actions, transitions, costs⟩, every algorithm in this module applies to it unchanged. In an exam, "formulate this as a search problem" means: fill in those five slots.

Search trees

Search tree
  • A node is a state.
  • An edge is an action taking you from one state to another.
  • The root is the initial state; a path from root to a node is a candidate plan.
Redundant paths make the tree infinite

A graph with a cycle (drive A→B, then B→A, then A→B…) unrolls into an infinite search tree, even though the state space is tiny. Two fixes:

  • Check the path back to the root — refuse to expand into a state already on the current branch. Cheap, only kills cycles on this path.
  • Track visited states (a reached set) — refuse to expand any state seen before anywhere. Stronger, costs memory.
Tree vs graph — why the distinction keeps showing up
The graph is the map, and it's finite. The tree is the set of all paths through that map, and it can be infinite. Algorithms walk the tree; the reached set is what keeps them from re-walking the same part of the graph forever. Whenever a slide says "complete if redundant paths are prevented", this is what it means.

Breadth-first search

Idea
Explore the tree in slices of the same depth: all nodes 1 action away, then all nodes 2 actions away, and so on. Implemented with a queue (first in, first out) plus a reached set.
PropertyBFS
Complete? (finds a solution if one exists)Yes
Optimal? (finds the best solution)Yes — if all action costs are equal
Timeb + b² + … + b^d
Spaceb + b² + … + b^d

b = branching factor (actions per state), d = depth of the shallowest solution, m = maximum depth of the tree.

Why "optimal only if costs are equal"
BFS returns the solution with the fewest actions. If every action costs the same, fewest actions = cheapest. If they don't — as on a road map — BFS will happily return a 2-hop route of length 310 while a 3-hop route of length 278 exists. That exact example appears under UCS below.
The space cost is the killer
BFS's memory is the same order as its time, because it must hold an entire depth slice at once. With b = 10 and d = 10 that's about ten billion nodes. Time you can wait for; memory you cannot buy.

Depth-first search

Idea
Always expand the deepest node first — dive down one branch to the bottom, then back up and try the next. Implemented with a stack (last in, first out).
PropertyDFS
Complete?Yes — if redundant paths are prevented (otherwise it can fall down an infinite branch)
Optimal?No — it finds the left-most solution, not the best one
Timeb^m
Spaceb · m
The trade in one line
DFS trades solution quality for memory. It only ever stores the current branch plus its siblings — b·m instead of b^d — which is the difference between a few thousand nodes and a few billion. In exchange it can return an absurdly long path, and its time bound depends on m (how deep the tree goes) rather than d (how deep the answer is), so a shallow solution hidden on the right can take exponentially long to reach.

Best-first search — the general framework

The idea that unifies everything
Keep the frontier in a priority queue ordered by an evaluation function f(n). Always expand the node with the lowest f. Every algorithm this week is just a different choice of f.
Algorithmf(n)Effect
BFSdepth(n)shallowest first
DFS−depth(n)deepest first
UCSg(n) — cost so farcheapest-so-far first
Greedy (Part 3)h(n) — estimate to goalclosest-looking first
A* (Part 3)g(n) + h(n)best total estimate first
This is the single most useful fact in the topic
You don't have five algorithms to memorise — you have one algorithm and five values of f. If you can write best-first search, you can write all of them. It also explains the exam favourite "what happens to A* when h ≡ 0?": f = g + 0 = g, which is literally the UCS row.

Uniform-cost search

Definition
f(n) = the sum of the action costs from the start state to n — usually written g(n). Expand the node with the smallest accumulated cost.

UCS finds the minimum-cost plan, not the minimum-action plan.

The slide's worked contrast
On the same map, from D to BUCHAREST:
  • BFS — D → F → BUCHAREST: 2 actions, total cost 99 + 211 = 310
  • UCS — D → E → G → BUCHAREST: 3 actions, total cost 80 + 97 + 101 = 278

BFS wins on hop count, UCS wins on distance. Neither is "wrong" — they optimise different things. 310 vs 278 is the number to remember.

PropertyUCS
Complete?Yes
Optimal?Yes (for non-negative costs)
Timeproportional to the number of nodes with cost less than the cost of the goal
Spacesame
Read that complexity carefully
UCS's cost is measured in cost contours, not depth: it expands every node cheaper than the optimal goal before it stops. If lots of cheap actions surround the start, that's a lot of nodes. And note that UCS uses no information about where the goal is — it expands outward in all directions equally. Fixing that is exactly what Part 3 does.

Tool · Search explorer

Interactive

Search explorer

The graph is drawn for you — drag the nodes apart, shift-click to move the start or goal, and step through the expansions one pop at a time watching the frontier light up. Switch between BFS, DFS, UCS, Greedy and A* with one click. Defaults to the Romania map from the slides.

Things worth trying in it
  • Press ▶ play on UCS and watch the frontier creep outwards in cost order. Then switch to A* and play it again — the heuristic drives it almost straight at the goal.
  • Shift-click D to make it the start, then compare BFS and UCS — 2 actions / cost 310 versus 3 actions / cost 278, exactly the slide.
  • Run DFS and notice the path it returns is neither shortest nor cheapest — it's simply the first branch it fell down.
  • Blank out the heuristics and run A*: with h ≡ 0 it expands exactly like UCS.
  • Compare the nodes expanded count for UCS and A* from ARAD — 13 against 6. Step both and watch where the six saved expansions were: UCS wastes them going the wrong way.
  • Drag the nodes into the shape of the real map (ARAD top-left, BUCHAREST bottom-right) and the greedy failure becomes obvious — it heads straight for F because F looks close.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 2
  1. The definition — search computes a sequence of actions that form a path to a goal.
  2. The five components — state space; initial state + goal test; actions; transition model; action costs. Be able to fill them in for an unfamiliar problem (tiles, navigation, coins).
  3. Search tree — node = state, edge = action; redundant paths make it infinite; prevent by checking parents up to the root, or by tracking visited states.
  4. BFS — queue + reached; complete yes; optimal yes if equal costs; time and space b + b² + … + b^d.
  5. DFS — deepest first; complete yes if redundant paths prevented; optimal no, returns the left-most solution; time b^m; space b·m.
  6. Best-first — priority queue on f(n); BFS is f = depth, DFS is f = −depth. Everything else is a choice of f.
  7. UCS — f(n) = g(n), the summed cost from the start; finds minimum-cost, not minimum-action plans; complete and optimal; time and space proportional to the number of nodes cheaper than the goal.
  8. The 310 vs 278 contrast — BFS's 2-action route costs more than UCS's 3-action route. It's the cleanest way to show you understand what "optimal" is relative to.

End of Part 2. Next: adding a heuristic — Greedy and A*.

Week 01 · Part 3 · Heuristic search

A* & Heuristics

using an estimate of what's ahead

The problem with UCS: it looks backwards

The observation the whole lecture turns on
UCS orders the frontier by g(n) — the cost already spent getting to n. That is information about the past. It says nothing about whether n is in the right direction.

So UCS is looking backwards, not forwards: it expands outward from the start in every direction equally, including directly away from the goal.

Heuristic
A rule of thumb — an estimate h(n) of the cost from n to the goal. It's a guess, computed cheaply, that lets the search look forwards.
Where a heuristic actually comes from
On a map, the obvious guess is the straight-line distance to the goal: easy to compute, and always less than or equal to the real road distance. For sliding tiles it might be the number of misplaced tiles. The pattern is the same — solve an easier version of the problem and use its answer as the estimate. That idea gets a name at the bottom of this page.

Greedy best-first search

Definition
f(n) = h(n) — expand whichever frontier node looks closest to the goal. Note h(goal) = 0, so the goal always wins once it's on the frontier.
What it costs you — the slide's number
On the Romania map, greedy best-first returns
ARAD → D → F → BUCHAREST  =  140 + 99 + 211 = 450

The optimal route costs 418. Greedy is fast and gets there, but it is not optimal — it walked into F because F looked close (h = 176), and only then discovered the last leg costs 211.

Why it fails, in one sentence
Greedy throws away g entirely, so it has no memory of what a route has already cost. UCS remembers the past and ignores the future; greedy predicts the future and ignores the past. Both are half-blind — which tells you exactly what to do next.

A*

Definition
f(n) = g(n) + h(n)
  • g(n) — the cost of the path from the start to n (backwards, known).
  • h(n) — the estimated cost from n to the goal (forwards, guessed).
  • f(n) — the estimated cost of the best route through n.
Read f as a question
"If the answer goes through this node, what would the whole trip cost?" Expanding the smallest f means always working on the most promising complete plan, rather than the cheapest fragment (UCS) or the nicest-looking next stop (greedy).

The worked example

Start ARAD, goal BUCHAREST. Straight-line heuristics to BUCHAREST:

ARAD366A329B374 C380D253E193 F176G100H160 I244L241M242 BUCHAREST0

Expanding ARAD gives three children — and f already picks the right one:

A f = 118 + 329 = 447 B f = 75 + 374 = 449 D f = 140 + 253 = 393
Notice what just happened
B is the cheapest child (g = 75) — UCS would expand it first. But B looks far from the goal (h = 374), so its f is the worst of the three. D costs nearly twice as much to reach, yet has the best f. This single step is the difference between UCS and A*.

Continuing — expand D (f = 393), which gives:

C f = 291 + 380 = 671 E f = 220 + 193 = 413 F f = 239 + 176 = 415

E wins (413). Expanding E gives G with f = 317 + 100 = 417 and H with f = 366 + 160 = 526. G (417) still beats F (415)? No — F at 415 is expanded first, offering BUCHAREST at f = 450 + 0 = 450. That's a goal node on the frontier, but A* does not stop: 450 is not the smallest f. G at 417 is. Expanding G offers BUCHAREST at f = 418 + 0 = 418, which is now the smallest — and that is the answer.

ARAD → D → E → G → BUCHAREST  =  140 + 80 + 97 + 101 = 418
The single most common exam mistake
A* does not stop when it generates the goal — only when it expands it. Had it stopped the moment BUCHAREST appeared via F, it would have returned 450, the greedy answer. The optimality guarantee lives entirely in that distinction.

Where do the heuristic numbers actually come from?

The question the table never answers
You are handed h(D) = 253 before you have explored anything. If we do not yet know the route to Bucharest, how can we possibly know it is 253 away?

Because 253 is not the road distance. It is the straight-line distance — measured off the map with a ruler, or computed from the two towns' coordinates. No roads are involved.

Two different pieces of knowledge
g(n)h(n)
What it isthe cost of the road you have actually travelledthe straight-line distance still to go
How you get itby adding up edges as you searchfrom the coordinates, before you search at all
Exact or estimate?exact — you drove itan estimate, and always an under-estimate
Changes during search?yes, it grows as you gono — it is a fixed property of the map

You know where Bucharest is. You do not know how to drive there. Those are separate facts, and A* uses the cheap one to find the expensive one.

The intuition, if the map is not helping
You are lost in a city and you can see a cathedral spire about two kilometres away. You know it is two kilometres away. You have no idea how to walk there — one-way streets, a river, dead ends. The two kilometres is h. The distance you actually end up walking is g, and it will be more than two kilometres.
Why the ruler is always wrong in the same direction
A straight line is the shortest thing between two points, so no road can beat it. Check it on D:
h(D) = 253   the ruler
true road = D → E → G → BUCHAREST = 80 + 97 + 101 = 278
253 ≤ 278   the estimate is 25 too low, as it must be

Never too high. That one-sided error is exactly the admissibility condition, and it is the whole reason A* can be trusted to return the cheapest path.

Two things worth knowing for the exam
  • You never compute h yourself. It is given to you in a table, exactly as in the worked example above. Computing it is the map-maker's job, not the search algorithm's.
  • When there are no coordinates to measure — an 8-puzzle, a planning problem — you get h by relaxing the problem: solve an easier version and use its cost as the estimate. Counting misplaced tiles is the relaxation "any tile may teleport". Week 3's RPG is the relaxation "actions have no delete effects". Same trick, twice.

Tool · The A* lab

Interactive

Drag the heuristics, switch the ranking rule, watch B wait

The towns sit at their real map positions, so the dashed lines are literally what h measures. Switch the ranking rule between g, h and g + h and step through — with g the dashed lines vanish, because UCS has no idea where the goal is. Drag any h slider and the search re-runs; push one above its true remaining distance and it turns red, because A* has stopped being safe. Set every h to 0 and A* collapses into UCS in front of you.

Three things to actually try in it
  1. Run A* to the end and watch B. It enters the frontier at expansion 1 with the cheapest g of the three, and it is still sitting there when the search finishes. UCS would have expanded it first. A* never expands it at all.
  2. Switch to f(n) = h(n). Greedy dives at whatever looks closest and stops caring what it has already spent — compare the final cost with A*'s.
  3. Drag h(D) up past its true remaining distance. D stops looking attractive, A* explores elsewhere, and the path it returns may no longer be the cheapest. That is what losing admissibility costs you.

Admissible heuristics

Definition
A heuristic is admissible if it never over-estimates the cost to the goal — that is, for every node,
actual cost to goal  ≥  h(n)
  • Straight-line distance is admissible — no road is shorter than the straight line.
  • A* with an admissible heuristic is optimal.
  • h ≡ 0 is admissible — but then f = g and A* degenerates into UCS.
Why over-estimating breaks it
If h over-estimates at some node, f at that node is too high, so A* may leave it sitting on the frontier and expand a goal through a worse route instead. In the worked example, if h(G) were 150 instead of 100, then f(G) = 467 > 450 and A* would have returned the 450 route. Over-estimating is exactly the failure that admissibility rules out.
The key challenge
Find a heuristic that is admissible AND informative.
  • Admissible alone is easy — h ≡ 0 qualifies, and is useless.
  • Informative means close to the true cost, so the search is strongly guided.
  • The higher h is without ever exceeding the truth, the fewer nodes A* expands.

How to get one: by relaxing the constraints of the problem — solve an easier version and use its cost as the estimate.

Relaxation, made concrete
Straight-line distance is a relaxation: drop the constraint "you must follow roads" and you get flying, whose cost is the straight line. For sliding tiles, drop "a tile can only move into the gap" and you get "number of misplaced tiles"; drop only "the target square must be empty" and you get the sum of Manhattan distances — a stronger, still-admissible heuristic. Removing a constraint can only make things cheaper, which is precisely why a relaxed solution never over-estimates.

Tool · Compare all five algorithms

Interactive

Algorithm comparison

Races all five algorithms side by side, one pop per step. Press play and watch A* march at the goal while UCS fans out in every direction. Uses the graph and heuristics from the Search explorer above.

Tool · Admissibility checker

Interactive

Admissibility checker

Every heuristic value is a slider — drag one above its true cost and watch A* break in real time. The true cheapest cost to the goal is computed exactly, and the verdict, the A* path and the optimality check all update as you drag.

Try breaking it
Drag the slider for G upwards. Its true cost to BUCHAREST is 101, so the moment you pass it the row turns orange, the verdict flips to not admissible — and the line at the bottom shows A* returning 450 instead of 418. That is the guarantee breaking, one pixel at a time.

Then press 0 (admissible, useless) and watch A* still find 418, but expand as many nodes as UCS. And press the true cost (perfect) to see A* walk straight to the goal with almost no wasted expansions.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 3
  1. UCS looks backwards — g is cost already spent, so UCS has no sense of direction.
  2. Heuristic = a rule of thumb estimating the cost from a node to the goal.
  3. Greedy best-first — f(n) = h(n), h(goal) = 0; on the map it returns 140 + 99 + 211 = 450, which is not optimal.
  4. A* — f(n) = g(n) + h(n): cost so far plus estimated cost remaining = estimated cost of the best route through that node.
  5. Be able to compute f-values by hand — from ARAD: A 447 = 118 + 329, B 449 = 75 + 374, D 393 = 140 + 253; then C 671, E 413, F 415; then G 417, H 526; goal via F = 450, via G = 418.
  6. The optimal path — ARAD → D → E → G → BUCHAREST = 140 + 80 + 97 + 101 = 418.
  7. A* stops when it expands the goal, not when it generates it — otherwise it would return 450.
  8. Admissible = never over-estimates; actual cost ≥ h(n); straight-line distance is admissible; A* + admissible ⇒ optimal.
  9. h ≡ 0 is admissible but useless — A* becomes UCS.
  10. The key challenge — admissible and informative; obtained by relaxing the constraints of the problem.

End of Week 1.

Week 02 · Part 1 · Adversarial search

Adversarial Search: Minimax

searching when someone is trying to stop you

A second agent changes everything

The setup
How do you solve a search problem when there is a second agent? They have their own goals, and they may:
  • act to help us — a cooperative agent;
  • act to hinder us — an adversarial agent.

This lecture takes the second case: two-player games.

The rules of the abstraction
  • Two players: MAX and MIN.
  • MAX moves first, then they take turns until the game is over.
  • At the end, points are awarded to the winner and penalties given to the loser.
Why the names
The whole game is scored on one number, from MAX's point of view. MAX wants it large, MIN wants it small — so MIN's goal is not "win" in some separate sense, it's "make MAX's number as small as possible". That single shared scale is what makes the algorithm work; you never need two sets of values.

Compare Week 1: there the world was indifferent, so a plan you found stayed valid. Here every second move is chosen by someone who wants your plan to fail, so you must plan for the worst reply, not the convenient one.

Game trees

Definition
A game tree is a tree where nodes are game states and edges are moves. Three types of node:
  • Max nodes — options for the Max-Player
  • Min nodes — options for the Min-Player
  • Terminal nodes — final outcomes
Structure
  • The root is either MAX or MIN.
  • Children of MAX nodes are MIN nodes or Terminal nodes.
  • Children of MIN nodes are MAX nodes or Terminal nodes.
  • Terminal nodes, and only them, have no children.

Evaluation function: values or payoffs associated with terminal nodes.

The layers alternate because the turns alternate
There is nothing deep about "MAX layer, MIN layer, MAX layer" — it's just whose turn it is at that depth. Depth 0 is MAX's move, depth 1 is MIN's reply, depth 2 is MAX again. The only place a number enters the tree from outside is at the terminals; every other value is computed from below.

Managing state spaces

GameSize
Tic-Tac-Toe~765 unique states (from an initial 19,683) once reflections and illegal states are removed — still over 250,000 possible matches
Draughts5 × 1020
Chess8.73 × 1039
Go2 × 10170
Read the jump
Tic-Tac-Toe is fully solvable by brute force — 765 states is nothing. Chess is 1037 times bigger; Go is beyond absurd. The rest of this week exists because you cannot look at the whole tree. Minimax is the correct-but-impossible algorithm; alpha-beta is the first thing you do about it.

The minimax value

Definition
The optimal strategy can be found from the minimax value of each node.

MINIMAX(n) = the utility for MAX of being in the corresponding state, assuming that both players play optimally.

  • MAX prefers to move to a state of maximum value.
  • MIN prefers to move to a state of minimum value.
The three words that carry the definition
"utility for MAX" — one scale, MAX's. "assuming both play optimally" — this is a worst-case guarantee, not a prediction; if MIN blunders, MAX does at least as well, never worse. And the value is computed bottom-up: a terminal's value is given, an internal node's value is the max or min of its children.
The recipe
  1. Terminal node → its payoff.
  2. MIN node → the smallest of its children's values.
  3. MAX node → the largest of its children's values.
  4. The move to play at the root is the edge leading to the child whose value equals the root's.

The worked example

The tree from the slides: root A is a MAX node with moves a₁, a₂, a₃ to MIN nodes B, C, D, each with three terminal children.

B = min(3, 12, 8) = 3 · C = min(2, 4, 6) = 2 · D = min(14, 5, 2) = 2 · A = max(3, 2, 2) = 3, so MAX plays a₁.
Notice the 12 and the 14
B contains a 12 and D contains a 14 — the two juiciest numbers in the tree — and neither has any effect on the answer. MIN will never hand them over. Only the worst child of each MIN node matters, which is exactly the fact alpha-beta exploits in Part 2.

Properties of the minimax algorithm

PropertyMinimax
Time complexityO(bd), where d is the number of levels and b the branching factor
Space complexityO(b · d)
Complete?Yes, if the tree is finite
Optimal?Yes, if the opponent is optimal
The line the lecture flags as important
Minimax explores the complete game tree using depth-first search. Can we improve the algorithm?
Why those two complexities, and why they matter
The space bound O(b·d) should look familiar — it's DFS's b·m from Week 1, because minimax is a DFS. That means memory is fine. The problem is entirely O(b^d) time: for chess, b ≈ 35 and d ≈ 100, so 35100 nodes. Alpha-beta attacks the exponent's base; it does not change the fact that the exponent is still there.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 1
  1. A second agent may be cooperative or adversarial; two-player games take the adversarial case.
  2. MAX moves first, players alternate, points to the winner and penalties to the loser.
  3. Game tree — nodes are game states, edges are moves; Max nodes, Min nodes, Terminal nodes; only terminals have no children; the evaluation function gives terminal payoffs.
  4. MINIMAX(n) = utility for MAX of being in that state, assuming both players play optimally.
  5. Compute bottom-up — MIN nodes take the minimum of their children, MAX nodes the maximum.
  6. The worked tree — leaves 3, 12, 8 | 2, 4, 6 | 14, 5, 2 give B = 3, C = 2, D = 2 and A = 3 via move a₁.
  7. Complexity — time O(bd), space O(b·d); complete if the tree is finite; optimal if the opponent is optimal.
  8. Minimax is a depth-first search over the complete game tree — this sentence sets up alpha-beta.
  9. The scale of the problem — Tic-Tac-Toe ~765 states, draughts 5×1020, chess 8.73×1039, Go 2×10170.

End of Part 1. Next: getting the same answer without looking at everything.

Week 02 · Part 2 · Adversarial search

Alpha-Beta Pruning

the same answer, fewer nodes

Two observations

At a MAX node → α

When some of the children of a MAX node have been evaluated, there is a lower bound α on how much MAX can get, even if the other children have not been evaluated yet.

≥ 3

At a MIN node → β

When some of the children of a MIN node have been evaluated, there is in turn an upper bound β on how much MIN can get, even if the other children have not been evaluated yet.

≤ 5
Why bounds, and why they only go one way
A MAX node that has already seen a child worth 3 can never end up below 3 — it can always just take that child. So its value is ≥ 3: a floor that only rises as more children are seen. Symmetrically, a MIN node that has seen a 5 can never end up above 5: a ceiling that only falls.

These are partial results computed before the node is finished — which is what makes them useful. If a floor from somewhere above already beats a ceiling here, nothing below this point can matter.

α, β, and the cut rule

Definitions
  • α is the minimum score the MAX player could get (the best MAX has secured so far anywhere on the path).
  • β is the maximum score the MIN player could get (the best MIN has secured so far anywhere on the path).

Two optimisations:

  • Skip the rest of a MIN node's children when β ≤ α.
  • Skip the rest of a MAX node's children when β ≤ α.
One rule, said in English
β ≤ α reads: "the best this branch can possibly offer MAX is already no better than something MAX can guarantee elsewhere." So MAX would never come here — and there is no point finishing the evaluation.

Notice the condition is the same at both node types. What differs is only which of the two values you were about to update. That is why it's one algorithm, not two.

What pruning does not do
Alpha-beta returns exactly the same value as plain minimax. It is not an approximation, not a heuristic, and it never changes the chosen move. The only thing it changes is how many terminal nodes get evaluated. If an exam question asks for "the minimax value with alpha-beta pruning", the value is the same number — the extra marks are for saying which nodes were skipped.

The worked example

Same tree as Part 1, evaluated left to right.

StepWhat happensState
1Descend to B, evaluate its leaves 3, 12, 8. B is done.B = 3, so root is ≥ 3 (α = 3)
2Descend to C, evaluate its first leaf: 2.C is ≤ 2 (β = 2)
3β = 2 ≤ α = 3 → prune. C's other two leaves are never looked at.C ≤ 2, marked ✗ ✗
4Descend to D, evaluate 14, then 5.D is ≤ 14, then ≤ 5
5Evaluate D's last leaf 2. D = 2.D = 2
6Root takes max(3, ≤2, 2).A = 3, play a₁
The result
Value 3 — identical to minimax · leaves evaluated 7 instead of 9 · pruned: C's second and third leaves (4 and 6)
Why C got cut but D did not
C's first leaf was 2, which instantly capped C at ≤ 2 — below the 3 MAX already had. Dead branch, stop.

D's first leaf was 14, which caps D at ≤ 14 — still above 3, so D might yet beat B and must be explored. Then 5 caps it at ≤ 5, still above 3. Only the final 2 settles it. The order the leaves happen to appear in decides how much you save — which is the next section.

Tool · Game tree solver

Interactive

Minimax & alpha-beta

Step through the alpha-beta walk one evaluation at a time and watch the bounds tighten until a cut fires. Enter any game tree as nested brackets; you also get the minimax value of every node and exactly which leaves get pruned. Defaults to the tree from the slides.

Things worth trying in it
  • Press ▶ play and watch the depth-first walk. Unvisited nodes are ghosted, so you see exactly how little of the tree alpha-beta ever touches.
  • The default tree — 7 of 9 leaves evaluated, the 4 and 6 under C pruned. That's the slide. Stop on the step marked "β ≤ α — prune" and look at the two bounds that caused it.
  • Reverse the last group to [[3,12,8],[2,4,6],[2,5,14]] — D now caps at ≤ 2 immediately and two more leaves vanish. Same answer, less work.
  • Try a 3-level tree such as [[[3,5],[6,9]],[[1,2],[0,7]]] to see pruning cascade through the layers.
  • Switch the root to MIN and watch every max and min swap while the pruning rule stays β ≤ α.

How much does pruning save?

It depends entirely on move ordering
  • Worst case — children arrive in the least helpful order and nothing is pruned: back to O(bd).
  • Best case — the best move is examined first at every node, and the cost drops to roughly O(bd/2).

Halving the exponent means you can search twice as deep in the same time — which, in a game, is the difference between a weak player and a strong one.

The intuition for "best move first"
Cuts happen when a bound gets tight early. Finding a strong move immediately raises α at once and makes every later sibling easy to dismiss; stumbling on it last means you carried a useless bound the whole way. Real engines therefore spend effort guessing a good move order before searching — which is why "try the move that was best last time" is such a common trick.
Summary of the deck
  • With more than one agent, we need different approaches.
  • Adversarial search like minimax lets us consider the best-worst outcomes and make decisions to guide towards them.
  • Alpha-beta pruning lets us trim and reduce the number of states we evaluate.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 2
  1. The two observations — a partly-evaluated MAX node has a lower bound α; a partly-evaluated MIN node has an upper bound β.
  2. α = minimum score the MAX player could get. β = maximum score the MIN player could get. Learn these two sentences verbatim.
  3. The cut rule — skip the remaining children of a MIN node when β ≤ α, and skip the remaining children of a MAX node when β ≤ α. Same condition both times.
  4. Alpha-beta returns the identical value to minimax — it only changes how many nodes are evaluated.
  5. Be able to run the worked tree by hand — B = 3 sets α = 3; C's first leaf 2 gives β = 2 ≤ 3, so C's remaining two leaves are pruned; D needs all three because 14 and 5 don't settle it. Answer 3, 7 leaves evaluated instead of 9.
  6. Savings depend on move ordering — worst case O(bd), best case about O(bd/2), i.e. twice the depth for the same effort.
  7. Show your working — in a pruning question the marks are for the α/β values at each node and the crossed-out leaves, not just the final number.

End of Part 2. Next: problems where the path doesn't matter at all.

Week 02 · Part 3 · CSPs

CSPs: Introduction

when only the answer matters, not how you got there

It's not the journey, it's the goal

The shift
Typically when you think of search you think of path planning — you know the goal and want to find out how to get there.

But in some problems we only care about finding a goal state: fill in all the values in a way that is valid.

  • Respect rules of where items/values can be placed.
  • Respect validity relationships.
  • All that matters is that we satisfy those rules and constraints — not in which order you filled in the puzzle.
Why this changes the algorithm
In Week 1 the path was the answer, so cost and ordering mattered. In a Sudoku or a colouring, the sequence you wrote the values in is irrelevant — nobody grades your filling-in order. That single observation is worth an exponential factor, and it's cashed in later under the word commutativity.
Why plain search wastes effort here
You can use an informed search on the map-colouring problem. But it is largely wasteful: there are lots of invalid states, and ordinary state-space search happily generates and stores them because it only checks whether a state is the goal, never whether it is valid.

What a CSP is

Definition — three components
  • A finite set of variables X {x₁ … xₙ} — defines all elements that need to be given a value in the problem.
  • A set of domains D {D₁ … Dᵢ} — defines what possible values can be assigned to each variable, {v₁ … vⱼ}.
  • A set of constraints C {C₁ … C_k} — the rules that dictate a relation between variables in X. Each constraint Cᵢ is a pairing of scope and relation.

A CSP solution is an instantiation of all variables in X using values in D that satisfies all constraints in C.

CSP solvers search through incomplete but consistent solutions (partial assignments).

"Scope and relation", and "incomplete but consistent"
A constraint has a scope (which variables it talks about — e.g. ⟨SA, WA⟩) and a relation (which combinations are allowed — e.g. all pairs where the two differ). Separating them is what lets a solver reason about a constraint without knowing what problem it came from.

"Incomplete but consistent" is the search space: partial assignments that break no constraint so far. Not every one leads to a solution, but every one is worth extending — and anything inconsistent is thrown away immediately rather than expanded.

Map colouring

The problem
Map of Australia. Colour each region {red, green, blue} so that no neighbouring regions are the same colour.
As a CSP — memorise this instantiation

X = {WA, NT, Q, NSW, V, SA, T}

D = {{red, green, blue}, {red, green, blue}, …} — one copy per variable

C = {SA≠WA, SA≠NT, SA≠Q, SA≠NSW, SA≠V, WA≠NT, NT≠Q, Q≠NSW, NSW≠V}

Two details people lose marks on
T (Tasmania) appears in X but in no constraint — it's an island, so it neighbours nothing. It still needs a value; it just can never fail. And SA appears in five of the nine constraints, because South Australia touches everything. That asymmetry is exactly what the variable-ordering heuristics in Part 4 detect.

The constraint graph

A CSP with binary constraints draws as a graph: nodes are variables, edges are constraints.

SA (degree 5) is the hub; T is isolated. Nine edges, matching the nine constraints.
Read the heuristics straight off the picture
Degree = how many constraints a variable is in. SA has degree 5, T has degree 0. "Most constraining variable" in Part 4 literally means "pick the highest-degree node" — so the graph is not decoration, it's the data structure the heuristics run on.

n-Queens as a CSP

The formulation from the slides
  • X = {xij} — one variable per square of the board.
  • D = {0, 1} — empty or queen.
  • C =
    Σi,j Xij = N
    (Xij, Xik) ∈ {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0)}
    (Xij, Xkj) ∈ {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0)}
    (Xij, Xi+k, j+k) ∈ {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0)}
    (Xij, Xi+k, j−k) ∈ {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0)}
Decoding those constraints
The set {(0,0), (0,1), (1,0)} is just "not both 1" written out as an explicit relation — the missing pair is (1,1). Applied to:
  • Xij, Xik — same row i, two columns → no two queens share a row;
  • Xij, Xkj — same column j → no two share a column;
  • Xi+k, j+k and Xi+k, j−k — the two diagonals.

And Σ Xij = N forces exactly N queens on the board — without it, all-zeros would satisfy everything.

This is a deliberately clumsy modelling
One variable per square means n² variables and a global sum constraint. A tighter model uses one variable per column with domain {1…n} = the row its queen sits in, which makes "no two in a column" free and reduces the problem to row and diagonal constraints. The slides use the square version because it shows off scope and relation explicitly — but if a question asks you to "model n-Queens efficiently", the column version is the better answer.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 3
  1. The shift — some problems care only about reaching a valid goal state, not about the path or the order of assignment.
  2. Ordinary search is wasteful here — it generates lots of invalid states because it tests for goal, not validity.
  3. The three components — variables X, domains D, constraints C. Each constraint is a pairing of scope and relation.
  4. A solution is an instantiation of all variables in X using values in D satisfying all constraints in C.
  5. Solvers search incomplete but consistent partial assignments.
  6. The Australia CSP verbatim — X = {WA, NT, Q, NSW, V, SA, T}; D = {red, green, blue} each; C = {SA≠WA, SA≠NT, SA≠Q, SA≠NSW, SA≠V, WA≠NT, NT≠Q, Q≠NSW, NSW≠V} — nine constraints.
  7. The constraint graph — nodes are variables, edges are constraints; SA has degree 5, T degree 0.
  8. n-Queens — X = {xij}, D = {0, 1}, and the constraints: Σ Xij = N plus "not both 1" on rows, columns and both diagonals.
  9. Be able to formulate an unseen problem as a CSP — this is the standard exam question. Name the variables, give each a domain, then list the constraints.

End of Part 3. Next: actually solving one.

Week 02 · Part 4 · CSPs

Solving a CSP

backtracking, heuristics, and inference

A CSP as a search problem

The four components
  • States — assignments of variables to values within domains.
  • Initial state — no variables assigned.
  • Action — assign a value to any unassigned variable, provided it does not violate a constraint. If no legal assignments, return failure.
  • Goal test — all variables are assigned values, satisfying all constraints.
The important word is "provided"
Compare Week 1's search problem: there, actions were legal or not by the transition model, and the goal test happened at the end. Here the constraint check is folded into the action itself — you never even generate an inconsistent state. That's the first efficiency, and it's free.
The size of the naïve tree
  • The complete search tree is only of depth n (one layer per variable) — every solution is at the bottom, so depth is not the problem.
  • But with m possible values per variable, there are n! × mn paths through the tree.

The n! is pure waste: it counts the orders in which you could have made the same assignments.

Backtracking search

What it is
A variation of depth-first search with two ingredients:
  • Single-variable assignments — only one variable is assigned at each level of the search tree.
    • Commutativity: [WA = red, NT = green] = [NT = green, WA = red].
    • This reduces paths from n! × mn to mn.
  • For each assignment — check for failure; backtrack on failure to the next assignment; if all assignments fail, return failure.
function RECURSIVE-BACKTRACKING(assignment, csp)
    if assignment is complete then return assignment
    var ← SELECT-UNASSIGNED-VARIABLE(VARIABLES[csp], assignment, csp)
    for each value in ORDER-DOMAIN-VALUES(var, assignment, csp)
        if value is consistent with assignment given CONSTRAINTS[csp]
            add {var = value} to assignment
            result ← RECURSIVE-BACKTRACKING(assignment, csp)
            if result ≠ failure then return result
            remove {var = value} from assignment
    return failure
Where the improvements plug in
Look at the two capitalised helper functions — they are deliberately left abstract:
  • SELECT-UNASSIGNED-VARIABLE → the variable-ordering heuristics (MRV, degree).
  • ORDER-DOMAIN-VALUES → the value-ordering heuristic (LCV).

The extended version adds a third: an INFERENCE step after each assignment, which is where forward checking and arc consistency live. Everything in the rest of this deck is one of those three slots.

Still not good enough
  • It's inefficient — still exhaustively trying all combinations until failure at a given level; arbitrary selection of values.
  • Improving the algorithm: decide which variable we assign at each level; decide the order in which values are tried.
function BACKTRACK(assignment, csp) /* the version with inference */
    if assignment is complete then return assignment
    var ← SELECT-UNASSIGNED-VARIABLE(csp)
    for each value in ORDER-DOMAIN-VALUES(var, assignment, csp) do
        if value is consistent with assignment then
            add {var = value} to assignment
            inferences ← INFERENCE(csp, var, value)
            if inferences ≠ failure then
                add inferences to assignment
                result ← BACKTRACK(assignment, csp)
                if result ≠ failure then return result
            remove {var = value} and inferences from assignment
    return failure

Which variable to assign next?

Most constrained variable

  • Choose the variable with the fewest legal values.
  • Known as the minimum remaining values (MRV) heuristic.

Most constraining variable

  • Imposes the most constraints on the remaining values (for other variables).
  • In graph terms: highest degree.
"Fail first" — and why that's a good thing
Both heuristics aim to hit the dead end as early as possible. If a variable has only one legal value left, assigning it can't go wrong; if it has zero, you find out now instead of after ten more pointless assignments. Pruning near the root of a tree removes an exponential amount of work; pruning near a leaf saves almost nothing.

In practice they're used together: MRV first, degree as the tie-breaker — which is why on Australia the first variable picked is SA (every variable starts with 3 values, so MRV ties, and SA wins on degree 5).

Variable selected — what value to try?

Least constraining value (LCV)
Choose the value that rules out the fewest values in the remaining variables.
Why value ordering pulls the opposite way to variable ordering
This looks contradictory — variables "fail first", values "fail last" — but the asymmetry is real:
  • You must assign every variable, so you want the hopeless one exposed immediately.
  • You only need one value per variable to work, so you want the most promising one tried first.

Same goal both times: reach a solution, or a refutation, with the least search.

Detecting failure early: forward checking

Definition
  • Keep track of remaining legal values for unassigned variables.
  • Terminate search when any variable has no legal values.

Forward checking propagates information from assigned to unassigned variables.

The slides' worked run, on the Australia map:

afterWANTQNSWVSAT
— start —
WA = red
Q = green
V = blue empty!
The failure is detected at V = blue
SA borders WA (red), Q (green) and V (blue), so after the third assignment it has no legal values left and the search backtracks — without ever having tried to assign SA. That is forward checking earning its keep.
But it isn't enough
Forward checking only detects constraints early. Constraint propagation enforces constraints.
Spot the missed inference
Look at the row after Q = green: NT = {blue} and SA = {blue}. NT and SA are neighbours, and both are down to the same single value — the position is already dead. Forward checking cannot see it, because it only ever compares an assigned variable with its unassigned neighbours; it never compares two unassigned variables with each other. Fixing exactly that is arc consistency.

Constraint propagation: arc consistency

Definition
The simplest form of constraint propagation — keep pairs of variables consistent.
  • X → Y is consistent iff for each value of X there are allowed values of Y.
  • When checking X → Y, throw out any values of X for which there isn't an allowed value of Y.
  • If X loses a value, all pairs Z → X need to be rechecked.
Arcs are directed — this trips everyone up
X → Y and Y → X are two different arcs and are checked separately. Checking X → Y only ever deletes values from X, never from Y. That's why the third bullet exists: shrinking X can break arcs that point into X, so they all go back in the queue.

Running it on the same problem, with only WA = red and Q = green assigned:

stepWANTQNSWVSAT
after FC
NSW → SA
V → NSW
SA → NT empty!
The headline result
Arc consistency detects failure earlier than forward checking — here with only two assignments instead of three. It can be run before or after each assignment is made.

AC-3

function AC-3(csp) returns the CSP, possibly with reduced domains
    inputs: csp, a binary CSP with variables {X₁, X₂, …, Xₙ}
    local variables: queue, a queue of arcs, initially all the arcs in csp

    while queue is not empty
        (Xᵢ, Xⱼ) ← REMOVE-FIRST(queue)
        if REMOVE-INCONSISTENT-VALUES(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) then
            for each X_k in NEIGHBORS[Xᵢ] do
                add (X_k, Xᵢ) to queue

function REMOVE-INCONSISTENT-VALUES(Xᵢ, Xⱼ) returns true iff succeeds
    removed ← false
    for each x in DOMAIN[Xᵢ]
        if no value y in DOMAIN[Xⱼ] allows (x, y) to satisfy the constraint Xᵢ ↔ Xⱼ
            then delete x from DOMAIN[Xᵢ]; removed ← true
    return removed
Reading AC-3 in three lines
1. Put every arc in a queue. 2. Pop one, prune the tail's domain against the head's. 3. If anything was pruned, push back every arc pointing at the tail, because they may have become stale.

It terminates because domains only ever shrink, and it costs O(n²d³) for n variables with domain size d. Failure = some domain becomes empty. Note it can also finish with all domains non-empty and still have no solution — arc consistency is a filter, not a solver.

Tool · CSP solver

Interactive

Backtracking search with heuristics and inference

The constraint graph is drawn for you — drag it apart, then step through the backtracking search one decision at a time watching nodes fill in and edges flash orange when violated. All the heuristic buttons re-solve instantly. Defaults to the Australia map-colouring problem.

Things worth trying in it
  • With MRV + degree, check that the first variable chosen is SA — every domain has 3 values so MRV ties, and SA wins the tie-break with degree 5.
  • Australia with three colours is too easy to show off the heuristics — every setting solves it in 7 assignments with no backtracking. To see them work, delete blue from every domain. Now the problem is impossible, and proving it takes 10 assignments with no inference, 4 with forward checking, and 2 with arc consistency.
  • For a solvable problem that needs real search, replace the CSP with a tangled chain: variables X1…X5 over a b c and X6 X7 over a b, constrained X1≠X2, X2≠X3, X3≠X4, X4≠X5, X5≠X6, X6≠X7, X7≠X1, X1≠X4, X2≠X5, X6≠X1, X7≠X2. Static order with no inference needs 69 assignments; MRV + degree needs 7.
  • Add the constraint WA != T and watch T stop being a free variable.

Tool · Forward checking vs AC-3

Interactive

Inference comparison

Click values to build any partial assignment, then walk AC-3 forward one arc at a time and watch the domains shrink next to what forward checking manages on the same input. Uses the CSP entered above.

The demonstration to run
With WA=red, Q=green, forward checking survives but AC-3 empties a domain — the slide's exact claim that arc consistency detects failure earlier. Then try WA=red, Q=green, V=blue and watch forward checking finally catch up.
Which variable empties is not fixed — and that's fine
The slide's trace ends with SA empty; the tool may report NT. Both are correct. After WA=red and Q=green, NT and SA are neighbours that have both been reduced to {blue}, so whichever arc — SA→NT or NT→SA — comes off the queue first is the one that wipes out.

AC-3 gives no guarantee about which domain empties, only that if the CSP is arc-inconsistent, some domain will. In an exam, name the variable your own trace produces and show the arc that did it.

Why constraint propagation pays off

The argument
  • Constraint propagation is often faster than traditional state-space search, because state-space search only cares if a state is the goal, not whether it is valid — and it is not immediately obvious what a good heuristic is for this kind of problem.
  • Constraint propagation eliminates areas of the state space that are no longer relevant: if we know this state isn't a valid solution, we can discard it and all further refinements of it.
The numbers from the slide
For {SA = blue}:
  • This state leaves 35 = 243 possible states for the neighbouring values — a lot of them invalid.
  • With constraint propagation: 25 = 32 possible states.
  • A reduction of 87%.

This enables dense or intractable problems to be searched through much faster.

Where 243 and 32 come from
SA has five neighbours (WA, NT, Q, NSW, V). Before propagation each has 3 colours: 3⁵ = 243. Setting SA = blue removes blue from every neighbour, leaving 2 each: 2⁵ = 32. And 32/243 ≈ 0.13, so 87% of that subtree is gone from a single assignment — which is the whole argument for inference in one line.
Summary of the deck
  • Problems of assignment are less concerned with the path taken than the solution.
  • CSPs let us define assignment problems with specific variables, domains and constraints.
  • Backtracking search is one approach towards solving a simple CSP.
  • We can improve variable selection through heuristics.
  • Forward checking and arc consistency help prevent wasted search.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 4
  1. CSP as a search problem — states are assignments; initial state has nothing assigned; an action assigns a value provided it violates no constraint; the goal test is all variables assigned and all constraints satisfied.
  2. The tree is only depth n, but has n! × mn paths.
  3. Commutativity — [WA=red, NT=green] = [NT=green, WA=red] — lets single-variable assignment cut n! × mn down to mn. Know this reduction.
  4. Backtracking search is depth-first search with one variable assigned per level, checking for failure and backtracking.
  5. MRV = most constrained variable = fewest legal values. Degree = most constraining variable = imposes the most constraints on others. LCV = least constraining value = rules out the fewest values elsewhere.
  6. Forward checking — track remaining legal values for unassigned variables; terminate when any variable has none; it propagates from assigned to unassigned variables.
  7. Arc consistency — X → Y is consistent iff for each value of X there is an allowed value of Y; checking X → Y deletes values from X; if X loses a value, all arcs Z → X must be rechecked.
  8. Arc consistency detects failure earlier than forward checking, and can be run before or after each assignment.
  9. Be able to reproduce both worked runs — FC fails after WA=red, Q=green, V=blue (SA empties); AC fails after just WA=red, Q=green.
  10. AC-3 — a queue of all arcs; pop, run REMOVE-INCONSISTENT-VALUES, and if it removed anything, add every arc (X_k, Xᵢ) for neighbours X_k back to the queue.
  11. The 87% figure — {SA = blue} goes from 3⁵ = 243 to 2⁵ = 32 states for its five neighbours.

End of Week 2.

Week 03 · Part 1 · Automated planning

Classical Planning

describing a world well enough that a general solver can act in it

What AI planning is

Definition

Given:

  • An initial state I
  • A goal state G
  • A set of actions A, each with preconditions and effects

Find:

  • A plan — a sequence of actions that bring the system from I to G.
  • More interesting: an optimal plan — the best way to reach the goal state.
Where it sits in the module
  • Problem modelling — graph search, heuristic search, adversarial search
  • Constraint satisfaction problems
  • Automated planning — in general, planning is more powerful than CSP (CSPs can be modelled as planning problems)
How this differs from everything so far
In Week 1 you were handed a graph. In Week 2's CSPs you were handed variables and constraints. Here you are handed nothing but a description in a language, and the state space is generated from it — the graph is implicit and astronomically large.

That's what "more powerful than CSP" means: a CSP has a fixed set of variables to fill in, whereas a planning problem has an unbounded sequence of actions to choose, and the same fact can be made true, destroyed and made true again.

The logistics domain

The running example
Cargos, trucks and locations. Initial state: cargos scattered across locations. Goal: all cargos at a destination point. Constraints in the real version include fuel, truck capacity, number of drivers…
Problem modelling — what we must define
  • The objects involved in the problem.
  • The relations between the objects.
  • The set of possible actions, with preconditions and effects.

And so: we need a formalism (a language) to describe objects, relations and actions.

Objects and relations

Objects

  • The cargos c1 … cn
  • The trucks t1 … tm
  • The locations l1 … lk

Relations

  • Pairs of locations can be connected: connected(li, lj)
  • Each truck is in a location: at(ti, lj)
  • Each cargo can be in a location: at(ci, lj)
  • Each cargo can be on a truck: on(ci, tj)
Note what a "relation" really is
These are predicates over objects, and a state is nothing more than the set of them that currently hold. at is used for both trucks and cargos — the same predicate, different object types — which is exactly the generality that lets one action definition cover every truck and every cargo at once.

From general description to specific problem

Initial state, goal state, and the closed-world assumption
  • Initial state — we have to list all the objects of our problem and all the true relations among the objects.
  • Closed-world assumption: what is not listed is assumed to be false.
  • Goal state — we have to list all the relations we want to be true.
The slides' instance — 2 trucks, 3 cargos, 8 locations
at(c1,l3)   at(c2,l4)   at(c3,l8)
at(t1,l1)   at(t2,l5)
connected(l1,l2)  connected(l2,l3)  connected(l3,l4)  connected(l3,l8)
connected(l4,l7)  connected(l5,l6)  connected(l6,l7)  connected(l7,l8)

From the closed-world assumption it follows that, for example: l1 and l6 are not connected, truck t1 is not at location l8, all trucks are empty, and so on.

Goal state: all cargos in location l6.

Why the closed-world assumption matters so much
Without it you would have to write down every false fact too — with 8 locations and 2 trucks that's already dozens of negative statements, and it grows quadratically. CWA lets the initial state be a short list of positives.

The price: the model must be complete. If you forget to state connected(l2,l3), the planner doesn't ask — it silently concludes the road doesn't exist and returns a worse plan, or none. Most "the planner gave a stupid answer" bugs are a missing fact in the initial state.

The actions

Informally
A truck can move from one location to another · a cargo can be loaded into a truck · a cargo can be unloaded from a truck.
More formally — for each action we define three things
  • The parameters — which objects are involved?
  • The preconditions — what needs to be true for the action to be applied?
  • The effects — how does the state change after execution?
ActionParametersPreconditionsEffects
Movetruck t
location from
location to		 at(t, from)
connected(from, to)		 + at(t, to)
− at(t, from)
Loadtruck t
cargo c
location l		 at(t, l)
at(c, l)		 + on(c, t)
− at(c, l)
Unloadtruck t
cargo c
location l		 at(t, l)
on(c, t)		 + at(c, l)
− on(c, t)
The two sentences to memorise
  • Preconditions are described through a set of relations that must be true in a state for the action to be applicable.
  • Effects are described by adding or deleting relations.
Read the delete effects carefully — they are where the meaning lives
Load adds on(c,t) and deletes at(c,l). Without the delete, the cargo would be on the truck and still lying at the location — the model would let you load one crate onto every truck in the country. The delete list is what stops the world from accumulating contradictions.

Also note Move has no connected(to, from): roads are directed unless you list both ways. And Load and Unload are exact mirrors — one action's add list is the other's delete list, which is what makes the two undo each other.

A plan

Truck1: l1, l2, l3, load(c1), l4, load(c2), l7, l6, unload(c1), unload(c2)
Truck2: l5, l6, l7, l8, load(c3), l7, l6, unload(c3)

Note that t1 and t2 can move in parallel.

And then the scaling question
What if we have 75 locations, 40 cargos, 12 trucks + aeroplanes (or more)?

You are not going to write that plan by hand. We need a planner.

The parallelism remark is a hint about Part 3
Classical planning produces a sequence, so it must arbitrarily interleave the two trucks even though nothing forces an order. Recovering the fact that independent actions can overlap is what durative actions and temporal planning are for.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 1
  1. Given I, G and A (each action with preconditions and effects); find a plan — a sequence of actions taking the system from I to G. Optimal = the best such sequence.
  2. Planning is more powerful than CSP — CSPs can be modelled as planning problems.
