  3. To model a domain you define objects, relations between them, and actions with preconditions and effects — and you need a language to write it in.
  4. An action has three parts: parameters (which objects), preconditions (what must be true), effects (how the state changes).
  5. Preconditions are relations that must hold; effects add or delete relations.
  6. Be able to fill in the Move / Load / Unload table from memory, delete effects included.
  7. Closed-world assumption — the initial state lists all objects and all true relations; anything not listed is assumed false.
  8. Domain vs problem — the domain formalises the space of all possible problems (relations and actions); a problem instance adds the initial state and the goal.

End of Part 1. Next: the actual language.

Week 03 · Part 2 · Automated planning

PDDL Basics

the language every planner speaks

Language + algorithm

The general approach to solving planning problems
  • A planning language — allows you to write the definition of a planning problem in text.
  • A planning algorithm — allows you to solve any problem given to it in that language.
This separation is the entire idea
Because the language is standard, your model and their solver are independent. Improve the model and every planner benefits; improve the planner and every model benefits. It is the same bargain as SQL: describe what, and someone else's engine works out how.

Hence the long list of planners in the slides — Zeno, FF, MetricFF, VHPOP, Marvin, Crikey, POPF, MIPS-XXL, LPGP, LPRPG, CoLin, Fast Downward, UPMurphi, Gamer, MBP — all competing in the International Planning Competition, all consuming the same input.

PDDL and its versions

PDDL — Planning Domain Definition Language
The standard language spoken by the planners. If you write a correct model of your planning problem in PDDL, you can use existing planners to solve it.

Different versions (levels), each able to handle different features:

PDDLpropositional planning
PDDL 2.1numbers + time
PDDL 3preferences
PDDL+continuous change, processes, events

Domain and problem files

Domain file — one

  • General description of the world.
  • Which types of objects are involved.
  • What actions can be applied, etc.

Problem file(s) — many

  • The specific situation you want to solve.
  • List of objects.
  • Initial state, goal state.
One domain, many problems
The slides draw one Domain in the middle with eight Problems orbiting it. That's the shape to remember: the rules of the world are written once, and each puzzle you want solved is a small file naming the objects, what's true at the start, and what you want true at the end.

Quick test of whether something belongs in the domain: would it still be true for a different puzzle in the same world? "A gripper can hold one ball" → domain. "There are four balls and they start in room A" → problem.

The Gripper domain

The problem
A robot can move between two rooms and pick up or drop balls with either of his two arms.
  • Initial state: balls b1..b5 in room A, robot in room A.
  • Goal state: balls b1..b5 in room B, robot in room B.
  • Actions: move from one room to the other; pick up a ball in a gripper; drop a ball.
ActionParametersPreconditionsEffects
MoveRoom x
Room y		at-robot(x) + at-robot(y)
− at-robot(x)
PickUpRoom x
Ball b
Gripper g		 at-robot(x)
at(b, x)
free(g)		 + carry(g, b)
− at(b, x)
− free(g)
DropRoom x
Ball b
Gripper g		 at-robot(x)
carry(g, b)		 + at(b, x)
+ free(g)
− carry(g, b)
Where the "two arms" constraint actually is
Nowhere explicit — it falls out of free(g). PickUp requires the gripper to be free and deletes that fact; Drop restores it. So each gripper holds at most one ball, and with two gripper objects the robot carries at most two. There's no counting anywhere. That's the classical-PDDL style: capacity limits are encoded as facts that get consumed and released. When you want to say "capacity 4" instead of "capacity 1", you need fluents — Part 3.

In PDDL

Objects and predicates:

(:objects roomA roomB
          ball1 ball2 ball3 ball4
          left right)

(:predicates (ROOM ?x) (BALL ?x) (GRIPPER ?x)
             (at-robot ?x) (at ?x ?y)
             (free ?x) (carry ?x ?y))
Why ROOM, BALL and GRIPPER are predicates here
This version of PDDL has no type system, so "x is a room" has to be stated as an ordinary fact — hence the upper-case type predicates, asserted in :init and tested in every precondition. With :typing (used in Part 3) you write ?x - room instead and the checking is free. Conventionally the type predicates are capitalised so you can see at a glance which preconditions are real and which are just type checks.

Initial state:

(:init (ROOM rooma) (ROOM roomb)
       (BALL ball1) (BALL ball2) (BALL ball3) (BALL ball4)
       (GRIPPER left) (GRIPPER right)
       (free left) (free right)
       (at-robot rooma)
       (at ball1 rooma) (at ball2 rooma)
       (at ball3 rooma) (at ball4 rooma))

Goal state:

(:goal (and (at ball1 roomb)
            (at ball2 roomb)
            (at ball3 roomb)
            (at ball4 roomb)))

The three actions:

(:action move
 :parameters (?x ?y)
 :precondition (and (ROOM ?x) (ROOM ?y)
                    (at-robot ?x))
 :effect
   (and (at-robot ?y) (not (at-robot ?x))))

(:action pick-up
 :parameters (?x ?y ?z)
 :precondition (and (BALL ?x) (ROOM ?y) (GRIPPER ?z)
                    (at ?x ?y) (at-robot ?y)
                    (free ?z))
 :effect
   (and (carry ?z ?x) (not (at ?x ?y)) (not (free ?z))))

(:action drop
 :parameters (?x ?y ?z)
 :precondition (and (BALL ?x) (ROOM ?y) (GRIPPER ?z)
                    (carry ?z ?x) (at-robot ?y))
 :effect
   (and (at ?x ?y) (free ?z) (not (carry ?z ?x))))
The syntax rules worth writing on a cheat sheet
  • Everything is a parenthesised list — Lisp style.
  • ?x is a variable; a bare name is an object.
  • An action has :parameters, :precondition, :effect.
  • Multiple conditions are joined with (and …).
  • Delete effects are written (not (fact)) inside the effect — there is no separate delete list.
  • The goal is (:goal (and …)), the start is (:init …).

The full domain file

(define (domain gripper-strips)
  (:predicates (room ?r) (ball ?b) (gripper ?g)
               (at-robot ?r) (at ?b ?r) (free ?g) (carry ?o ?g))

  (:action move
     :parameters (?from ?to)
     :precondition (and (room ?from) (room ?to) (at-robot ?from))
     :effect (and (at-robot ?to) (not (at-robot ?from))))

  (:action pick
     :parameters (?ball ?room ?gripper)
     :precondition (and (ball ?ball) (room ?room) (gripper ?gripper)
                        (at ?ball ?room) (at-robot ?room) (free ?gripper))
     :effect (and (carry ?ball ?gripper) (not (at ?ball ?room))
                  (not (free ?gripper))))

  (:action drop
     :parameters (?ball ?room ?gripper)
     :precondition (and (ball ?ball) (room ?room) (gripper ?gripper)
                        (carry ?ball ?gripper) (at-robot ?room))
     :effect (and (at ?ball ?room) (free ?gripper)
                  (not (carry ?ball ?gripper)))))
Summary of the deck
  • PDDL allows us to define problems in a set-theoretic language.
  • Domain files store all the predicates and actions we require.
  • We store the actual problem instances in other files.

Appendix: the Blocks World domain

Five predicates, four actions. This is the domain Part 4 uses, so it's worth knowing well.

(:predicates (on ?x ?y) (ontable ?x) (clear ?x) (handempty) (holding ?x))
(define (domain blocks)
  (:predicates (on ?x ?y) (ontable ?x) (clear ?x) (handempty) (holding ?x))

  (:action pick-up
     :parameters (?x)
     :precondition (and (clear ?x) (ontable ?x) (handempty))
     :effect (and (not (ontable ?x)) (not (clear ?x))
                  (not (handempty)) (holding ?x)))

  (:action put-down
     :parameters (?x)
     :precondition (holding ?x)
     :effect (and (not (holding ?x)) (clear ?x)
                  (handempty) (ontable ?x)))

  (:action stack
     :parameters (?x ?y)
     :precondition (and (holding ?x) (clear ?y))
     :effect (and (not (holding ?x)) (not (clear ?y)) (clear ?x)
                  (handempty) (on ?x ?y)))

  (:action unstack
     :parameters (?x ?y)
     :precondition (and (on ?x ?y) (clear ?x) (handempty))
     :effect (and (holding ?x) (clear ?y) (not (clear ?x))
                  (not (handempty)) (not (on ?x ?y)))))
The four actions come in two mirror pairs
pick-up ↔ put-down (table) and unstack ↔ stack (another block). Each pair swaps handempty for holding ?x and back.

Note that (clear ?x) is deleted when you pick a block up — because while you're holding it, nothing can be placed on it either. And the table is never mentioned as an object: "on the table" is its own predicate, ontable. Part 4's slides simplify all four of these into a single action, Put X on Y from Z, by treating the table as just another destination.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 2
  1. Language + algorithm — a planning language lets you write the problem down; a planning algorithm solves any problem written in it.
  2. PDDL = Planning Domain Definition Language, the standard language spoken by planners.
  3. The versions — PDDL propositional · PDDL 2.1 numbers + time · PDDL 3 preferences · PDDL+ continuous change, processes, events.
  4. Two file types — one domain file (types, predicates, actions) and many problem files (objects, initial state, goal).
  5. Be able to write an action: :parameters, :precondition, :effect, with (and …) and delete effects as (not (…)).
  6. Be able to reproduce the Gripper table — Move / PickUp / Drop with their parameters, preconditions and effects, and translate it into PDDL.
  7. Type predicates like (ROOM ?x) exist because plain PDDL has no type system.
  8. Blocks World — predicates on, ontable, clear, handempty, holding; actions pick-up, put-down, stack, unstack.
  9. A likely exam task: given an informal domain description, write the PDDL predicates and one or two actions. Practise on something unfamiliar.

End of Part 2. Next: numbers and clocks.

Week 03 · Part 3 · Automated planning

PDDL 2.1: Fluents & Time

resources that run out, actions that take a while

What classical planning cannot say

The four limitations
  • Actions are instantaneous.
  • The planner has to decide which actions to apply and in what order.
  • Plans are sequential.
  • Actions don't define quantity or resource, and goals cannot define resource constraints.

All actions take uniform time and have no costs.

The fix
"PDDL 2.1: An Extension to PDDL for Expressing Temporal Planning Domains" adds:
  • Numbers, resources, costs ("metrics")
  • Time
Why you can't fake numbers with predicates
You could in principle write fuel-30, fuel-29, … as separate facts, but the state space explodes and nothing can express "enough fuel" or "minimise total fuel". Fluents make quantity first-class: you can compare it in a precondition and change it by an amount in an effect.

Fluents

Definition
  • PDDL 2.1 introduces the ability to model numeric values through fluents.
  • We identify a particular resource within the domain by having action effects increase or decrease the value of that resource.
  • This helps maintain an understanding of the costs of actions.
The new syntax
  • (:requirements :typing :fluents) — declare what the domain uses.
  • (:types vehicle location) — real types, so ?v - vehicle replaces type predicates.
  • (:functions …) — declares the numeric fluents, exactly as :predicates declares the boolean ones.
  • In preconditions: comparisons — (>= (fuel-level ?v) (fuel-required ?from ?to)).
  • In effects: updates — (decrease …), (increase …), also (assign …).
  • In the problem file: assignments — (= (fuel-level truck) 100).
  • In the problem file: (:metric minimize …) — what "optimal" means for this problem.

The metric vehicle domain

(define (domain metricVehicle)
(:requirements :typing :fluents)
(:types vehicle location)
(:predicates (at ?v - vehicle ?p - location)
             (accessible ?v - vehicle ?p1 ?p2 - location))

(:functions (fuel-level ?v - vehicle) (fuel-used ?v - vehicle)
            (fuel-required ?p1 ?p2 - location) (total-fuel-used))

(:action drive
 :parameters (?v - vehicle ?from ?to - location)
 :precondition (and (at ?v ?from) (accessible ?v ?from ?to)
                    (>= (fuel-level ?v) (fuel-required ?from ?to)))
 :effect (and (not (at ?v ?from)) (at ?v ?to)
              (decrease (fuel-level ?v) (fuel-required ?from ?to))
              (increase (total-fuel-used) (fuel-required ?from ?to))
              (increase (fuel-used ?v) (fuel-required ?from ?to)))))
Three kinds of fluent in one action
  • fuel-level ?v — a consumable resource: guarded by a precondition, decreased by the effect. This is what makes plans fail when you run dry.
  • fuel-used ?v and total-fuel-used — accumulators: never tested, only increased. They exist purely so the metric has something to minimise.
  • fuel-required ?p1 ?p2 — a static table: set in the problem file, never modified. It's a numeric fact about the map, not a resource.

Notice total-fuel-used has no parameters — a single global number. That's the standard way to write a plan metric.

The problem file:

(define (problem metricVehicle-example)
(:domain metricVehicle)
(:objects truck car - vehicle
          Paris Berlin Rome Madrid - location)
(:init
  (at truck Rome)
  (at car Paris)
  (= (fuel-level truck) 100)      (= (fuel-level car) 100)
  (accessible car Paris Berlin)     (accessible car Berlin Rome)
  (accessible car Rome Madrid)      (accessible truck Rome Paris)
  (accessible truck Rome Berlin)    (accessible truck Berlin Paris)
  (= (fuel-required Paris Berlin) 40)   (= (fuel-required Berlin Rome) 30)
  (= (fuel-required Rome Madrid) 50)    (= (fuel-required Rome Paris) 35)
  (= (fuel-required Rome Berlin) 40)    (= (fuel-required Berlin Paris) 40)
  (= (total-fuel-used) 0) (= (fuel-used car) 0) (= (fuel-used truck) 0))

(:goal (and (at truck Paris) (at car Rome)))
(:metric minimize (total-fuel-used)))
Work the example out — it rewards a close look
Truck: Rome → Paris. Two options: direct (35) or via Berlin (40 + 40 = 80). Direct wins.
Car: Paris → Rome. Only route is Paris → Berlin → Rome (40 + 30 = 70). Note the car cannot use Rome → Paris — accessible takes the vehicle as an argument, so the two have different road networks.
Total = 35 + 70 = 105, and both start with 100 units, so both stay in range.

Also notice accessible and fuel-required are directed — (accessible car Paris Berlin) does not give you Berlin → Paris. Missing reverse edges are a classic modelling bug.

Durative actions (temporal planning)

Why time is a separate problem from resources
  • Fluents handle resources and how they change during execution — but we still need to handle the passage of time. How long does an action take?
  • This influences conditions as well as effects: conditions might hold true at different times, and effects can occur at different times.
(:durative-action move-up-slow
  :parameters (?lift - slow-elevator ?f1 - floor ?f2 - floor)
  :duration (= ?duration (travel-slow ?f1 ?f2))
  :condition (and (at start (lift-at ?lift ?f1))
                  (at start (above ?f1 ?f2))
                  (at start (reachable-floor ?lift ?f2)))
  :effect (and (at start (not (lift-at ?lift ?f1)))
               (at end (lift-at ?lift ?f2))))

; problem file
(above f0 f1)
(reachable-floor slow1 f1)
(= (travel-slow f0 f1) 12)
The four slots — this is the diagram to be able to draw
at startover allat end
Conditionsmust hold when the action beginsmust hold throughoutmust hold when it finishes
Effectsapplied when it begins—applied when it finishes
Read the lift action as a story
At the start, the lift is at f1, f1 is above f2, and f2 is reachable. The instant it starts moving, lift-at f1 is deleted — the lift is now between floors and nowhere in particular. Only at the end does lift-at f2 become true, 12 time units later.

That gap is the whole point. Splitting one action into a start effect and an end effect means another action can be happening in the interval — which is how temporal plans get genuine parallelism, unlike the sequential plans of Part 1.

The board action — and over all

(:durative-action board
  :parameters (?p - passenger ?lift - elevator ?f - floor)
  :duration (= ?duration 3)
  :condition (and (over all (lift-at ?lift ?f))
                  (at start (passenger-at ?p ?f))
                  (at start (< (passengers ?lift) (capacity ?lift))))
  :effect (and (at start (not (passenger-at ?p ?f)))
               (at end (boarded ?p ?lift))
               (at start (increase (passengers ?lift) 1))))

; problem file
(above f0 f1)   (reachable-floor slow1 f1)   (= (travel-slow f0 f1) 12)
(passenger-at p0 f1)   (= (passengers slow1) 0)   (= (capacity slow1) 4)
Everything worth noticing here
  • over all (lift-at ?lift ?f) — the lift must stay at that floor for the whole three seconds. Not just at the start: the doors must not close mid-boarding. This is the condition type the previous action didn't have.
  • Fixed duration — (= ?duration 3), a constant rather than a fluent lookup. Both forms are legal.
  • Fluent + durative combined — the capacity check (< (passengers ?lift) (capacity ?lift)) is exactly the Part-3-fluents machinery inside a temporal action. This is how you say "capacity 4" rather than the gripper's one-ball-per-free trick.
  • The counter increases at start, not at end — deliberately. It reserves the seat the moment boarding begins, so a second passenger deciding at the same instant sees the space already taken. Putting it at end would let five people board a lift with capacity 4.
Summary of the decks
  • PDDL 2.1 handles more complex temporal and resource-heavy problems.
  • Fluents allow management of resources — check a resource is within a limit, increase/decrease it.
  • Temporal planning considers how planning must execute within fixed time frames: the overall duration; conditions that must hold at the start, until the end, or throughout; effects applied at the start or upon completion.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 3
  1. Classical PDDL's limits — instantaneous actions, sequential plans, no quantities or resources, goals cannot express resource constraints.
  2. PDDL 2.1 adds numbers, resources, costs (metrics) and time.
  3. Fluents = numeric values; effects increase/decrease them; preconditions compare them.
  4. Know the sections — :requirements, :types, :predicates, :functions, :action; and in the problem :objects, :init with (= (f x) n), :goal, :metric minimize ….
  5. Be able to write a fluent action — the drive action is the model answer: a >= guard plus a decrease and matching increasees.
  6. Durative actions — :durative-action with :duration, :condition and :effect.
  7. The three condition types: at start, over all, at end. The two effect types: at start, at end. Be able to draw the timeline.
  8. What over all is for — something that must remain true for the whole duration, e.g. the lift staying at the floor while a passenger boards.
  9. Why the delete happens at start — the object leaves its old state immediately; the new state only becomes true at the end. That interval is what lets other actions run concurrently.

End of Part 3. Next: how a planner actually searches, and where its heuristic comes from.

Week 03 · Part 4 · Automated planning

Forward Chaining & RPG

where a domain-independent heuristic comes from

Forward-chain planning

The algorithm
  • Choose a state s and expand it, beginning with the initial state Sinit.
  • Consider the actions applicable in s — those whose preconditions are satisfied in s.
  • One successor state s′ is generated for each applicable action a:
    S′ = S − {delete effects of a} + {add effects of a}
  • Create a plan for S′ by chaining a to the end of the plan for s.
  • A goal state is a state containing the goal conditions. If the state does not satisfy them, loop and expand more states.
This is Week 1's search, with the graph generated on the fly
Node = a set of facts. Edge = a ground action. "Expand" means: find every action whose preconditions are in this fact set, and apply the delete-then-add rule.

Delete first, then add — the order matters when an action both deletes and adds the same fact. And note the goal test is a subset test, not equality: a goal state is any state containing the goal conditions, so many different full states can be goals.

What a planner is
A planner takes the domain, the initial state and the goal, and generates a plan — a sequence of actions from A which transforms Sinit into Sgoal. It performs search to consider the different possible plans available until Sgoal is found.

The Blocks World, simplified to one action

Put X on Y from Z
PreconditionsAddDelete
clear X
on X Z
clear Y		 clear Z
on X Y		 on X Z
clear Y
One action instead of four
Part 2's Blocks World needed pick-up, put-down, stack and unstack because the hand was modelled. Here the move is atomic — X goes straight from Z to Y — so handempty and holding disappear entirely, and the table T behaves as a block that is always clear (it never appears in a delete list because infinitely many things fit on it).

Read the effects as a swap: X vacates Z (so Z becomes clear) and occupies Y (so Y stops being clear). Fewer actions means a smaller branching factor, which is exactly what you want when demonstrating a search by hand.

The state the rest of this page works with — C on A, A and B on the table, goal A on B, B on C:

C
A
B
initial state
A
B
C
goal
Initial facts: onCA, onAT, onBT, clearB, clearC · Goal: onAB, onBC

"How do we know this is the best state?"

The question the lecture leaves hanging
Forward chaining generates a tree of states. Fine — but which one should you expand next? Week 1's answer was A*, which needs h(n). So: is it possible to define heuristics that work for any PDDL domain?

Yes — domain-independent heuristics. No knowledge about the specific problem is used.

Why this is harder than the Romania map
In Week 1 you had straight-line distance handed to you — a human looked at the map and supplied it. A planner is given an arbitrary PDDL file it has never seen and must invent its own heuristic from the domain description alone. The recipe is the one from Week 1: relax the problem. The only question is which constraint to drop.

The Relaxed Planning Graph

Definition
The Relaxed Planning Graph (RPG) is a domain-independent heuristic used in actual planners (e.g. the FF planner).
  • It involves finding a plan from the current state S which achieves the goals G but ignores the delete effects of each action.
  • The length of this plan is used as the heuristic value for the state S.

J. Hoffmann and B. Nebel, 2001, "The FF Planning System: Fast Plan Generation through Heuristic Search", Journal of AI Research vol. 14.

Ignoring deletes is the relaxation — and it's the perfect one
Drop the delete lists and facts can only ever become true, never false. Nothing you do can undo anything, so there is no such thing as a wrong move and no need to backtrack. The relaxed problem is solvable in polynomial time.

And because the relaxed problem is easier — every real plan is still a valid relaxed plan — its optimal length can never exceed the real one. That's admissibility, straight from Week 1. (The relaxed plan that FF actually extracts isn't guaranteed optimal, so hFF is not strictly admissible — but the idea is the same, and it works extremely well in practice.)

Fact layers and action layers

The construction rules
  • The RPG is made of alternating fact layers and action layers.
  • The first fact layer f(0) is the initial state of the problem.
  • Fact layer f(n) determines which actions can appear in action layer a(n+1) — those whose preconditions are satisfied in f(n).
  • f(n+1) = f(n) plus all the add effects of the actions in a(n+1) — remember we ignore delete effects!
  • Hence fact layers get bigger and bigger as more actions become applicable.
Two consequences of "fact layers only grow"
It always terminates. There are finitely many ground facts, so eventually a layer adds nothing new — a fixpoint. If the goals aren't in that fixpoint, no relaxed plan exists, so no real plan exists either, and the state can be discarded outright. That's a free dead-end detector.

And the layer at which a fact first appears is a measure of how hard it is to achieve — that number is what the extraction phase turns into a heuristic.

For our state, the graph builds like this:

LayerContents
f(0)onAT, onBT, onCA, clearB, clearC — the initial state
a(1)C to T from A · C to B from A · B to C from T
f(1)f(0) + clearA, onCT, onCB, onBC
a(2)A to B from T · A to C from T · B to A from T · B to A from C · B to T from C · C to A from T · C to A from B · C to B from T · C to T from B
f(2)everything — including onAB, the last goal to appear
Why nothing involving A appears in a(1)
A has C sitting on it, so clearA is false in f(0) and no action can move A. Once any action in a(1) shifts C off A, clearA enters f(1) — and a pile of actions become applicable at once. Watch clearA: it is the fact that unlocks the layer.
a(2) is bigger than it looks — and that's the relaxation showing through
The slide lists six actions in a(2); the true count is nine. The extra three are B to A from C, C to A from B and C to T from B, and they are applicable for a revealing reason.

f(1) contains both onBT and onBC — B is on the table and on C at the same time. That is physically impossible, and it happens precisely because we deleted nothing. So the relaxed graph offers moves the real world never would.

This is exactly why the RPG under-estimates: the relaxed world is more permissive than the real one. It doesn't affect the answer here — the extraction still picks the same three actions and h = 3 — but if you're listing a(2) by hand, don't stop at six. The RPG builder tool below shows all nine.

Extracting the relaxed plan

The backwards pass
To get a solution, work backwards through the RPG. At each fact layer f(n) we have goals to achieve, g(n). Start with g(n) containing the problem goals. For each fact in g(n):
  • If it was already in f(n−1), add it to g(n−1).
  • Otherwise, choose an action from a(n) that achieves it, and add its preconditions to g(n−1).

Stop when you are at g(0).

The worked extraction

g(2) = {onAB, onBC} — the problem goals.

  • onAB was not in f(1) → need the action "A to B from T", whose preconditions are clearA, onAT, clearB.
  • onBC was already in f(1) → carry it straight down.

g(1) = {clearA, clearB, onAT, onBC}

  • clearB and onAT were in f(0) → carry down.
  • onBC was not in f(0) → need "B to C from T" (preconditions clearB, onBT, clearC).
  • clearA was not in f(0) → need "C to T from A" (preconditions clearC, onCA).

g(0) = {clearB, onAT, clearC, onBT, onCA} — all in the initial state. Done.

Final relaxed plan:
O₀ = { Put C on T from A , Put B on C from T }
O₁ = { Put A on B from T }
h(s) = |O₀| + |O₁| = 2 + 1 = 3
Constructing the RPG value — the formal statement
For each state S reached during forward search, the length of the relaxed plan P′ which achieves the goals G starting from S is computed. This is an estimate of the goal distance.

P′ = ⟨O₀, O₁, …, Om−1⟩, where each Oi is the set of actions selected in parallel at time step i, and m is the number of the first fact layer containing all goals.

h(s) := Σ |Oi|

i.e. the heuristic is an estimate of the sequential solution length.

h is the number of actions, not the number of layers
Here m = 2 layers but h = 3, because O₀ contains two actions. Summing |O_i| rather than counting layers is what makes it an estimate of the sequential plan length — you still have to execute those two actions one after another. Confusing the two is the standard mistake.
Sanity-check it against the real plan
The genuine plan here is also three moves: C→table, B→C, A→B. So h = 3 is exact for this state — the relaxation cost nothing, because no action needed to undo another. RPG becomes an under-estimate precisely in the states where you must dismantle something you built, since the relaxed version never has to take it apart again.

Tool · RPG builder

Interactive

Build the graph, extract the plan, get h

Click the blocks to rearrange the towers and the whole graph rebuilds; step through the layers one at a time to see exactly which fact unlocks the next set of actions. Defaults to the state from the demo — you should get h = 3.

Things worth trying in it
  • Press ▶ play and watch the graph grow one layer at a time. Stop on action layer 1 and note that nothing involving A is there — then step to fact layer 1 and see clearA arrive and unlock six more actions.
  • The default — reproduce the demo exactly: a(1) has three actions, onAB first appears in f(2), and h = 3.
  • Click C, then click the table. A is now clear from the start, the graph reshapes, and h drops — you have just made the problem easier with two clicks.
  • Set the goal to onBC alone. It's in f(1), so h drops to 1 — the graph stops a layer earlier.
  • Set the goal to something already true, e.g. onCA: h = 0, which is the definition of a goal state.
  • Use four blocks (A B C D) and watch the layers grow — this is why real planners rebuild the RPG for every node they evaluate.

Tool · Forward-chain planner

Interactive

Search the state space, with or without the heuristic

Rearrange the blocks by clicking, then walk the plan action by action and watch the towers rebuild themselves. Expand the initial state one step, or solve with breadth-first search versus A* using the RPG heuristic and compare the expansion counts.

How the RPG is used in a planner
  • RPG provides a heuristic automatically — no domain knowledge.
  • Use it in heuristic search (e.g. A*) where h comes from the RPG.
  • Every time we want to add a new node to the open list, we solve a simplified version of the problem (the RPG) to find out h.
Read that last bullet twice
The heuristic is not a lookup — it is an entire sub-problem solved from scratch for every single node. That is enormously more expensive per node than Week 1's straight-line distance. It pays off anyway, because the reduction in nodes expanded is far larger than the extra cost per node — and it is the reason FF beat the field in 2000.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 4
  1. Forward-chain planning — expand a state, find the applicable actions, and for each one produce S′ = S − {delete effects} + {add effects}, chaining the action onto the plan.
  2. A goal state is a state containing the goal conditions — a subset test, not equality.
  3. Put X on Y from Z — pre: clear X, on X Z, clear Y; add: clear Z, on X Y; del: on X Z, clear Y.
  4. Domain-independent heuristics work for any PDDL domain using no problem-specific knowledge.
  5. RPG — find a plan from S achieving G that ignores the delete effects; the length of that plan is h(S). Used in FF (Hoffmann & Nebel 2001).
  6. Construction — f(0) is the initial state; a(n+1) holds the actions whose preconditions are satisfied in f(n); f(n+1) = f(n) + the add effects of a(n+1); layers only grow.
  7. Extraction — start with g(m) = the goals; a fact already in f(n−1) drops straight down, otherwise pick an action from a(n) and add its preconditions to g(n−1); stop at g(0).
  8. h(s) := Σ |Oi|, where Oi is the set of actions chosen at step i and m is the first fact layer containing all goals. It estimates the sequential plan length.
  9. Be able to run the demo by hand — from onCA, onAT, onBT, clearB, clearC to onAB, onBC: a(1) = {C to T from A, C to B from A, B to C from T}; the plan is Put C on T from A, Put B on C from T, Put A on B from T; h = 3 over 2 layers.
  10. Using it — A* with h from the RPG, recomputing the RPG for every node added to the open list.

End of Week 3.

Week 04 · Start here

MDPs, Slowly

read this before the other three parts — no equations until the end
If Week 4 is not going in, it is almost always one of four things
  1. Not seeing what problem any of this solves.
  2. Thinking U(s) means the reward of a square. It does not.
  3. Not noticing that the definition of U is circular, so wondering why we iterate at all.
  4. Meeting the Bellman equation as one long line of symbols instead of four separate ideas.

This page does those four, in that order, with no equation until the last one. Then the formal parts will read like notes rather than code.

1 · The one thing that changed

You press Up. You do not always go up.
In every search problem so far, actions did exactly what they said. Here they do not. You command Up and:
0.8  you go up
0.1  you veer left instead
0.1  you veer right instead

That is the only new ingredient in Week 4. Everything else — policies, utilities, Bellman, value iteration — is a consequence of it. If you keep that one line in your head, the rest has somewhere to attach.

Why that one change breaks everything you already know
A plan is a list: Up, Up, Right, Right. It only works if step 1 lands you where you expected, so that step 2 still makes sense. With slipping, step 1 might not. Two squares in you are somewhere the list never anticipated, and the rest of it is nonsense.

So you cannot answer “what should I do?” once. You have to answer it for every square you might end up standing on. That answer — one action per state — is a policy, written π(s).

Plan (Weeks 1–3)Policy (Week 4)
Shapea sequence of actionsan action for every state
Read itfrom the start, in orderlook up wherever you are
Survives a surprise?noyes — that is the point

2 · What U(s) actually means

The single most common misreading
U(s) is not the reward of square s. The reward is R(s), and on this grid it is −0.04 almost everywhere — a small fee for taking one more step.

U(s) is the total value of everything that happens from here on, if you stand on s and then behave optimally forever. It bundles up: the fee you pay now, the fees you will pay on the way, and the +1 or −1 you eventually hit.

R(s)U(s)
Iswhat this square pays you right nowwhat standing here is worth in total
Given or computed?given in the problemcomputed — it is the whole answer
On the grid−0.04 nearly everywherenear +1 by the goal, near −1 by the pit

So a square right next to the +1 has a bad reward (−0.04) and a great utility (about 0.9), because of where it lets you go next. Utility is about location, not payout.

3 · Why we cannot just work it out

The circle
Ask what a square is worth and you get:
U(3,3) depends on U(4,3), U(3,2), U(3,3) …
U(3,2) depends on U(3,3), U(3,1), U(4,2) …
U(3,1) depends on U(3,2), U(2,1), U(4,1) …

Every square's value is defined in terms of its neighbours' values, and theirs in terms of it. There is no square you can start from and no substitution that unwinds it. This is not a gap in the notes — the definition really is circular, and that is exactly why an algorithm is needed rather than a formula.

4 · How iteration breaks the circle

Guess, then let the truth spread
  1. Set every non-terminal square to 0. Not because it is worth nothing — because we have to start somewhere, and 0 is as good a lie as any.
  2. The terminals are not a guess. +1 and −1 are given. They are the only true numbers on the board.
  3. Do one sweep: recompute every square from its neighbours' current values.
  4. Repeat until the numbers stop moving.
And here is the bit that makes it click
On the first sweep, almost every square averages over neighbours that are all still 0, so it gets R + γ·0 = −0.04 and learns nothing. The only squares that learn anything are the ones touching a terminal.

On the second sweep, their neighbours can finally see a non-zero number. On the third, the next ring out. One Bellman sweep carries information exactly one square — a square four steps from a terminal cannot possibly move before sweep four. The +1 spreads outward like a stone dropped in water, and value iteration is just waiting for the ripple to reach every corner.

Watch it happen — the outlined ring is the squares whose value moved for the first time this sweep:

Interactive

Tool · Watch the value spread

Step through the sweeps. “Unmoved” means the square is still sitting on the do-nothing baseline — its number is nothing but accumulated step-fees. The outlined ring is what moved this sweep, and it spreads out from the +1 one square at a time.

One asymmetry the tool will show you
The +1 spreads visibly. The −1 mostly does not — squares right next to the pit sit on the baseline for several sweeps, looking as though they have heard nothing.

They have heard. It just does not change what they are worth yet. The best action next to a pit is to step away from it, and stepping away costs exactly what any other pointless step costs. Bad news only changes a square's value once it starts closing off the good routes — which happens later, when the surrounding values have risen and avoiding the pit finally means giving something up.

Worth knowing, because it is the sort of thing that looks like a bug in your own hand-computed table when it is not.

5 · One number, computed very slowly

Where 0.76 comes from
Take square (3,3) — one to the left of the +1 goal — on the very first sweep, when every non-terminal square is still 0. Try the action Right.

Step 1 — list what could actually happen. You command Right, so:

with probabilityyou end up atwhose current value iscontribution
0.8(4,3) — the +1 goal10.8 × 1 = 0.80
0.1veer up → off the grid → stay at (3,3)00.1 × 0 = 0
0.1veer down → (3,2)00.1 × 0 = 0
expected value of taking Right0.80

Step 2 — do the same for Up, Down and Left. All three point away from the goal, and every square they can reach is still 0, so they all score 0. Right wins.

Step 3 — add the fee for being here.

U₁(3,3) = R + γ × 0.80 = −0.04 + 1 × 0.80 = 0.76

That is the entire Bellman update, done once, by hand. Value iteration is that calculation, repeated for every square, over and over. Nothing more happens.

Two things that trip people up in that table
  • Bumping into a wall or an edge leaves you where you were. You do not lose a turn or vanish — you stay put, and the value you "land on" is your own current value.
  • The slips are perpendicular to the direction you asked for. Command Right and you can veer up or down — never backwards. That is why every action has exactly three outcomes, not four.

6 · Now the equation, read out loud

Four ideas, not one line
Ui+1(s)  =  R(s)  +  γ  maxa  Σs′ P(s′|s,a) · Ui(s′)
piecesaysin the worked example
R(s)the fee for standing here−0.04
γhow much the future is worth relative to now1 — the future counts fully
maxayou choose, so take the best actionRight beat Up, Down and Left
Σs′ P(·)·U(·)the world chooses, so average over what it might do0.8×1 + 0.1×0 + 0.1×0 = 0.80

Read right to left it is a sentence: average over what the world might do, take the best action you could pick, discount it, and add the fee for being here.

Max over your options, average over the world's. That one line is the Bellman equation, and it is the only thing you have to remember.

Why there is a max at all
Drop the maxa and you have a Markov chain — a world that evolves on its own with nobody steering. The max is the agent. It is the single symbol that turns "watching a process" into "making decisions", and it is what makes this an MDP.

7 · Two things that happen after the numbers settle

Stopping, and then reading off the answer
  • When to stop. Track δ, the largest change any square made this sweep. When δ < ε(1 − γ)/γ, the numbers are close enough and you stop. In practice: stop when nothing is moving.
  • Getting the policy. The utilities are not the answer you wanted — you wanted what do I do? Once U has settled, go to each square and run the same expected-value calculation one last time, but instead of keeping the best number, keep the best action. That is π(s).

So the pipeline is: guess zeros → sweep until still → read off the arrows. Value iteration computes numbers; policy extraction turns them into behaviour.

The one genuinely surprising result in Week 4
Change R and the optimal policy changes shape, not just slightly. Make the step fee harsh enough and the best policy is to run at the nearest terminal — including the −1 — because dying quickly beats paying the fee forever.

That is Week 1's value alignment problem arriving as arithmetic. The reward function is the specification: you did not tell it to survive, you told it to maximise a sum, and R = −1.65 quietly means "please die quickly". The reward sweep tool shows exactly where the policy flips.

Where to go next
  1. Part 1 · Uncertainty — why the earlier weeks' methods stop working.
  2. Part 2 · What an MDP is — the formal definition, now that you know what it is for.
  3. Part 3 · Expected value — the coin-flip version of the sum you just did by hand.
  4. Part 4 · The Bellman calculator — click any square and it prints the table from step 5 for you, for any sweep.

If Part 3's E[U | s, a] = Σ P(s′|s,a) U(s′) still looks alien, it is exactly the "expected value of taking Right" column you already computed. Same sum, formal name.

Now the rest of Week 4 should read like notes.

Week 04 · Part 1 · Uncertainty in AI

Uncertainty in AI

everything so far assumed the world does what it's told

Uncertainty in search

The two assumptions we have been making all along
Search algorithms — BFS, DFS, A* — typically assume:
  • The current state is known → "fully observable"
  • Actions always execute as intended → "deterministic"

These don't apply in many real-world applications:

  • Current state uncertain → "partially observable"
  • Results of actions uncertain → "stochastic"
You have seen these four words before
They are two of the seven dimensions from Week 1. Every algorithm in Weeks 1–3 quietly sat at the easy end of both. This week we drop one of them — actions become stochastic — and keep full observability. Dropping the other gives you a POMDP, which is a much harder object and not on this course.

Uncertainty in supervised learning

The setup
  • Training set: examples of input data (images, features) and output labels.
  • Models then predict labels in new examples.
Four places uncertainty enters
  • Training labels uncertain — was the human annotation done correctly?
  • Input data noisy — is this the real distance from the pedestrian to the car?
  • Model predictions uncertain — how confident are we in the model's prediction? Is this a cat or a dog? Will that pedestrian try to cross?
  • The world is uncertain — some things are stochastic and can never be predicted 100% accurately:
    • pedestrian movement prediction for autonomous vehicles;
    • text generation with language models — many different ways of completing "Mary crossed the road and then ______".
The fourth one is different in kind from the first three
Noisy labels, noisy inputs and an unconfident model are all problems you could in principle fix — annotate more carefully, buy a better sensor, train a bigger model. The world being stochastic is not fixable. No amount of data tells you which way a pedestrian will step, because they have not decided yet.

That is the kind of uncertainty MDPs are for. You do not try to eliminate it — you build it into the model as a probability distribution and then optimise the expected outcome.

Where this sits

DimensionWeeks 1–3Week 4 (MDPs)
Environment observabilityfully observablefully observable — unchanged
Action outcomesdeterministicstochastic ← the change
What a solution isa sequence of actions (a plan)a policy — an action for every state
What we optimisepath cost / plan lengthexpected sum of discounted rewards
The row that matters most
A plan is no longer a useful answer. If your actions can go wrong, a fixed sequence stops being valid the moment one of them does — and you would have to replan. A policy says what to do in every state, so it is still valid no matter where you end up. That single shift is what the rest of the week is about.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 1
  1. Search's two assumptions — current state known (fully observable) and actions execute as intended (deterministic).
  2. When they break — uncertain current state gives a partially observable problem; uncertain action results give a stochastic one.
  3. MDPs relax exactly one: fully observable but stochastic.
  4. Four sources of uncertainty in supervised learning — uncertain training labels, noisy input data, uncertain model predictions, and a genuinely stochastic world.
  5. Be able to give the examples — annotation quality, sensor distance to a pedestrian, cat-or-dog confidence, pedestrian movement for AVs, language-model text completion.
  6. Irreducible vs reducible uncertainty — the first three could be improved with better data or models; a stochastic world cannot be, which is why it has to be modelled rather than removed.

End of Part 1. Next: what a search problem becomes when actions can go wrong.

Week 04 · Part 2 · Uncertainty in AI

Markov Decision Processes

stop planning a route; start deciding what to do everywhere
Before this page
If any of this stops making sense, go back to MDPs, Slowly — it builds the same ideas up from scratch with no notation. This page is the formal version.

The grid everything runs on

One picture, used for the whole week

A robot in a 4×3 grid. It starts bottom-left. There is a wall at (2,2). Two squares end the game: +1 at the top right, and −1 just below it.

−0.04−0.04−0.04+1end
−0.04−0.04−1end
−0.04start−0.04−0.04−0.04

Every ordinary square pays −0.04 when you stand on it. Think of it as a small fee for taking another step.

Squares are named (column, row), counting from the bottom left. So the start is (1,1) and the +1 is (4,3). Getting this the wrong way round is the commonest way to lose marks on an otherwise correct answer.

Why this needs anything new
As a plain search problem this maze is trivial — Week 1 would solve it in seconds. It only gets hard when the moves stop being reliable. That is the next section, and it is the whole reason Week 4 exists.

Actions that don't do what you asked

The rule

You command Up. What actually happens:

0.8  you move up
0.1  you move left instead
0.1  you move right instead

The two slips are sideways, at right angles to what you asked for. You never go backwards. So every action has exactly three possible outcomes, not four.

And if the square you would move into is a wall or off the grid, you stay where you are. You do not lose a turn; you just do not move.

The same thing as a picture
Why this kills the Week 1 answer

Search says: go Up, Up, Right, Right, Right. Five actions. The chance that all five do what you asked is

0.85 = 0.328

So about a third of the time the sequence runs as written. The other two thirds, something slipped.

The deeper problem is not the odds — it is that the list stops meaning anything. Instruction 3 says "Right" because instructions 1 and 2 were supposed to have put you two squares up. If they did not, "Right" is advice about a square you are not standing on.

A small precision, if you want it
0.328 is the chance of the plan executing exactly, not the chance of reaching the +1. Some slips are harmless — bump a wall and you stay put, so the next instruction still applies. Some are fatal — drift into the −1 and it is over. The true chance of reaching the goal while blindly following that list is a different number. The point stands either way, so do not get stuck here.

Markov chains, and what "Markov" buys you

A Markov chain
A model of a world that moves between states at random, with nobody steering. Each state has a probability of leading to each other state, and that is the whole model.

The defining feature is the Markov property: where you go next depends only on where you are now. How you got here is irrelevant.

The same sentence in symbols
P(St+1 | St, St−1, …, S0)  =  P(St+1 | St)

In words: the probability of the next state, given the entire history, equals the probability given just the current state. Everything before now adds nothing.

Read the notation as: St is "the state at time t", and P(A | B) is "the probability of A given that B happened".

Why this is a design choice, not a restriction
If history does matter, you put the history into the state. A chess position includes castling rights for exactly this reason — so that the position alone is enough.

And you need this property for value iteration to be possible at all. Without it, a square would not have a value — it would have a different value depending on how you arrived, and you would need a number per history rather than per square. There are infinitely many histories.

What an MDP is

The definition to be able to write down
A Markov Decision Process is a sequential decision making problem for a fully observable but stochastic environment.

Taking that apart:

phrasemeans
sequential decision makingyou choose repeatedly, and each choice affects what comes next
fully observableyou always know which square you are on
stochasticyour actions do not reliably do what you asked

It rests on two assumptions:

  • the Markov property holds for the action transitions;
  • the probabilities are stationary — they never change.
Markov chain vs MDP — one difference
Markov chainMDP
Who steersnobody — you watch it happenan agent chooses
Probabilitiesone distribution per stateone distribution per state per action
Question it answerswhat will happen?what should I do?

Fix a policy and an MDP collapses back into a Markov chain — once the action at every square is decided, nobody is choosing any more.

What "stationary" rules out
Moving up is 0.8-reliable on turn 1 and still 0.8-reliable on turn 400. If that were not true, the best action would depend on when you are as well as where — and then a single utility per square could not exist, because a square would be worth different amounts at different times.

The transition model

T(s, a, s′), also written P(s′ | s, a)

In words: the probability that you end up in square s′, given that you were in square s and took action a.

s  — the square you are on now
a  — the action you chose
s′  — a square you might land on  (read "s prime")

On this grid it is just the 0.8 / 0.1 / 0.1 rule written formally. From (1,1) taking Up: P((1,2) | (1,1), Up) = 0.8, and P((2,1) | (1,1), Up) = 0.1, and the leftward slip hits the wall so P((1,1) | (1,1), Up) = 0.1.

And immediately, a problem
In Week 1 an action had an outcome, so it had a cost, so you could compare actions. Here an action has a distribution over outcomes, so it has no single value, so there is nothing obvious to compare.

We need a way to turn "a spread of possible outcomes" into one number. That number is an expected value, and it is what Part 3 is about.

Rewards, and why they are negative

Three statements from the lecture
  • Every state has a reward, R(s).
  • The agent's total utility is the sum of the rewards of every state it visits.
  • Negative rewards encourage the agent to be efficient.

For the five-step route Up, Up, Right, Right, Right, if nothing slips:

(5 × −0.04) + 1 = 0.8

Five step fees, then the goal.

Why the small negative number is doing real work
Suppose empty squares paid 0 instead. Then wandering in circles forever costs nothing, and an agent that never reaches the goal scores the same as one that does. It has no reason to hurry, or to finish at all.

Charging −0.04 per step makes time expensive. Now the agent wants to finish — and nobody had to tell it to take the short route. That preference falls out of the reward function on its own.

Turn that dial and the behaviour changes completely, which is what the four grids below are about. R(s) is not a detail. It is the specification.

Policies

What we are actually looking for

A policy, written π, is an action for every square. The best one is written π*. It must be:

propertymeanswhat goes wrong without it
completeit has an answer for every stateyou slip somewhere it says nothing about, and you are stuck
optimalthe best action in each stateyou are following a policy, just not a good one
stationarydepends on where you are, not what time it isyou could not store one action per square
properguaranteed to reach a terminalthe agent circles forever and never collects the +1
The value of following a policy
Uπ(s) = E[ Σt=0∞ γt R(St) ]

In words: start at s, follow policy π, and add up every reward you collect along the way. Since slips make that total uncertain, take the average over all the ways it could go — that is what E[…] means.

symbolread it as
E[ … ]"the average value of", over all the ways things might turn out
Σt=0∞add up over every time step, from now until the end
R(St)the reward of whichever square you are on at time t
γtshrink rewards that arrive later — see below
What γ is for
γ (gamma) is the discount factor, a number between 0 and 1. It says how much a reward arriving later is worth compared with the same reward now. γ = 0.9 means a reward one step away counts for 0.9 of its face value, two steps away 0.81, and so on.

The practical reason it exists: it keeps an infinite sum finite. If the agent might wander forever, adding up infinitely many rewards could blow up. With γ < 1 the total is bounded no matter what.

This grid uses γ = 1, so nothing is discounted at all. That is only safe because the policy is proper — the run is guaranteed to end, so the sum is finite anyway.

The optimal policy when R(s) = −0.04
→→→+1
↑↑−1
↑start←←←

The lecture's three comments on it: the policy balances risk against reward; it gives the best action regardless of how the execution goes; and it is very sensitive to the action probabilities.

Look at the bottom-right arrow — that one arrow is the whole lecture
At (4,1), directly below the −1, the policy says Left. That is away from the goal.

Going Up would be the short way round. But a 10% sideways slip while moving Up puts you in the −1 and ends the game badly. Going the long way costs a few more −0.04 fees and avoids that risk entirely.

Nobody programmed caution. It came out of the arithmetic, because the expected value of the long route is higher. This is the single most quotable thing in Week 4.

How R(s) changes everything

Four rewards, four completely different agents
R(s)behaviourwhy
R < −1.6284run at the nearest exit, including the −1living costs more than dying; ending it quickly is the best available deal
−0.4278 < R < −0.0850take the short, risky routethe fee hurts enough to be worth some risk
−0.0221 < R < 0take the long, safe routesteps are cheap, so avoid the −1 at all costs
R > 0never finishexisting pays, so reaching a terminal would end the income

Same grid, same probabilities, same algorithm. Only the reward changed.

This is Week 1's value alignment problem, in numbers
Nobody wrote "die quickly" anywhere. They wrote R = −1.65 and asked for the sum to be maximised, and the arithmetic did the rest.

The reward function is the specification of what you want. Get it slightly wrong and you get an agent that is behaving perfectly correctly and doing something you never intended. Use the reward sweep tool to watch the policy flip as R crosses each boundary.

Exam-style takeaways

What to have ready
  • MDP = sequential decision making, fully observable, stochastic. Assumes Markov + stationary probabilities.
  • Markov property: the next state depends only on the current state, not the history. If history matters, put it in the state.
  • Chain vs MDP: a chain has one distribution per state; an MDP has one per state per action, because an agent chooses. Fix a policy and an MDP becomes a chain.
  • T(s, a, s′) = P(s′ | s, a) — probability of landing in s′ from s via a. Here: 0.8 intended, 0.1 to each side, never backwards, walls leave you put.
  • 0.85 = 0.328 — why a fixed plan fails. The real problem is that the list stops meaning anything after a slip.
  • A policy π(s) gives an action for every state. π* must be complete, optimal, stationary and proper.
  • γ discounts future rewards and keeps infinite sums finite. This grid uses γ = 1, which is safe only because the policy is proper.
  • The (4,1) arrow points Left — away from the goal, to avoid a 10% slip into the −1. Caution emerged from the arithmetic.
  • R(s) is the specification. Four regimes, four different agents, from one number.

Part 3 turns "a spread of outcomes" into one number.

Week 04 · Part 3 · Uncertainty in AI

Expected Utility

turning a spread of possible outcomes into one number
The job of this page
Part 2 ended with a problem. An action no longer has an outcome, so it no longer has a value — and if actions have no values, you cannot compare them. This page builds the one number that lets you compare them. It is called an expected value, and you already know how to compute one.

Expected value, with a coin

The idea

I flip a fair coin. Heads pays you £5, tails pays £0. What is a flip worth?

Not £5 — you only get that half the time. Not £0 either. The honest answer is what you would average if you did it many times:

(0.5 × £5) + (0.5 × £0) = £2.50

£2.50 is not a possible outcome of a single flip. It is still the right number to make decisions with — if someone charged £2 a flip you should play, and at £3 you should not.

The recipe, and it never changes
expected value = Σoutcomes (probability of it) × (value of it)

For each thing that could happen, multiply how likely it is by what it is worth. Add those up. That is all an expectation ever is, in any subject.

The Σ (sigma) just means "add up the following, once for each outcome". E[X] is the standard shorthand for "the expected value of X".

The three probability facts you need

That is genuinely all
factmeaningon the grid
0 ≤ P ≤ 10 is impossible, 1 is certainP(you move up) = 0.8
the options sum to 1something must happen0.8 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 1 ✓
P(A | B)probability of A given B already happenedP(land on (1,2) given you were at (1,1) and pressed Up) = 0.8

The vertical bar is read "given". It is not division. P(s′ | s, a) is just "the chance of ending at s′, given you were at s and did a" — the transition model from Part 2, written the standard way.

A check worth doing on every exam question
Add up the probabilities of an action's outcomes. If they do not come to 1, you have missed an outcome — usually a slip that bumps a wall and leaves you where you started. That single check catches most arithmetic slips in these questions.

The expected utility of an action

The coin formula, with the names changed
E[U | s, a]  =  Σs′ P(s′ | s, a) · U(s′)

In words: for each square you might land on, multiply the chance of landing there by what that square is worth. Add them up. That is what taking action a from square s is worth.

the cointhe grid
the things that could happenheads, tailsthe squares you might land on
how likely each is0.5 each0.8, 0.1, 0.1
what each is worth£5 or £0U(s′), the utility of that square

It is literally the same sum. If you can price a coin flip you can price an action.

The one genuine difference — and it is the reason for Part 4
With the coin, you were told that heads is worth £5. On the grid, nobody tells you what U(s′) is.

A square's worth depends on where you can get to from it, which depends on what those squares are worth, which depends back on the first one. The definition is circular.

So you cannot just look the numbers up. You have to compute them, and the way to break the circle is to guess and repeat. That is value iteration, and it is Part 4.

A worked example on the grid

You are at (3,3), one square left of the +1. Suppose every ordinary square is currently valued at 0, and you take action Right.

probabilityyou land onworthcontribution
0.8(4,3), the +110.8 × 1 = 0.8
0.1slip up → off the grid → stay at (3,3)00.1 × 0 = 0
0.1slip down → (3,2)00.1 × 0 = 0
E[U | (3,3), Right] =0.8

Do the same for Up, Down and Left and they all come out 0, because every square they can reach is still 0. So Right is the best action here, worth 0.8.

The Bellman calculator in Part 4 prints this table for any square, any action and any stage of the computation.

Exam-style takeaways

What to have ready
  • Expected value = Σ (probability × value), over everything that could happen. Same formula for coins and for actions.
  • E[U | s, a] = Σs′ P(s′ | s, a) · U(s′) — the value of taking action a from square s.
  • P(A | B) is read "A given B", and the bar is not division.
  • Probabilities of an action's outcomes must sum to 1 — use it as a check. Missing outcome is usually a wall bump.
  • Every action has three outcomes here: 0.8 intended, 0.1 each side. Never backwards.
  • U(s′) is not given to you. Its definition is circular, and value iteration exists to break the circle.
  • An expected value need not be a possible outcome — £2.50 is not a coin result, and it is still the right number to decide with.

Part 4 breaks the circle.

Week 04 · Part 4 · Uncertainty in AI

Value Iteration

guess zeros, sweep until still, read off the arrows

The Bellman update

The equation
Ui+1(s)  =  R(s)  +  γ  maxa  Σs′ P(s′ | s, a) Ui(s′)

The Σ part is exactly E[U | s, a] from Part 3. Nothing new has appeared — the update just wraps that expected value in two more steps.

Read it in four pieces, right to left
piecewhat it doeswho is in charge
Σs′ P(s′|s,a) Ui(s′)the expected value of one actionthe world — so average over what it might do
maxatry every action, keep the best numberyou — so take the best
γshrink it, if the future is worth less than nowa setting
R(s)add the fee for standing herethe problem

As a sentence: the new value of a square is what it pays you now, plus the best you can expect to get from here.

One line to remember
Max over your options, average over the world's.

The max is the agent. Take it away and there is nobody choosing — the world just drifts, and you are back to a Markov chain. That single symbol is the difference between watching a process and making decisions.

And notice the subscripts: the new values Ui+1 are computed from the old values Ui. You do a whole sweep using last round's numbers, then swap them in.

The algorithm

Four steps
  1. Set every non-terminal square to 0. Terminals keep their +1 and −1 forever — they are given, not guessed.
  2. Sweep: apply the Bellman update to every square, using the previous round's values.
  3. Measure δ — the largest amount any single square changed this sweep.
  4. Stop when δ is small enough. Otherwise go back to step 2.

That is the entire algorithm. There is no cleverness in it — the cleverness is that repeating a local rule enough times solves a global problem.

Why starting at 0 is not cheating
The starting values are wrong and it does not matter. Each sweep pulls every square a little closer to the truth, and the terminals anchor the whole thing because they were never a guess. Start from any numbers you like and you converge to the same answer.

Watching it run

The 4×3 grid, R(s) = −0.04, γ = 1
U₀ — the guess
000+1
00−1
0000
U₁ — one sweep
−0.04−0.040.76+1
−0.04−0.04−1
−0.04−0.04−0.04−0.04
U — converged
0.8120.8680.918+1
0.7620.660−1
0.7050.6550.6110.388
Why U₁ is almost entirely −0.04

Every square looked at its neighbours. They were all still 0. So the expected value of every action was 0, the max of a set of zeros is 0, and the square got

−0.04 + 1 × 0 = −0.04

One square is different. (3,3) touches the +1, so one of its actions could actually see a non-zero number:

U₁(3,3) = −0.04 + 1 × [ 0.8×1 + 0.1×0 + 0.1×0 ] = 0.76
And (3,2) touches the −1 — so why is it still −0.04?
Because its best action simply avoids the pit, and avoiding costs nothing yet. Its best move is Left into the wall: you stay put, expected value 0. Moving Up would risk the −1 for no gain, so the max never picks it.

Good news changes a square's value immediately. Bad news does not — not until it starts closing off good routes. That happens later, once the surrounding squares are worth something and dodging the pit finally means giving something up.

This trips people up when they check their hand-worked table and think they have made a mistake. They have not.

How information travels
Utility spreads outwards from the terminals, one square per sweep. After one sweep only (3,3) has heard about the +1. After two, its neighbours have. And so on.

That is why (4,1) is the last to settle — it is furthest from anything good — and why the number of sweeps grows with the size of the world. Value iteration is a flood fill, carrying value backwards from the rewards. Watch it happen here.

A note on the lecture slide's U₁ map
The slide shows −0.02 in the U₁ cells and 0.60 at (3,3). But its converged map shows 0.812 / 0.868 / 0.918, which are the published values for R(s) = −0.04, γ = 1.

Those two maps cannot come from the same parameters. The U₁ picture appears to have been drawn with a different reward or discount. The numbers above are what you get from the parameters the rest of the deck uses, and the solver below reproduces them exactly.

If an exam asks for one iteration by hand: state your R and γ, and show the arithmetic. That is where the marks are.

When to stop

The figure

Recomputed from the same grid. (3,3) shoots up almost immediately. The far squares — (1,1), (3,1), (4,1) — start negative, because at first all they know about is the step fee piling up, and only climb once the good news reaches them. Everything has settled by about iteration 25, with (4,1) lowest at 0.388.

The stopping rule
stop when   δ  <  ε(1 − γ) / γ
symbolis
δ (delta)the biggest change any square made this sweep
ε (epsilon)how much error you are willing to accept in the final answer
γ (gamma)the discount factor

In practice: stop when the numbers have stopped moving. The formula just makes "stopped moving" precise, and ties it to how wrong you are prepared to be.

Reading Figure 17.5
graphshowsthe point
(a) utility vs iteration(4,3) is correct instantly; (3,3) shoots up almost at once; (1,1), (3,1), (4,1) start negative and climb, settling after about 20–30 sweepsdistant squares take longest, and (4,1) settles lowest at ≈ 0.388
(b) iterations vs γabout 10–20 sweeps at γ = 0.5, rising steeply as γ → 1γ costs far more than the error tolerance does
Two things worth understanding rather than memorising

Why large γ is expensive. γ controls how far ahead the algorithm must look. At γ = 0.5, a reward ten steps away is worth 0.510 ≈ 0.001 — invisible, so a few sweeps are enough. At γ = 0.99 nothing fades, so information has to cross the entire grid before anything settles.

Why the curves dip negative first. Early on, a distant square has only seen step fees piling up and has no idea a +1 exists. It genuinely looks like a bad place to be. Only when the good news arrives does the estimate climb. Intermediate values are not meaningful — only the final fixpoint is.

Getting the policy out

The utilities are not the answer you wanted
Value iteration gives you a number per square. What you actually wanted was an action per square. One more pass converts one into the other:
π(s) = arg maxa  Σs′ P(s′ | s, a) U(s′)

In words: at each square, work out the expected value of every action one last time — and keep the action that scored highest, instead of the score.

max vs arg max — the only difference between the two equations
maxarg max
Returnsthe best valuethe action that achieved it
Used byvalue iteration — it needs a number to keep iteratingpolicy extraction — it needs behaviour
Examplemax = 0.8arg max = Right
Why R(s) and γ vanished from the policy formula
Neither can change which action wins. R(s) is the same whatever you choose — it is the fee for the square you are already standing on. And γ multiplies every action's score by the same amount, so it cannot reorder them.

So the policy is a single arg max over the converged utilities — one cheap pass at the very end, after all the iterating is done.

Tool · Grid-world solver

Interactive

Value iteration, step by step

Click cells to build your own maze, drag the sliders to reshape the policy live, and step through the Bellman sweeps one at a time. Defaults to the 4×3 grid from the slides — press ⏭ and it reproduces 0.812 / 0.868 / 0.918.

Things worth trying in it
  • The default — check U₁ has 0.76 at (3,3) and −0.04 everywhere else, and that the final grid matches Russell & Norvig exactly.
  • Press ▶ play. Utility floods outwards from the +1, one square per sweep — the far corner (4,1) is the last to settle. The small numbers under each value are the change since the previous sweep.
  • Drag the R(s) slider slowly from 0 down to −2 with the policy shown. You can watch the four regimes appear one after another, and find the exact reward at which (3,2) flips from pointing away from the −1 to diving into it.
  • Drag γ from 0.5 up through 0.9, 0.99, 0.999 and watch both the stopping threshold tighten and the iteration count climb — 9 → 18 → 26 → 31 sweeps. (See the caveat below about how this compares to Figure 17.5(b).)
  • Build your own maze: pick a paint, click cells, add rows and columns. Put a −1 in a corridor and see the policy take the long way round it.
  • Set P(intended) = 1. The world becomes deterministic and the bottom row flips to Up, Right, Up, Left — the agent now cuts up column 3, straight past the −1, the risky shortcut it refuses to take when actions can slip. (4,1) still avoids Up, because Up from there enters the −1 with certainty.)
  • Set P(intended) = 0.5 and see how much more cautious the policy becomes — "highly sensitive to the action probabilities".
  • Draw your own grid. More walls, several terminals, any shape — it all still works.
An honest note about the γ blow-up
Figure 17.5(b) shows iterations rocketing to 105 and beyond as γ → 1. On this 11-state grid you will not see that: with the same stopping rule the count only goes from about 9 sweeps at γ = 0.5 to 31 at γ = 0.999.

The shape of the curve is right and the cause is right — the threshold ε(1−γ)/γ tightens towards zero while convergence slows to rate γ — but the magnitude in the figure reflects a general worst-case bound, not this particular tiny world. Value spreads across 11 squares in a handful of sweeps no matter what γ is. Quote the trend in an exam, not a number.

Tool · Bellman calculator

Interactive

One state, four actions, term by term

Click any square on the grid and see Σ P(s′|s,a) U(s′) written out for all four actions, with the winner starred — the argmax that becomes π(s). Buttons switch which utility map you read from.

The two cells to look at first
(3, 3) with U₀ — reproduces the 0.8 calculation from Part 3 and shows where U₁'s 0.76 comes from once you add R(s).
(4, 1) with the converged U — the square below the −1. This is where you can see, in the numbers, why the policy chooses Left over Up.

Tool · Reward sweep

Interactive

How the optimal policy changes with R(s)

Drag the scanner and watch the optimal policy snap between regimes. Also lays out a fixed list of rewards side by side — the four slides reproduced, including the answers to the question marks in the R(s) > 0 case.

What to look for
Find the value of R at which the policy at (3,2) flips from pointing left (away from the −1) to pointing right (into it), and the value at which (4,1) starts stalling against the wall. Those are the boundaries between the regimes — the policy is piecewise constant in R(s), changing only at a handful of critical values.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 4
  1. The Bellman update — Ui+1(s) = R(s) + γ maxa Σs′ P(s′|s,a) Ui(s′). Write it from memory.
  2. Max over your actions, average over the world's outcomes.
  3. Initialisation — U(s) = 0 everywhere except end states, where U(s) = R(s).
  4. Stop when Ui+1(s) = Ui(s) for all s; formally when δ < ε(1−γ)/γ, where δ is the largest change in any state this sweep and ε the error you'll tolerate.
  5. Be able to do one iteration by hand. On the standard grid with R = −0.04, γ = 1: everything is −0.04 after one sweep except (3,3) = −0.04 + 0.8 = 0.76.
  6. The converged utilities — 0.812, 0.868, 0.918 / 0.762, wall, 0.660 / 0.705, 0.655, 0.611, 0.388.
  7. Extracting the policy — π(s) = arg maxa Σs′ P(s′|s,a) U(s′). Note R(s) and γ drop out.
  8. max vs arg max — one returns the value, the other the action.
  9. Convergence behaviour — distant states dip negative before climbing; ~20–30 iterations on this grid; iterations blow up as γ → 1, and depend only weakly on the error tolerance.
  10. Utility spreads outwards from the terminals, roughly one square per iteration.
  11. The policy stabilises before the utilities do — worth a sentence if you're asked when you can stop.

End of Week 4.

Week 05 · Part 1 · Introduction to Machine Learning

Machine Learning: Overview

the other half of the field, finally

What machine learning is

The classic definition
"The field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed."

— Arthur Samuel, 1959

This is the right-hand column of Week 1, at last
Week 1 split AI into model-based (explicit knowledge, symbolic, classical — "pretends to think") and data-driven (tacit knowledge, machine learning — "pretends to learn"). Weeks 1–4 were entirely the left-hand column: search, adversarial search, CSPs, planning, MDPs — all of them require you to write the world down first.

Samuel's phrase "without being explicitly programmed" is precisely the boundary. In a PDDL domain you state that loading a cargo deletes at(c,l). In machine learning nobody states anything; the rule is extracted from examples.

The running example
A classification problem: muffin or chihuahua? A grid of photos where blueberry muffins and chihuahua faces are genuinely, uncomfortably similar.

Note what makes it a good example: nobody can write down the rule. You cannot state, in code, what distinguishes a muffin from a small dog — but you can produce ten thousand labelled photos. That gap is the entire reason machine learning exists.

Four definitions, and what each emphasises

SourceDefinition
Arthur Samuel
1959		 "The field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed."
Mohri, Rostamizadeh
& Talwalkar
2018		 "Computational methods using experience to improve performance or to make accurate predictions."
Russell & Norvig
2022		 "A computer observes some data, builds a model based on the data, and uses the model as both a hypothesis about the world and a piece of software that can solve problems."
Murphy
2012		 "A set of methods that can automatically detect patterns in data, and then use the uncovered patterns to predict future data."
They are not four different things — they are four angles on one thing
  • Samuel — what it is not: hand-written rules.
  • Mohri et al. — the mechanism: experience (data) improving performance. Note it takes a measurable view — you must be able to say how good you are, which is Part 2.
  • Russell & Norvig — the dual nature of the product: a model is both a hypothesis (a claim about how the world works) and a program (something you can run). That's a very AI-textbook framing.
  • Murphy — the statistician's view: detect patterns, then predict future data.

If an exam asks "define machine learning", give one verbatim and attribute it, then say what it emphasises. Naming the source is free marks.

"For the mathematicians out there…"

The honest caveat
For several machine learning algorithms, there are no mathematical proofs that they actually work.

The slide illustrates this with the xkcd cartoon (#1838) in which a machine learning system is a pile of linear algebra, and the fix for wrong answers is to stir the pile until they start looking right.

Why this matters more than it sounds
Everything in Weeks 1–4 came with guarantees: A* is optimal if h is admissible; alpha-beta returns exactly the minimax value; AC-3 terminates; value iteration converges to the unique fixpoint. You could prove all of them.

Machine learning largely cannot offer that. So the field replaces proof with measurement — you cannot show the model is right, so you must show it performs well on data it has never seen. That substitution is what Parts 2 and 3 are about, and it's why they take up two thirds of the week.

Three types of machine learning

Learn all three definitions
  • Supervised learning — the program is 'trained' on a given set of examples (with labels). It learns how to reach an accurate conclusion when given new data.
  • Unsupervised learning — the program is given a bunch of unlabelled data and must discover patterns and relationships in them.
  • Reinforcement learning — the program learns from the consequences of its actions (reward or punishment), rather than from being explicitly taught, and selects its actions on the basis of its past experiences (exploitation) and also by new choices (exploration).
The distinguishing question is "where does the feedback come from?"
  • Supervised — someone hands you the right answer for every example.
  • Unsupervised — there is no right answer; you're looking for structure.
  • Reinforcement — no one tells you the right answer, but the world eventually tells you whether things went well.
You have already met reinforcement learning's world — from the other side
Reward, punishment, actions, past experience, exploration versus exploitation: this is Week 4's MDP vocabulary exactly. The difference is what you're given.
  • In an MDP you are handed P(s′|s,a) and R(s) and you compute the optimal policy with value iteration.
  • In reinforcement learning you are handed neither. You must learn the policy by acting and observing what happens.

And that's why exploration vs exploitation exists in RL but never appeared in Week 4: when you already know the transition model, there is nothing to explore.

Four classes of learning problem

ProblemTypeWhat it does
ClassificationsupervisedOrganises data in classes and determines the class of new data-points.
RegressionsupervisedFits functions to data and determines values of new data-points.
ClusteringunsupervisedSeparates data in groups and determines the group of new data-points.
Dimensionality reductionunsupervisedTransforms high-dimensional data into lower-dimensional data while preserving desired properties.
Two pairs, two distinctions
Classification vs regression — both supervised; the difference is the output type. Classification predicts a label from a fixed set (muffin / chihuahua); regression predicts a number (house price, temperature). That difference is exactly why they need different metrics in Part 2 — you cannot take the "mean absolute error" of "chihuahua".

Classification vs clustering — these look identical and are not. Classification is given the classes and told which points belong to which. Clustering is given neither and has to invent the groups. "Determines the class of new data-points" versus "determines the group" is the giveaway wording.

Bibliography from the deck
  • Mohri, Mehryar, Afshin Rostamizadeh, and Ameet Talwalkar (2018). Foundations of Machine Learning. MIT Press.
  • Russell, Stuart J. and Peter Norvig (2022). Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 4th edition. Pearson Education.
  • Murphy, Kevin P. (2012). Machine Learning: A Probabilistic Perspective. MIT Press.

The deck also points at Quanta Magazine for accessible write-ups, and names the venues where the field publishes: conferences ICML (International Conference on Machine Learning) and NeurIPS (Neural Information Processing Systems), and the journal JMLR (Journal of Machine Learning Research).

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 1
