  1. Samuel 1959 — "the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed". Know the quote and the year.
  2. The other three definitions and their sources — Mohri et al. 2018 (experience → performance), Russell & Norvig 2022 (observes data, builds a model that is both hypothesis and software), Murphy 2012 (detect patterns, predict future data).
  3. Supervised = trained on labelled examples. Unsupervised = unlabelled data, discover patterns. Reinforcement = learns from reward or punishment, balancing exploitation of past experience against exploration of new choices.
  4. Classification and regression are supervised; clustering and dimensionality reduction are unsupervised. Be able to state what each does.
  5. Classification vs regression — label versus number. Classification vs clustering — the classes are given versus the groups are discovered.
  6. Many ML algorithms have no mathematical proof that they work — which is why empirical evaluation on held-out data is so central.
  7. Where this sits — this is the data-driven / tacit knowledge half of Week 1's split, after four weeks entirely in the model-based half.

End of Part 1. Next: if you can't prove it works, how do you tell?

Week 05 · Part 2 · Introduction to Machine Learning

Is My Algorithm Any Good?

measurement instead of proof

Training and test sets

Definitions — supervised learning vocabulary
  • Training set — the portion of the data used for the learning. We give our program both data and labels for a portion of the data.
  • Test set — the untouched portion of data used to evaluate our model after it is trained. We 'hide' the test labels from the algorithm in that phase.
The word doing the work is "untouched"
Measuring a model on the data it was trained on tells you nothing — a model that simply memorises every training example would score perfectly and be useless. The test set is a stand-in for data the model will meet in the real world, and it only works as a stand-in for as long as the model has never seen it.

Hold on to that word. In Part 3 a third split appears — the validation set — for exactly this reason, and "untouched" is why.

Accuracy, and its trap

Definition
Given a classification algorithm and a test set, the accuracy is the proportion of correct predictions done by the algorithm over all predictions in the test set.
The slide's question: "an algorithm has 99% accuracy. Is it good?"
Well, it depends.

Example. An algorithm takes an X-ray image of a person's lungs and predicts a rare disease D. Assume 1% of the population has disease D.

A very simple algorithm achieves 99% accuracy. Which one?

One that says "no" to every single input.

Work the numbers — take 10,000 patients
100 have the disease, 9,900 don't. The always-"no" model:
  • gets all 9,900 healthy people right,
  • gets all 100 sick people wrong,
  • accuracy = 9,900 / 10,000 = 99%.

It is 99% accurate and catches zero cases of the disease. This is called the class imbalance problem, and the general lesson is: accuracy is only meaningful relative to the base rate. On a problem where 99% of answers are "no", 99% accuracy is what you get for doing nothing at all.

Precision, sensitivity, F1

This example suggests accuracy alone may not be a sufficient metric
  • Precision — proportion of true positives over true positives and false positives.
    precision = TP / (TP + FP)
  • Sensitivity (or recall) — proportion of true positives over true positives and false negatives.
    recall = TP / (TP + FN)
  • F1 score — harmonic mean between sensitivity and precision.
    F1 = 2 / (recall−1 + precision−1)  =  2·P·R / (P + R)

The four boxes everything is built from — the confusion matrix:

Actually
positivenegative
predicted positiveTPtrue positiveFPfalse positive
predicted negativeFNfalse negativeTNtrue negative
How to remember which is which, and never mix them up
Both fractions have TP on top. Only the denominator differs, and each denominator is a column or a row of the matrix:
  • Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — the predicted-positive row. "Of everything I flagged, how much was real?" It punishes false alarms.
  • Recall = TP / (TP + FN) — the actually-positive column. "Of everything that was real, how much did I catch?" It punishes misses.

Note that neither uses TN. That is the whole point: in the rare-disease problem TN is the enormous number that lets accuracy hide the failure, and precision and recall simply refuse to look at it.

Why the harmonic mean, and not the ordinary average?
Because the harmonic mean is dragged down by the smaller number, so you cannot score well by being brilliant at one and hopeless at the other.

Take precision = 1.0 and recall = 0.02:

  • ordinary mean = (1.0 + 0.02) / 2 = 0.51 — looks respectable;
  • F1 = 2(1.0)(0.02) / (1.02) = 0.039 — correctly awful.

F1 is high only when both are high. Every classifier can trade one for the other (flag everything → recall 1, precision terrible; flag only the single most certain case → precision 1, recall terrible), so a single number that resists that trade is what you want.

The slide's question, worked

"Which of precision or sensitivity would have highlighted the weakness of the previous algorithm? Assume 0.01% of true positives."
Sensitivity (recall).
Why — on 10,000 patients with the always-"no" model

The model never predicts positive, so TP = 0 and FP = 0, and all 100 sick patients are missed: FN = 100, TN = 9,900.

  • Accuracy = (0 + 9900) / 10000 = 0.99 — hides everything.
  • Recall = 0 / (0 + 100) = 0 — exposes it immediately.
  • Precision = 0 / (0 + 0) = 0/0, undefined — it cannot even be computed, so it tells you nothing.

That is what the slide's "assume 0.01% of true positives" is for. Let the model be very slightly less useless, so it flags a handful of cases and gets them right: now FP = 0 still, so precision = 1.0 — a perfect score — while recall stays near 0.

Precision would have looked perfect. Recall is the one that exposes the weakness.

The general rule this illustrates
Recall is the metric that catches "does nothing" models. Whenever the cost of a miss is much worse than the cost of a false alarm — disease screening, fraud detection, safety systems — recall is the metric to lead with.

Flip it and precision leads: for spam filtering, a missed spam is a mild annoyance but a real email in the junk folder is a disaster, so false positives are what hurt.

The deck's closing note on balanced test sets
"What about a balanced test set, in which classes have equal number of samples? Accuracy not terrible, F1 score still interesting."

Balance the classes 50/50 and the always-"no" trick collapses — it now scores 50%, not 99% — so accuracy becomes informative again. But F1 is still worth reporting, because accuracy still treats a miss and a false alarm as equally bad, and in most real problems they are not.

Tool · Confusion matrix & classification metrics

Interactive

Every metric, from four numbers

Two modes. Type the four counts for the slide's presets — or slide a decision threshold across two overlapping score distributions and watch precision and recall trade against each other in real time, with the precision–recall curve drawn underneath.

Things worth trying in it
  • Switch to slide a decision threshold, set prevalence to about 1%, and drag the threshold slowly to the right. Accuracy barely moves off 99% the entire way while recall collapses to zero — the rare-disease argument, as one continuous motion.
  • In that mode, drag how good the model is to 0. The two distributions sit on top of each other and no threshold can separate them; the precision–recall curve flattens onto the prevalence line.
  • Step through the first four presets in order. Watch accuracy stay near 99% while recall swings from 0 to 1 — the whole argument of this lecture in four clicks.
  • The flags 0.01% preset is the slide's question: precision 1.00, recall 0.01. Precision says the model is perfect.
  • Compare rare disease against balanced test set for the same model and see accuracy become informative again.
  • Set TP = 0, FP = 0 and see the tool report precision as undefined rather than quietly printing 0.
  • On the precision–recall curve, notice you cannot move right without moving down. That trade is why a single number never settles the question, and why F1 (the dashed line) peaks somewhere in the middle.

Metrics for regression problems

The three definitions
Assume our regression predicts real numbers. Call the predictions ŷ₁ … ŷₙ and the true values y₁ … yₙ. Then:
MetricFormula
MAE
Mean Absolute Error		 (1/n) Σi=1n |ŷi − yi|
MSE
Mean Squared Error		 (1/n) Σi=1n (ŷi − yi)²
RMSE
Root-Mean-Squared Error		 √[ (1/n) Σi=1n (ŷi − yi)² ]
Why three of them, when they measure the same thing
  • MAE treats every unit of error equally. Being wrong by 10 is exactly ten times as bad as being wrong by 1.
  • MSE squares first, so being wrong by 10 is a hundred times as bad as being wrong by 1. It is dominated by the worst predictions, which makes it very sensitive to outliers.
  • RMSE is MSE's square root, purely so the number is back in the original units. If you're predicting prices in pounds, MSE is in pounds-squared and means nothing to a human; RMSE is in pounds.

Useful fact: RMSE ≥ MAE always, with equality only when every error has the same magnitude. The gap between them tells you how uneven your errors are.

Tool · Regression metrics

Interactive

MAE, MSE and RMSE, term by term

Drag any prediction up or down and watch MAE crawl while MSE explodes. Every residual, its absolute value and its square are listed underneath; the dashed diagonal is a perfect prediction.

The experiment to run
Note the metrics, then drag the last dot up to about 11 — one bad outlier in six points. MAE rises by about 1.6; MSE rises by roughly 16. Same data, same single mistake, ten times the effect. Watch the "share of squared error" line: that one point ends up owning over 90% of MSE while contributing a fraction of MAE.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 2
  1. Training set = the portion used for learning, data and labels. Test set = the untouched portion used to evaluate after training, with the labels hidden.
  2. Accuracy = proportion of correct predictions over all predictions in the test set.
  3. Be able to tell the 99% story — with 1% prevalence, an algorithm that always says "no" scores 99% accuracy and catches nothing.
  4. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — of what I flagged, how much was real. Punishes false alarms.
  5. Sensitivity / recall = TP / (TP + FN) — of what was real, how much I caught. Punishes misses.
  6. F1 = 2 / (recall−1 + precision−1), the harmonic mean — high only when both are high.
  7. Recall is the metric that exposes the always-"no" model; precision would report 1.00 or be undefined. This is the slide's question.
  8. Neither precision nor recall uses TN — which is exactly why they survive class imbalance.
  9. On a balanced test set accuracy is "not terrible", but F1 is still interesting.
  10. MAE, MSE, RMSE — write all three formulas. MSE punishes large errors quadratically; RMSE restores the original units; RMSE ≥ MAE.

End of Part 2. Next: the two ways a model goes wrong.

Week 05 · Part 3 · Introduction to Machine Learning

Underfitting & Overfitting

the two ways a model goes wrong

Generalisation error

The definition, and the problem with it
  • When we develop a model, we want to minimise the error it will have on unseen data. This is, informally, the generalisation error.
  • We rarely have a model for the unseen data, and we only have samples to deal with. We can, then, minimise the empirical error — the one we have control of.
The gap between those two sentences is this entire lecture
The thing you care about is not the thing you can measure. You want low error on data that does not exist yet; all you can compute is error on the data in front of you. So you minimise the empirical error and hope it stands in for the generalisation error.

Underfitting and overfitting are the two ways that hope fails:

  • Underfitting — empirical error is high, so generalisation error is high too. At least it's honest about it.
  • Overfitting — empirical error is tiny and generalisation error is enormous. The measurement actively lies to you, which is what makes it the dangerous one.

Underfitting

Definition
Underfitting is when the model fails to capture the complexity of the (training) data — or fails to find a pattern in the data.

The model is too simple.

Overfitting

Definition
Overfitting is when the model fits too much to the training data and fails to generalise to unseen data.

The model is too complex.

The mental image
The data is a true underlying pattern plus noise. A model that is too simple can't even follow the pattern. A model that is too complex follows the noise as well — and the noise is different next time, so everything it learned about it is worthless.

Overfitting is memorisation. A model with enough parameters can pass exactly through every training point and score zero training error while knowing nothing at all — which is precisely why the test set has to be untouched.

The three plots

The slides fit polynomials of increasing degree to the same noisy sample of a smooth curve:

ModelTrain MSEValidation MSEVerdict
Degree 1
a straight line		 1.89e−013.79e−01 Underfitting — both errors high; the line cannot bend.
Degree 4 6.91e−031.20e−02 Just right — both errors low and close to each other.
Degree 29 3.22e−031.76e+15 Overfitting — best training score of the three, and catastrophically wrong on new data.
The same three fits, drawn

Dots are the 30 data points. The dashed grey line is the true smooth curve they were sampled from — the model never sees it. The blue line is what each polynomial actually fitted.

Notice the blue line vanishing off the top and bottom of the third panel. Degree 29 passes through every dot exactly, and to do that it swings out to roughly +234 and −15 in the gaps between them. Any new point landing in one of those gaps is missed by an enormous margin, which is the entire content of that 1.76e+15.

"Degree" is simply how bendy the curve is allowed to be: degree 1 cannot bend at all, degree 4 bends a few times, degree 29 can bend 28 times. (Figures recomputed here from 30 samples of cos(1.5πx) with noise; the exact numbers depend on the sample, the pattern never does.)

Read the two columns separately — they tell opposite stories
Training MSE falls the whole way: 0.189 → 0.0069 → 0.0032. By that number alone, degree 29 is the best model of the three.

Validation MSE does not: 0.379 → 0.012 → 1,760,000,000,000,000. Degree 29 is worse than a straight line by roughly fifteen orders of magnitude.

That is the single most important pair of rows in the week. Training error can only ever go down as you add complexity — a more flexible model can always reproduce whatever a simpler one did. So training error can never tell you when to stop. Only held-out error can.

Where a number like 1015 even comes from
A degree-29 polynomial through ~30 points has enough freedom to pass through every single one exactly — and to do it, its coefficients become gigantic and of alternating sign. Between the points it therefore swings wildly, shooting to ±107 in the gaps. Square that and average, and you get 1015.

You can see it in the third plot: the fitted curve is a set of near-vertical spikes. It is perfect at the training points and insane everywhere between them.

Increasing model complexity

The slide
In this example, the degree of the polynomial can be understood as our model complexity. We would choose in this case the lower validation error, so degree of 4.

Plotting both errors against degree gives the shape you should be able to draw from memory:

Training error falls and flattens. Validation error is U-shaped. Pick the bottom of the U.
The three things to say about this curve
  1. Training error is monotonically decreasing (then flat). More complexity can never fit the training data worse.
  2. Validation error is U-shaped. Left of the minimum you are underfitting; right of it you are overfitting.
  3. Choose the complexity at the minimum of the validation curve — here, degree 4.

A fourth, worth a mark: the widening gap between the two curves is itself the diagnosis. Both high and close together = underfitting. Training near zero while validation climbs = overfitting.

"Why validation and not test?"

The question in green on the final slide — answer it properly
Because the moment you use a set to make a decision, it stops being untouched — and an untouched set was the entire point of having one.

If you try all eight degrees and pick the one with the lowest test error, you have fitted your choice of model to the test set. Its error is now an optimistic estimate of generalisation error: you selected it precisely because it happened to do well there, noise included. Report that number and you are quoting a best-of-eight, not an honest estimate.

So the data splits three ways
SetUsed forSeen by
Trainingfitting the model's parametersthe learning algorithm
Validationchoosing between models — the degree, the hyperparametersyou, the person choosing
Testthe final honest estimate of generalisation errornothing, until the very end
Note the vocabulary shift in the slides — it is deliberate
Part 2 defined only training and test. Part 3's plots are all labelled "Validation MSE". That is not an inconsistency: as soon as the polynomial degree became something to choose, a set was needed to choose it with, and the test set could not be spent on that.

The rule in one line: train on the training set, choose on the validation set, report on the test set — once.

Tool · Fitting explorer

Interactive

Underfit it, fit it, then destroy it

Drag the degree slider and watch the curve go from a straight line to a scribble — or press play and let it sweep through every degree. Samples noisy points from cos(1.5πx) exactly as the slides do, splits them into training and validation, and plots both the fit and the U-shaped error curve.

Things worth trying in it
  • The three defaults reproduce the slides' three plots. On the default sample:
    DegreeTrainValidation
    19.97e−024.13e−01underfitting — a straight line through a curve
    41.21e−021.07e−02the minimum — both low and close
    143.87e−038.57e+04overfitting — best training score of the three

    Same story as the lecture's 1.89e−01 / 6.91e−03 / 3.22e−03 against 3.79e−01 / 1.20e−02 / 1.76e+15 — different random draw, identical shape.

  • Push the degree towards the number of training points and watch the fitted curve start spiking between the data while training error keeps falling.
  • Look at the sweep table: the training column never rises; the validation column is U-shaped. The tool marks the minimum for you — that is the degree you would choose.
  • Drop the training points to 8 and look at degree 7: training MSE 5.9e−22 — the polynomial passes exactly through all eight points, because 8 coefficients can always fit 8 points — while validation MSE is 4.3e+02. That is overfitting in its purest possible form. Everything above degree 7 is reported as singular: more coefficients than data, and the fit is not even defined.
  • Set noise to 0 and the U disappears — validation error just keeps falling, all the way to 1.9e−16 at degree 13. With no noise there is nothing to memorise, so extra complexity costs nothing. Overfitting is a disease of noisy data, not of complexity by itself.
  • Change the seed to redraw the sample. The exact numbers move and the ★ may land on a neighbouring degree — the shape never changes. I checked 40 seeds: training error was monotonically non-increasing in all 40, and the validation minimum was strictly interior (a real U) in all 40.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 3
  1. Generalisation error = the error the model will have on unseen data. We can't compute it, so we minimise the empirical error, the one we have control of.
  2. Underfitting = the model fails to capture the complexity of the training data. Too simple.
  3. Overfitting = the model fits too much to the training data and fails to generalise. Too complex.
  4. Be able to draw the two curves — training error monotonically decreasing then flat; validation error U-shaped.
  5. Choose the complexity at the minimum of the validation curve — in the slides' example, degree 4.
  6. Know the three sets of numbers — degree 1: train 1.89e−01, validation 3.79e−01. Degree 4: 6.91e−03, 1.20e−02. Degree 29: 3.22e−03, 1.76e+15.
  7. Training error alone can never tell you when to stop, because it only ever goes down as complexity rises.
  8. Diagnose from the gap — both errors high and close = underfitting; training near zero and validation climbing = overfitting.
  9. "Why validation and not test?" — because choosing with a set means fitting to it, and the test error would then be an optimistic estimate rather than an honest one. Train / choose / report, on three separate sets.

End of Week 5.

Week 06 · Part 1 · Unsupervised Learning

K-Means Clustering

finding groups when nobody tells you what they are

Unsupervised learning

The setting
In the unsupervised learning setting, we look for patterns in the data without having the labels of such data points.

For example, given pictures of cats and dogs, an unsupervised algorithm may be able to identify two groups of similar pictures in the dataset — without, of course, being able to 'name' them.

A very common technique to do that is clustering. This week covers two: K-Means and Hierarchical clustering.

"Without being able to name them" is the whole difference from Week 5
A supervised classifier trained on labelled photos outputs "cat". A clustering algorithm outputs "group 2" — it has found that some photos resemble each other more than others, and that is all. Nothing in the data says which group is the cats.

This also means there is no accuracy, no precision, no F1 — there is no right answer to compare against. So the quality of a clustering has to be judged from the data's own geometry, which is exactly what "within-cluster variance" is for.

Example 6.1 — where should p₄ go?

The set-up
Six points, and we want K = 2 clusters. It is unclear which cluster point p₄ should belong to. Should we have
C̃₁ = {p₁, p₂, p₃, p₄}   and   C̃₂ = {p₅, p₆}   (6.1)

or, instead,

Ĉ₁ = {p₁, p₂, p₃}   and   Ĉ₂ = {p₄, p₅, p₆}   (6.2)
Figure 6.1 — p₄ sits awkwardly between the lower-left trio and the upper-right pair.

Within-cluster variance

The key question, and the answer
What does it mean to be a better cluster assignment than another? To answer, we need a metric for within-cluster variance, V(Ck) — the value we want to minimise. We use the squared Euclidean distance:
V(Ck) = (1 / |Ck|)  Σi,i′ ∈ Ck  d(pi, pi′)²   (6.3)
d(pi, pi′)² = Σj=1D (pij − pi′j)²   (6.4)
Three details that decide whether your answer is right
  1. We do not count each pair i, i′ twice. For a cluster of 4 points there are 6 terms, not 12 — it is every unordered pair.
  2. The distance is squared, and stays squared. No square root anywhere in V.
  3. You divide by |Ck| — the number of points, not the number of pairs. A 4-point cluster with 6 pair-terms is divided by 4.

The notes even flag their own abuse of notation here: Ck is made of points pi, not indices i, so strictly the sum should be over pi, pi′ ∈ Ck. "You would be correct to feel something is off."

The notes' worked calculation — V(Ĉ₂) where Ĉ₂ = {p₄, p₅, p₆}
V(Ĉ₂) = (1/3) [ d(p₄,p₅)² + d(p₄,p₆)² + d(p₅,p₆)² ]
        = (1/3) [ 13 + 13 + 2 ]
        ≈ 9.33

Checking the three terms: d(p₄,p₅)² = (4−6)² + (4−7)² = 4 + 9 = 13 · d(p₄,p₆)² = (4−7)² + (4−6)² = 9 + 4 = 13 · d(p₅,p₆)² = (6−7)² + (7−6)² = 1 + 1 = 2.

Where this is going
Compute V for both candidate clusterings, add up each pair, and the one with the lower total wins. That is Exercise 1 — worked in full in Part 3, and the answer settles where p₄ goes. Do it yourself first; the calculator below will mark it.

Tool · Within-cluster variance

Interactive

Every pair, every term, the total

Drag the points and every V recomputes; shift-click a point to move it between clusters. Every thin line on the canvas is one of the pairs being counted. Defaults to Example 6.1's two candidate clusterings — drag p₄ and watch which one wins change.

The algorithm

Why we need one at all
There are too many cluster assignments to check. Considering only K = 2, the number of assignments for n = 20 is
220 − 1 = 1,048,575

That may not look like much, but the number grows exponentially in n, becoming intractable very quickly on realistic data sets.

Definition 6.2 — the K-Means Clustering Algorithm
Let p₁ … pn ∈ ℝD be a set of points and K the desired number of clusters. Then:
  1. Select K different data points to be the initial cluster centres at time t = 0, µk(0). There are no clusters yet at t = 0. Move time to t = 1.
  2. At time t, assign each data point pi to the cluster Ck(t) with the closest cluster centre µk(t−1). Break ties by assigning the point to the cluster centre with the lowest index among the closest ones.
  3. For each cluster, recalculate the cluster centre as the average of all its points:
    µk(t) = (1 / |Ck(t)|) Σi ∈ Ck(t) pi   (6.5)
  4. If clusters changed, go back to step 2 with t + 1. If clusters have not changed, stop and return the final clusters.
Four things worth noticing in that definition
  • The initial centres are actual data points — "select K different data points" — not arbitrary coordinates. Later centres are averages and generally are not data points.
  • The tie-break is specified: lowest index wins. This is unusual for a textbook and it matters — Exercises 2 and 3 both hinge on a tie at p₄, and the tie-break is what sends it one way or the other.
  • The stopping test is on the clusters, not the centres. If no point changes cluster, the centres cannot change either, so it is equivalent — but the notes phrase it in terms of clusters.
  • K is an input. K-means does not discover how many clusters there are; you have to tell it. (Hierarchical clustering, in Part 2, gives you every K at once.)
In two words
Assign, then average. Assign every point to its nearest centre; move every centre to the mean of what it caught; repeat until nothing moves.

The worked example

Eight points, K = 3, with the first three points as the initial centres:

p₁ = (2,5)   p₂ = (2,6)   p₃ = (6,4)   p₄ = (1,8)
p₅ = (4,5)   p₆ = (4,4)   p₇ = (1,1)   p₈ = (4,7)

µ₁(0) = p₁ = (2,5)  ·  µ₂(0) = p₂ = (2,6)  ·  µ₃(0) = p₃ = (6,4)
End ofC₁C₂C₃µ₁µ₂µ₃
iteration 1p₁ p₅ p₇p₂ p₄ p₈p₃ p₆ (2.33, 3.67)(2.33, 7.00)(5.00, 4.00)
iteration 2p₁ p₇p₂ p₄ p₈p₃ p₅ p₆ (1.50, 3.00)(2.33, 7.00)(4.67, 4.33)
iteration 3p₇p₁ p₂ p₄ p₈p₃ p₅ p₆ (1.00, 1.00)(2.25, 6.50)(4.67, 4.33)
iteration 4p₇p₁ p₂ p₄ p₈p₃ p₅ p₆ (1.00, 1.00)(2.25, 6.50)(4.67, 4.33)
The note under Figure 6.2, and why it matters for exam bookkeeping
"In a real implementation, iteration number 5 would not even start. That is because at the end of iteration 4 we would identify that clusters have not changed from the end of iteration 3, and therefore terminate."

So the figure draws five panels but the algorithm does four iterations. If asked "how many iterations does it take?", the answer is the number at which the clusters first repeat — here 4, because iteration 4 reproduced iteration 3's clusters.

Watch p₁ across the table: it starts as its own centre in C₁, and by iteration 3 it has migrated to C₂. A point can leave the cluster it seeded. And C₁ shrinks to the single outlier p₇ = (1,1) — K-means will happily spend a whole cluster on one distant point.

Tool · K-means tracer

Interactive

Every assignment, every centroid, every iteration

Drag the points and centres around, add and delete them, and step through the algorithm one phase at a time. Runs Definition 6.2 exactly, including the lowest-index tie-break. Defaults to the worked example; the presets load Exercises 2 and 3.

Things worth trying in it
  • Press ▶ play on the default and watch it converge. The phases alternate: assign draws a dashed line from every point to the centre that claimed it, then recompute slides each ✕ to the mean of what it caught, leaving a ghost where it was.
  • The default reproduces Figure 6.2 exactly — check the centroids against the table above, and note it reports 4 iterations, not 5.
  • Switch to Exercise 2, then Exercise 3. Same six points, same K, only the two centres swapped over — and they converge to different clusterings with total variance 14.75 and 16.00. That is a local minimum, live.
  • In both of those runs, look for the point ringed in orange and marked TIE: p₄ is exactly 13 from both centres, and the lowest-index rule decides everything that follows. Now drag p₄ one square in any direction and watch the tie break on its own.
  • Drag a centre into the middle of the other cluster and step through. You can watch K-means climb back out — or get stuck, if you place it badly enough.
  • The shaded regions are the decision boundaries for the current centres: perpendicular bisectors between neighbouring centres. Drag a centre and watch the whole partition of the plane move with it.
  • Hit + K a few times, then ⟳ reseed centres repeatedly. The final variance changes from run to run — that is exactly the n_init problem from §6.2.4, and you are watching it happen.
  • Click empty space to drop in an outlier far from everything, and see K-means spend an entire cluster on it.

A few words on initialisation

The problem and the two fixes
Definition 6.2 does not specify how to choose the initial centres, and a bad choice can lead to a local minimum that is not a global minimum — as Exercise 3 demonstrates. Two main ways to address this (which can be combined):
  1. Run the clustering several times, with several random initialisations, and pick the best one.
  2. Select your initial centres in a smart way — for example, do not take points that are too close to each other, as it may lead to bad local minima or take too long to finish.

Both are used by scikit-learn's K-means: the number of restarts is the parameter n_init, and k-means++ selects initial centres from an empirical probability distribution over the points.

The terminology footnote is worth reading twice
The notes are careful: "a global minimum is, in particular, a local minimum. So our worry is to land on another local minimum, that is, one that does not happen to also be a global minimum." And: there may be more than one global minimum — several assignments that are equally good and better than anything else.

So the correct phrasing in an exam is "a local minimum that is not global", not "a local rather than a global minimum".

Why comparing to centres is enough

The nagging question
Step 2 assigns each point to its nearest centre. But V(Ck) was defined over all pairs of points. How can just looking for the closest cluster centre be enough?
Proposition 6.3  — flagged in the notes as non-examinable
Let Ck be a cluster and µk its centre. Then its within-cluster variance is equal to two times the sum of squared distances from each point to the cluster centre:
(1/|Ck|) Σi,i′ ∈ Ck d(pi, pi′)²  =  2 Σi ∈ Ck d(pi, µk)²   (6.7)

By reducing the sum of distances to cluster centres, one also reduces the sum of within-cluster variances. That is what makes step 2 legitimate.

Remark 6.4 — and why this justifies squared Euclidean distance specifically
The proposition justifies the use of Euclidean distances (or their squares) as what we minimise. If we had used Manhattan distance instead, it is not clear how we would be minimising distances by deciding a point's cluster only from the closest cluster centre.

In other words: the identity is a property of the squared Euclidean metric and the arithmetic mean, not a general fact. Swap the metric and "assign to nearest centre, then average" stops being guaranteed to reduce the objective. That is not an idle remark — Part 2's hierarchical clustering deliberately uses Manhattan distance, and it can, precisely because it never uses centres.

Careful — the factor of 2 only works if you count each pair twice
Check Proposition 6.3 on the notes' own cluster. Ĉ₂ = {p₄, p₅, p₆} has V = 9.33, and its centre is µ = (17/3, 17/3). Summing squared distances to that centre:
d(p₄,µ)² = (4 − 17/3)² + (4 − 17/3)² = 2 × (5/3)² ≈ 5.556
d(p₅,µ)² = (6 − 17/3)² + (7 − 17/3)² ≈ 0.111 + 1.778 = 1.889
d(p₆,µ)² = (7 − 17/3)² + (6 − 17/3)² ≈ 1.778 + 0.111 = 1.889
Σ = 9.333

That is V exactly — so with the chapter's own convention the identity is V(Ck) = Σi d(pi, µk)², without the 2. Doubling it would give 18.67.

The two statements are reconciled by which pairs the left-hand sum runs over. Equation 6.3 as used in the chapter counts each unordered pair once — "we do not count each pair i, i′ twice", and V(Ĉ₂) = (1/3)(13 + 13 + 2). Proposition 6.3's factor of 2 needs the sum over ordered pairs, which is twice as big. It is the same theorem, stated against a different reading of Σi,i′.

This changes none of the exercises and the proposition is non-examinable, but if you are asked to verify it numerically, use the convention you computed V with and say so. The variance calculator above prints both columns so you can see them line up.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 1
  1. Unsupervised learning looks for patterns without labels; clustering can find the groups but cannot name them.
  2. V(Ck) = (1/|Ck|) Σi,i′∈Ck d(pi,pi′)² with d² the sum of squared coordinate differences. Each pair counted once; divide by the number of points.
  3. Be able to compute V by hand — V(Ĉ₂) = (1/3)(13 + 13 + 2) ≈ 9.33 is the model answer.
  4. A better clustering is the one with lower total within-cluster variance.
  5. The four steps of Definition 6.2 — pick K data points as centres; assign each point to the nearest centre (ties to the lowest index); recompute each centre as the mean of its cluster; repeat until the clusters stop changing.
  6. Why we need it — brute force is exponential; for n = 20 and K = 2 there are 220 − 1 = 1,048,575 assignments.
  7. K-means can converge to a local minimum that is not global, and the initialisation decides which. Two fixes: many random restarts (n_init), and choosing initial centres cleverly (k-means++).
  8. Proposition 6.3 (non-examinable) — within-cluster variance equals twice the sum of squared distances to the centre, which is what licenses "assign to nearest centre". Remark 6.4: this is specific to Euclidean distance.
  9. Be able to run K-means by hand for two or three iterations on six to eight 2-D points. This is the most likely calculation question in the whole topic.

End of Part 1. Next: clustering without having to pick K in advance.

Week 06 · Part 2 · Unsupervised Learning

Hierarchical Clustering

every K at once, from n clusters down to one

The idea

The motivation
Instead of finding a fixed number of clusters, we create a process in which the number of clusters progressively changes as steps go by. We can then stop when we reach the desired number of clusters.

The process is simple: at step 1 there are K = n clusters — each point is its own cluster. At each time-step, we select the closest pair of clusters and merge them into one.

Informally, the algorithm
  1. At the start, assign each point to their own cluster.
  2. Merge the two closest clusters according to a given criterion.
  3. If all points are in one cluster, stop. Otherwise, go back to step 2.
Two things to pin down before you can run it
  • Linkage criterion — how do we define distance between two clusters?
  • Metric — which metric do we use to define distance between two points?

These are related, since both reason about distances. But — and this is the point to remember — the criterion for cluster distance is independent of the choice of metric. Any of the three linkages combines with any metric, giving the six dendograms at the end of this page.

The trade against K-means, in one line each
K-means: you must choose K up front, it can land in a bad local minimum, and the answer depends on the initialisation. Hierarchical: no K needed, no initialisation, and it is deterministic — but it is greedy, so an early merge can never be undone, and it is far more expensive (you recompute a whole distance table every step).

The two metrics

Definition 6.5 — Manhattan, L₁

‖p₁ − p₂‖₁ := Σi=1D |p1i − p2i|

The sum of the absolute coordinate differences, where |x| is the usual modulus. Also called the L₁ norm — hence the subscript 1.

Definition 6.6 — Euclidean, L₂

‖p₁ − p₂‖₂ := ( Σi=1D (p1i − p2i)² )½

Straight-line distance. Also called the L₂ norm.

Note the square root is back
Part 1's V(Ck) used squared Euclidean distance with no root. These definitions are the genuine norms, root and all. Hierarchical clustering compares distances rather than summing them into an objective, so there is no reason to drop the root — and dropping it would change nothing about the order of merges anyway.

The three linkage criteria

Definitions 6.7, 6.8 and 6.9
Let C₁ and C₂ be two clusters and ‖·‖ a norm (L₁ or L₂, say).
CriterionDefinitionIn words
Single-linkage distSL(C₁,C₂) := minp∈C₁, q∈C₂ ‖p − q‖ the shortest distance between points from one cluster to the other
Complete-linkage distCL(C₁,C₂) := maxp∈C₁, q∈C₂ ‖p − q‖ the longest distance between points from one cluster to the other
Average-linkage distAL(C₁,C₂) := (1/mn) Σi=1n Σj=1m ‖pi − qj‖ the average distance between points from one cluster to the other

Note that mn is the number of pairs of points between clusters — every point of C₁ against every point of C₂.

What each one actually does to the shape of your clusters
  • Single-linkage only needs one close pair, so clusters can grow along a chain of near-neighbours — long, straggly shapes. Good at finding elongated structure, notoriously prone to "chaining" two blobs together through a bridge of stray points.
  • Complete-linkage requires every pair to be close before it merges, so it produces tight, compact, roughly equal-sized clusters — and refuses to merge anything with an outlier hanging off it.
  • Average-linkage sits between the two and is the usual compromise.

This is not cosmetic. On the notes' own six points, single and complete linkage produce genuinely different clusterings at K = 3, which is Exercise 6. And the difference is exactly what Exercise 7's helicopter question turns on.

The worked example

Six points, single-linkage and Manhattan (L₁) distance:

p₁ = (−10, 8)   p₂ = (7, −6)   p₃ = (8, −10)
p₄ = (−6, −4)   p₅ = (−8, 6)   p₆ = (2, −4)

At iteration 0 every point is its own cluster, so the cluster distance table is just the point distance table:

{1}{2}{3}{4}{5}
{2}31
{3}365
{4}161520
{5}4273212
{6}24712820

Check one: d₁(p₁,p₅) = |−10 − (−8)| + |8 − 6| = 2 + 2 = 4, the smallest entry — so {1} and {5} merge first.

Where single-linkage first bites
At iteration 1 we need the distance from {1,5} to {4}. Should that be d(p₁,p₄) = 16 or d(p₅,p₄) = 12? "The former is worse, the latter is better, so what is the correct one? Well, that is where the criterion comes in."

Single-linkage takes the shortest distance between any two points, one in each cluster — so 12.

The full run, with the threshold at each step:

tThresholdMergeResulting clustersK
0——{1} {2} {3} {4} {5} {6}6
14{1} + {5}{1,5} {2} {3} {4} {6}5
25{2} + {3}{1,5} {2,3} {4} {6}4
37{2,3} + {6}{1,5} {2,3,6} {4}3
48{2,3,6} + {4}{1,5} {2,3,4,6}2
512everything{1,2,3,4,5,6}1
The thresholds are the merge distances — and they only ever increase
4, 5, 7, 8, 12. That monotone sequence is what gets plotted as the heights of a dendogram, and it is also why "a big jump" is meaningful: it means the next two things to join were much further apart than anything joined so far.

The notes observe that a threshold of 12 is enough to amalgamate all points into a single cluster — i.e. reading the final threshold tells you the diameter of the whole data set under this linkage.

The formal algorithm, and what happens on ties

Definition 6.10 — Hierarchical Clustering Algorithm
  1. Create n clusters, one per data point. At t = 0, C₁ = {p₁} … Cn = {pn}. Move time to t = 1.
  2. At time t, merge clusters that have the smallest distance between each other, according to the given criterion. Evaluate, over every distinct pair:
    threshold(t) := minCi,Cj dist(Ci(t), Cj(t))   (6.11)
    If only one pair achieves it, merge them (assuming i < j): Ci(t+1) = Ci(t) ∪ Cj(t). In case of ties, merge all clusters that are a distance of threshold(t) away from each other.
  3. Stop if there is only one cluster containing all points. Otherwise go back to step 2 with t + 1.

Naming convention: the lower index at time t is used when naming the merged cluster at t + 1.

Remark 6.11 — the two tie scenarios
  1. Two separate pairs. C₁ and C₂ are 10 apart, and C₃ and C₄ are also 10 apart, and 10 is the smallest distance overall. Then perform two merges: C₁∪C₂ and C₃∪C₄. K drops by 2 in one step.
  2. A chain. C₁ and C₂ are 10 apart and C₂ and C₃ are also 10 apart. Then merge all three into one big cluster. K drops by 2 here too, but into a single cluster rather than two.
The honest caveat, and the consequence
The notes are explicit that "there are no correct answers for the points we raised… there are often arguments both ways". Merging every pair at the threshold has a real cost:

it makes it impossible to have all values of K — you can "jump" from x clusters to x − 2 or fewer, so some K simply never occurs. On the other hand, it ties really nicely into dendograms, because everything at the same height merges at the same height.

If an exam asks you to justify the tie rule, that is the trade: lose some values of K, gain a clean dendogram.

Dendograms

The figure

Complete linkage, L₂, on the six points from Part 1. The height of each bar is the distance at which that merge happened. Read it bottom-up: p1+p2 and p5+p6 join cheaply at 1.41, then p3 joins at 3.16, then p4 joins p5p6 at 3.61 — and the last merge costs 7.62. That big jump is where to cut, and cutting there gives K = 2.

What they are for
A dendogram visualises the entire hierarchical clustering process at once. Leaves are points; each horizontal join is a merge; the height of a join is the threshold at which it happened.

They also help decide a suitable K. If we need to increase the threshold a lot before the next pair merges, that indicates the clusters were 'far away'. Long vertical parts of the dendogram mark those points.

The notes' worked reading — Figure 6.9, complete linkage with L₁
"It looks like K = 2 may be a good choice, since one needs to increase the threshold from around 20 to around 35 to go from 2 clusters to 1 cluster."

Running that combination gives merge thresholds 4, 5, 8, 20, 36. The jump from 20 to 36 is the long vertical bar at the top — by far the biggest gap in the sequence — so cutting just below it, at K = 2, is the natural choice.

All six combinations, as merge-threshold sequences (the heights you would draw):

LinkageMetricMerge thresholds (t = 1 … 5)Final clustering at K = 2
SingleL₁4, 5, 7, 8, 12{1,5} · {2,3,4,6}
CompleteL₁4, 5, 8, 20, 36{1,5} · {2,3,4,6}
AverageL₁4, 5, 8, 13.5, 24.75{1,5} · {2,3,4,6}
SingleL₂2.83, 4.12, 5.39, 8, 10.20{1,5} · {2,3,4,6}
CompleteL₂2.83, 4.12, 8, 15.23, 25.46{1,5} · {2,3,4,6}
AverageL₂2.83, 4.12, 6.94, 11.42, 17.42{1,4,5} · {2,3,6}
Read the last column — the notes say "clustering changes significantly", and here is where
Five of the six agree at K = 2. Average linkage with L₂ is the odd one out: it puts p₄ with {1,5} instead of with {2,3,6}, giving {1,4,5} · {2,3,6}. That is why Figure 6.12 has a completely different leaf order (6 2 3 4 1 5) from the other five.

And note the axis maxima match the figures: single L₁ tops out at 12 (Fig 6.7), single L₂ at ~10 (6.8), complete L₁ at ~36 (6.9), complete L₂ at ~25 (6.10), average L₁ at ~25 (6.11), average L₂ at ~17.5 (6.12). The final threshold is the height of the dendogram.

Tool · Hierarchical tracer & dendogram

Interactive

Distance tables at every step, plus the dendogram

Drag the points, step through the merges, and drag the cut line on the dendogram to choose K. Runs Definition 6.10 including the "merge everything at the threshold" tie rule, showing the cluster-distance table for the next merge with the minimum highlighted. Defaults to the notes' six points; the two dropdowns re-cluster instantly, so you can flip between all six figures.

Things worth trying in it
  • Press ▶ play and watch the clusters swallow each other one merge at a time, with the dashed line showing which pair is about to join and the dendogram colouring in behind it.
  • Drag the cut line up and down the dendogram. The plot on the left recolours instantly — that is what "choosing K from a dendogram" actually means, and you can feel the long vertical gaps as the K that the cut sits in for the longest.
  • The default reproduces Figures 6.3–6.6 exactly: thresholds 4, 5, 7, 8, 12 and the distance table for each merge.
  • Switch to complete linkage, keep L₁, and compare the K = 3 row against single linkage. They differ — that is Exercise 6, and the tool marks the highest K at which the two disagree. The dropdowns re-cluster instantly, so you can flip back and forth.
  • Drag a point into the gap between two clusters, then switch between single and complete linkage. Single-linkage will chain the two groups together through your new point; complete-linkage will refuse. That is Exercise 7's helicopter argument, drawn.
  • Run all six linkage × metric combinations and check the threshold sequences against the table above. Average + L₂ is the one that splits differently at K = 2.
  • Look for the biggest gap in each dendogram — that is the K the notes would recommend. With complete + L₁ the jump is 20 → 36, pointing at K = 2.

Exam-style takeaways

Key things to nail for Part 2
  1. Start with n singleton clusters; repeatedly merge the closest pair; stop at one cluster.
  2. Two independent choices — the linkage criterion (cluster-to-cluster) and the metric (point-to-point). Any combination is legal.
  3. L₁ (Manhattan) = Σ|p₁ᵢ − p₂ᵢ|. L₂ (Euclidean) = (Σ(p₁ᵢ − p₂ᵢ)²)½. Write both.
  4. Single = min, complete = max, average = mean over all cross-cluster pairs; average divides by mn, the number of such pairs.
  5. Be able to build the distance table and run the merges by hand. On the notes' points with single + L₁: thresholds 4, 5, 7, 8, 12, merging {1,5}, then {2,3}, then {2,3,6}, then {2,3,4,6}, then everything.
  6. Ties (Remark 6.11) — merge all clusters at the threshold; two separate pairs give two merges, a chain gives one big cluster. The cost is that some values of K become unreachable.
  7. Dendograms — leaves are points, join height is the merge threshold; a long vertical gap indicates a good place to cut, i.e. a good K.
  8. The maximum number of steps is n − 1 (Exercise 5) — each merge reduces the cluster count by at least one.
  9. Single-linkage chains; complete-linkage keeps clusters compact. This is the reasoning Exercise 7 wants.

End of Part 2. Next: the seven exercises, worked out.

The Seven Exercises, Worked

the notes' "Solution to Exercise N" buttons don't contain the answers — so here they are
Read this first
Every answer below is worked from scratch and verified numerically against the definitions in the notes. They are not the official solutions, so if the module publishes its own, trust those — but the arithmetic here has been checked term by term, and the runs reproduce every figure in the chapter.

Attempt each one before reading. The three tools in Parts 1 and 2 will mark your working: the variance calculator for Exercise 1, the K-means tracer for 2 and 3, and the hierarchical tracer for 6.

Exercise 1 · within-cluster variance

Recall the cluster options from Example 6.1. Either C̃₁ = {p₁,p₂,p₃,p₄} and C̃₂ = {p₅,p₆}, or Ĉ₁ = {p₁,p₂,p₃} and Ĉ₂ = {p₄,p₅,p₆}. Calculate V(C̃₁), V(C̃₂) and V(Ĉ₁). Then use V(Ĉ₂) too, to determine which of the two cluster assignments has the lower within-cluster variance.

V(C̃₁), where C̃₁ = {p₁,p₂,p₃,p₄} — four points, so 6 pairs, divided by 4:

d(p₁,p₂)² = (1−2)² + (2−3)² = 1 + 1 =  2
d(p₁,p₃)² = (1−3)² + (2−0)² = 4 + 4 =  8
d(p₁,p₄)² = (1−4)² + (2−4)² = 9 + 4 = 13
d(p₂,p₃)² = (2−3)² + (3−0)² = 1 + 9 = 10
d(p₂,p₄)² = (2−4)² + (3−4)² = 4 + 1 =  5
d(p₃,p₄)² = (3−4)² + (0−4)² = 1 + 16 = 17
sum = 55  →  V(C̃₁) = 55 / 4 = 13.75

V(C̃₂), where C̃₂ = {p₅,p₆} — one pair, divided by 2:

d(p₅,p₆)² = (6−7)² + (7−6)² = 1 + 1 = 2
V(C̃₂) = 2 / 2 = 1.00

V(Ĉ₁), where Ĉ₁ = {p₁,p₂,p₃} — three pairs, divided by 3:

2 + 8 + 10 = 20  →  V(Ĉ₁) = 20 / 3 ≈ 6.67

And V(Ĉ₂) ≈ 9.33 is given in the notes.

Answer
AssignmentV of cluster 1V of cluster 2Total
C̃ — {p₁,p₂,p₃,p₄} / {p₅,p₆}13.751.0014.75
Ĉ — {p₁,p₂,p₃} / {p₄,p₅,p₆}6.679.3316.00
C̃ has the lower total within-cluster variance (14.75 < 16.00), so p₄ should join {p₁,p₂,p₃}.
Why the answer is counter-intuitive, and worth a sentence in an exam
Look at the picture: p₄ = (4,4) is closer to the centre of {p₅,p₆} than to the centre of {p₁,p₂,p₃}. Ĉ₁ on its own is also far tighter than C̃₁ (6.67 vs 13.75). Yet Ĉ loses.

The reason is the 1/|Ck| normalisation. Adding p₄ to the trio adds three new pair-terms (13 + 5 + 17 = 35) but also raises the divisor from 3 to 4. Adding it to the pair adds two terms (13 + 13 = 26) and raises the divisor only from 2 to 3, which is proportionally much worse. Dividing by the number of points, not the number of pairs, systematically favours putting the awkward point in the bigger cluster.

Exercise 2 · running K-means

Consider the data points of Figure 6.1. Define K = 2 and µ₁(0) = (1,2), µ₂(0) = (6,7). What are C₁(1), C₂(1), µ₁(1) and µ₂(1)? What about C₁(2), C₂(2), µ₁(2) and µ₂(2)?

Iteration 1 — squared distances to each centre (comparing squares is the same as comparing distances, and avoids square roots):

µ₁(1) = ((1+2+3+4)/4, (2+3+0+4)/4) = (2.5, 2.25)
µ₂(1) = ((6+7)/2, (7+6)/2) = (6.5, 6.5)

Iteration 2 — reassign against the new centres. p₄ is now 5.31 (squared) from µ₁ and 12.5 from µ₂, so it stays in C₁; nothing else is close. No point changes cluster.

C₁(2) = {p₁, p₂, p₃, p₄}    C₂(2) = {p₅, p₆}
µ₁(2) = (2.5, 2.25)    µ₂(2) = (6.5, 6.5)  — unchanged

The clusters did not change, so the algorithm terminates. Total within-cluster variance = 14.75 — the good clustering from Exercise 1.

Exercise 3 · the same run with the indices swapped

Same data points, K = 2, but now invert the cluster indexes: µ₁(0) = (6,7) and µ₂(0) = (1,2). What are C₁(1), C₂(1), µ₁(1), µ₂(1)? What about iteration 2?

Every distance is identical to Exercise 2 — the two centres are the same two points, just labelled the other way round. So p₁, p₂, p₃ go to C₂ and p₅, p₆ go to C₁.

And p₄ is still exactly tied — 13 from both
But now the lowest index is C₁, which is the (6,7) centre. The same tie-breaking rule that sent p₄ down-left in Exercise 2 sends it up-right here. This single line is the entire exercise.
Answer — iteration 1
C₁(1) = {p₄, p₅, p₆}    C₂(1) = {p₁, p₂, p₃}
µ₁(1) = ((4+6+7)/3, (4+7+6)/3) = (17/3, 17/3) ≈ (5.67, 5.67)
µ₂(1) = ((1+2+3)/3, (2+3+0)/3) = (2, 5/3) ≈ (2.00, 1.67)

Iteration 2 — check p₄ = (4,4) again: squared distance to µ₁ is 2.78 + 2.78 = 5.56, to µ₂ is 4 + 5.44 = 9.44. It stays in C₁. Nothing moves.

Answer — iteration 2
C₁(2) = {p₄, p₅, p₆}    C₂(2) = {p₁, p₂, p₃}
µ₁(2) ≈ (5.67, 5.67)    µ₂(2) ≈ (2.00, 1.67)  — unchanged, so it terminates.
The point of the exercise
Same data, same K, same algorithm, the only difference is which centre got called number 1 — and K-means converges to a different answer, with total within-cluster variance 16.00 instead of 14.75.

Both runs are stable: neither can improve by moving a single point, so both are genuine local minima. Exercise 1 already told us 14.75 is the better of the two, so Exercise 3's run has landed on a local minimum that is not global — which is exactly what Section 6.2.4 then goes on to discuss, and why n_init and k-means++ exist.

Exercise 4 · Manhattan distance

Compute the Manhattan distance between p₁ = (3, 6, 1, −1) and p₂ = (−3, 6, 2, 5).

‖p₁ − p₂‖₁ = |3 − (−3)| + |6 − 6| + |1 − 2| + |−1 − 5|
            =    6   +   0   +  1   +   6
Answer13
Two easy marks to lose
The second coordinate contributes 0 — it is the same in both points, and it is easy to skip a term when one vanishes. And |−1 − 5| = |−6| = 6, not 4: subtract first, then take the modulus.

For comparison, the Euclidean distance here is √(36 + 0 + 1 + 36) = √73 ≈ 8.54 — always ≤ the Manhattan distance, which is a useful sanity check.

Exercise 5 · how long does it run?

If n > 1 is the number of initial points in a hierarchical clustering algorithm, what is the maximum time t until the algorithm ends?

We start at t = 0 with n clusters and stop when there is 1. Step 2 always merges at least two clusters, so every step reduces the cluster count by at least one. To get from n down to 1 therefore takes at most n − 1 steps.

Answert = n − 1
Why the question says maximum
Because of the tie rule in Remark 6.11. If several pairs sit at the threshold, one step can remove two or more clusters at once, and the run finishes early. So n − 1 is the upper bound, achieved exactly when every step merges a single pair — which is what happens in the chapter's example: n = 6 and it takes 5 steps.

This is also the reason a dendogram of n points has at most n − 1 join heights, and why some values of K may be skipped.

Exercise 6 · single vs complete linkage

The example in this section used single-linkage and L₁. The clustering process differs if we use complete-linkage instead (keeping Manhattan distance). What is the highest value of K for which the algorithms differ? For K = 6 the clustering is the same; for K = 5, although the distances change, the actual cluster assignment is the same. What is the highest K for which it isn't?

Run both from the same distance table. The first two merges agree, because at that stage the clusters involved are singletons or their nearest pair is unambiguous:

KSingle-linkage (L₁)Complete-linkage (L₁)
6{1}{2}{3}{4}{5}{6}{1}{2}{3}{4}{5}{6}same
5{1,5}{2}{3}{4}{6} @4{1,5}{2}{3}{4}{6} @4same
4{1,5}{2,3}{4}{6} @5{1,5}{2,3}{4}{6} @5same
3{1,5} {2,3,6} {4} @7{1,5} {2,3} {4,6} @8DIFFER
2{1,5}{2,3,4,6} @8{1,5}{2,3,4,6} @20same again
1all @12all @36same
AnswerK = 3

Where they part company. At K = 4 the clusters are {1,5}, {2,3}, {4}, {6}. Now compare the two candidate merges:

single:   dist({2,3},{6}) = min(7, 12) = 7  ·  dist({4},{6}) = 8  → merge {2,3} with {6}
complete: dist({2,3},{6}) = max(7, 12) = 12  ·  dist({4},{6}) = 8  → merge {4} with {6}
The one number that does it
d(p₃, p₆) = 12. Single-linkage ignores it — {2,3} is only 7 from {6} because p₂ is close — so {6} joins the pair. Complete-linkage is forced to use it, which pushes {2,3} out to 12 and lets {4} win at 8 instead.

Note the two then re-converge at K = 2. Different intermediate structures can lead to the same final split, so "the algorithms differ" has to be checked at every K, not just the end.

Exercise 7 · the helicopter problem

Cities are points, with Euclidean distances. Your helicopters have limited fuel and can travel non-stop between cities at most 100 miles apart. You want to cluster cities so that a helicopter can go from any city to any other city within the same cluster without stopping for fuel. You set the threshold to 100. Which criterion should you use?

AnswerComplete-linkage.

Why. The requirement is about every pair of cities in a cluster, not some pair. Complete-linkage defines the distance between two clusters as the maximum over cross-cluster pairs, so it only merges when the furthest apart pair is within the threshold. Merging at threshold 100 therefore guarantees every pair inside a cluster is at most 100 miles apart — precisely the guarantee the helicopters need.

Why single-linkage would strand a helicopter
Single-linkage merges when the closest pair is within 100. So take three cities in a line: A is 90 from B, B is 90 from C, and A is 180 from C. Both of those 90s are the joint-smallest distance, so under the tie rule single-linkage merges all three in one step at threshold 90 — comfortably under your limit of 100. A helicopter then asked to fly A → C runs out of fuel halfway. That is chaining, and here it is not a stylistic quirk but a crash.

Average-linkage fails for the same reason, more subtly: an average below 100 says nothing about the worst pair.

The general principle worth stating in an answer
Match the linkage to the guarantee you need. Complete-linkage gives you a bound on the diameter of every cluster; single-linkage gives you a bound on connectivity — that you can get between any two members via a chain of short hops. If refuelling were allowed at intermediate cities, single-linkage would be the right answer.

End of Week 6.

Week 07 · Part 1 · Supervised Learning

Linear Regression

the one algorithm in this course whose optimum you can prove

Supervised learning, and the two tasks inside it

The setting
In supervised learning we capture the patterns of a set of training data with labels, in order to predict new samples.

Take predicting the value of a house. We have data on several houses — size, number of bedrooms, and so on — together with their market value. The challenge is an algorithm that learns how these features should be combined to predict the value of a given, often unseen, house.

Regression vs classification — the split that decides which algorithm you reach for
RegressionClassification
What you predicta continuous numberwhich of a fixed set of classes C a point belongs to
Example in this chapterthe value of a house; y at x = 5credit risk ∈ {High, Low, Medium}
Algorithm coveredLinear RegressionDecision Trees
Error measured bySSE / MSE / MAE (Week 5)accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (Week 5)

Both are supervised: both need labels. The contrast with Week 6 is that clustering had none.

Where the boundary is not where you expect
A decision tree can predict continuous values too — that is Decision Tree Regression, and it is outside the scope of this course. What is in scope is the reverse direction: continuous values can appear as attributes of the data points in a classification problem. Salary, for instance, is a perfectly good feature for predicting credit risk; you split on it with a test like Salary ≤ 30000. That is why every node in the course's figures is labelled with a ≤ test rather than a bare feature name.

Modelling the data: a line plus noise

Equation (7.1)
Before fitting anything, we say where the data came from. Figure 7.1 shows samples drawn from a function but with some error:
y = ½x + ε   (7.1)

Here ε has a normal distribution, ε ∼ N(0, 0.09). The blue points are not on the grey line, and the green dotted segments between point and line are the error, or the residual.

The regression problem, stated exactly
Given the blue points, but not the grey line, how would I estimate the line?

Defining a line is nothing more than defining two parameters:

ŷ = β₀ + β₁x

We write ŷ rather than y to signal that these are predictions, not observed values. β₀ is the intercept; β₁ is the slope.

Three symbols that get mixed up in exam answers
  • y — the value actually observed in the data.
  • ŷ — what the fitted line says y should be at that x.
  • ε — the gap, ε = y − ŷ. Called the error when you are talking about the true generating process, and the residual when you are talking about a fitted line. The notes use both words for the same green segments.

The normal distribution, recapped

The two figures

Left is the data: dots scattered around the line y = ½x. Right is a close-up of the scatter at one x value — at x = 5 the line gives 2.5, and the noise spreads y around it in a bell shape.

µ = 2.5 is where the bell is centred. σ = 0.3 is how wide it is. The shaded band is µ ± σ, which always holds about 68% of the area — whatever µ and σ happen to be.

Figure 7.2, in words
The curve in Figure 7.2 has mean µ = 2.5 and standard deviation σ = 0.3, so by definition the variance is σ² = 0.09. We write normal distributions as N(µ, σ²) — the second argument is the variance, not the standard deviation. Therefore
f(5) ∼ N(2.5, 0.09)

where f(5) denotes the distribution of y when x = 5. That is Figure 7.2 matching the middle bell of Figure 7.1 on purpose: at x = 5 the line y = ½x gives 2.5, and the noise spreads y around it.

Two facts that get asked
  • Normal distributions are continuous, so the chance of getting any one specific value is always zero. You can only talk about intervals, and the probability of landing in one is the area under the curve over that interval.
  • The probability of a value between µ − σ and µ + σ — here 2.2 to 2.8 — is approximately 68%. That number does not depend on µ or σ, which is exactly why σ is worth quoting.

Tool · The normal curve behind ε

Interactive

µ, σ, and the area you are actually allowed to ask about

Drag µ and σ and watch the ±1σ figure refuse to move off 68%. The second pair of sliders sets an arbitrary interval in units of σ, and the panel gives you its exact area — the only kind of probability a continuous distribution has to offer.

The worked example — Table 7.1

The data
xy
−12
00
20
5?

Three points, and we want the line that best approximates them — and then the best value at x = 5. The notes stress the point of the exercise: we want to be able to find it “by hand”.

Step 1 — one residual per point
We minimise the sum of the squares of the residuals. For x = −1, y = 2 we have 2 = β₀ + β₁·(−1) + ε₁, so:
ε₁² = (2 − β₀ + β₁)²
ε₂² = (0 − β₀)²
ε₃² = (0 − β₀ − 2β₁)²

Notice the sign flip on the first line: −β₁xᵢ with xᵢ = −1 becomes +β₁. This is where most by-hand attempts go wrong.

Step 2 — add them up and collect
SSE = (2 − β₀ + β₁)² + (0 − β₀)² + (0 − β₀ − 2β₁)²
      = 4 − 4β₀ + 4β₁ + 3β₀² + 5β₁² + 2β₀β₁

There are two routes from here to the minimum, and which one you take is “down to how much calculus you have seen in school”:

  • Option 1 — partial derivatives. Take ∂SSE/∂β₀ and ∂SSE/∂β₁, set both to zero. (If you go this way you can jump straight to the answers.)
  • Option 2 — parabola vertices. No calculus needed. This is the route the notes take, and it is the one worth being able to reproduce.

Option 2 in full — minimising without calculus

Step 3 — freeze one β and you are left with a parabola
If we make β₁ constant, SSE is a function of β₀ that happens to be a parabola — call it g(β₀). Same in the other direction for h(β₁). Written in the shape f(x) = ax² + bx + c, they are the same six terms sorted differently:
g(β₀) = 3β₀² + (−4 + 2β₁)β₀ + (4 + 4β₁ + 5β₁²)
h(β₁) = 5β₁² + (4 + 2β₀)β₁ + (4 − 4β₀ + 3β₀²)
Step 4 — a parabola is lowest at x = −b/2a
For each β₁ there is a parabola g(β₀) whose minimum we can write down, and vice versa:
β̂₀ = (4 − 2β₁) / 6   (7.2)
β̂₁ = (−4 − 2β₀) / 10   (7.3)

Both β² terms have vanished, so this is now an ordinary pair of simultaneous linear equations.

Step 5 — solve the system
6β₀ = 4 − 2β₁  and  5β₁ = −2 − β₀
6β₀ = 4 − 2(−2 − β₀)/5  ⟹  30β₀ = 24 + 2β₀  ⟹  28β₀ = 24
β̂₀ = 6/7 ≈ 0.86   (7.4)
β̂₁ = −4/7 ≈ −0.57   (7.5)
ŷ = −(4/7)x + 6/7   (7.6)
Two small slips in the printed notes — worth knowing so they do not confuse you
  • Equation (7.6) is introduced as “the best fit line in Figure 7.1”. It is the best fit line of Figure 7.3 — Figure 7.1 is the y = ½x sampling picture, whose line has a positive slope.
  • Equation (7.2) is written with a tilde, β̃₀, in the line above and a hat, β̂₀, in the equation itself. They mean the same thing: the minimising value.

The mathematics is right; only the cross-reference is off. β̂₀ = 6/7 and β̂₁ = −4/7 check out exactly, and the resulting SSE is 8/7 ≈ 1.1429.

Tool · Least squares, by hand and by formula

Interactive

Drag the data, watch the derivation rewrite itself

Drag any point; click empty space to add one; shift-click to delete. The six-step derivation underneath is the notes' Option 2 carried out on your points — residuals, the collected SSE, the two parabolas, the two vertex equations, the solve, and the prediction. Step through it with ▶, or turn on compare my own line and try to beat the least-squares SSE by hand. (You cannot. That is the point of Theorem 7.3.)

The formal definitions

Definition 7.1 — Linear Regression
Let x₁, …, xn ∈ ℝD be a set of points in D dimensions and y₁, …, yn the values associated with them. In a linear regression we look for values β₀, …, βD such that
ŷj = h(xj) = β₀ + β₁xj,1 + β₂xj,2 + ⋯ + βDxj,D   (7.7)

and that best approximate the set of points — in other words, minimise SSE (or MSE) between y₁ … yn and ŷ₁ … ŷn. This is also known as multiple linear regression.

Definition 7.2 — Simple Linear Regression
The same, with D = 1. One feature, two parameters, and everything above applies.
The trap in the word “linear” — this is exam material
“Linear” refers to the parameters βi, not to the variables xi. So polynomial regression,
ŷj = h(xj) = β₀ + β₁xj + β₂xj² + ⋯ + βDxjD

— a curve, obviously — is a special case of linear regression. Treat x, x², x³ as D separate features and Definition 7.1 applies unchanged. This is also the honest answer to “why did the degree-9 curve in Week 5 still count as a linear model”.

Theorem 7.3 — and why it is remarkable

Why squared error at all?
It is not set in stone. Other algorithms minimise the absolute error — look up Least Absolute Deviations. What is nice about SSE is that we can compute a formula that gives us the solution.

This is very rare in machine learning. Not often can we actually prove that a method gives the best solution possible; most algorithms are useful because they work well in practice. K-means, for one, only converges to a local optimum. Linear regression hands you the global one in closed form.

Theorem 7.3 — Solution for Simple Linear Regression
For a simple linear regression yᵢ = β₁xᵢ + β₀ + εᵢ, the least-squares estimates are
β̂₁ = ( n·Σxᵢyᵢ − (Σxᵢ)(Σyᵢ) ) / ( n·Σxᵢ² − (Σxᵢ)² )
β̂₀ = ( (Σxᵢ²)(Σyᵢ) − (Σxᵢ)(Σxᵢyᵢ) ) / ( n·Σxᵢ² − (Σxᵢ)² )

Four sums and a count. Σxᵢ, Σyᵢ, Σxᵢ², Σxᵢyᵢ, and n — the entire dataset reduces to these five numbers as far as the fit is concerned.

The proof, in three lines (explicitly non-examinable)
Differentiate SSE and set both derivatives to zero:
∂SSE/∂β₀ = −2 Σ (yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0
∂SSE/∂β₁ = −2 Σ xᵢ(yᵢ − β₀ − β₁xᵢ) = 0

which rearrange into the two normal equations

n·β̂₀ + β̂₁·Σxᵢ = Σyᵢ
β̂₀·Σxᵢ + β̂₁·Σxᵢ² = Σxᵢyᵢ

and solving that 2×2 system gives the theorem. Note what is not used: the normality of the errors. You need that assumption only to prove further properties of the estimators, such as unbiasedness.

A free check on any answer you write
The first normal equation says Σyᵢ = n·β̂₀ + β̂₁Σxᵢ, which is exactly the statement that the residuals sum to zero at the optimum — equivalently, that the fitted line passes through the point of means (x̄, ȳ). Add your residuals up. If they do not cancel, your βs are wrong, and it takes ten seconds to find out.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • Supervised = labelled. Regression predicts a number; classification picks a class. Decision Tree Regression is out of scope, but continuous features in a classification tree are in.
  • N(µ, σ²) carries the variance. σ = 0.3 ⟹ N(µ, 0.09). µ ± σ ≈ 68%. P(exactly one value) = 0 for any continuous distribution.
  • ŷ = β₀ + β₁x; residual εᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ; we minimise Σεᵢ².
  • Know both routes to the minimum. Partial derivatives, or freeze one β and use the vertex of a parabola at −b/2a. The by-hand route is the one the notes work, so it is the one likely to be asked for.
  • Theorem 7.3 is five numbers: n, Σx, Σy, Σx², Σxy. Memorise the shape β̂₁ = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) / (nΣx² − (Σx)²) and note that β̂₀ reuses the same denominator.
  • “Linear” is about the βs. Polynomial regression is a special case of linear regression.
  • Normality of ε is not used in the proof — only for further properties of the estimators. This is a favourite “state whether the following is true” item.
  • Check your answer by summing the residuals; they must come to zero.

Part 2 turns to classification — and to trees.

Week 07 · Part 2 · Supervised Learning

Decision Trees

Gini, Gini-Split, and choosing what to ask first

Using a tree before building one

Figure 7.4 — the credit-risk classifier
A person has attributes HasJob and OwnsHome, each 0 (False) or 1 (True). The tree assigns them to one of C = {High, Low, Medium} — their credit risk.

Someone with HasJob = 0 is classified High, regardless of OwnsHome — the feature simply never gets consulted on that branch. That is a decision tree's whole appeal: the questions you get asked depend on your earlier answers.

Two conventions to state before you draw anything
  • For binary trees (two children at every non-leaf), the left branch is where the statement is True.
  • For a non-binary branch, label each arrow with the attribute value it stands for. Nothing forces a tree to be binary — a feature profession with values journalist / mathematician / historian gives three branches out of one node.

Table 7.3 — the dataset behind the figures

Fifteen people
IDOwnsHomeHasJobCreditRisk
1YesYesLow
2NoYesMedium
3NoNoHigh
4YesNoHigh
5YesYesLow
6NoYesMedium
7YesNoHigh
8NoNoHigh
9YesYesLow
10NoYesMedium
11YesNoHigh
12YesYesLow
13NoYesMedium
14YesNoHigh
15YesYesLow

Class totals: High 6, Low 5, Medium 4. The figures print them as the vector [6, 5, 4], and that ordering is alphabetical — High, Low, Medium — which is what makes “lowest index” a well-defined tie-break.

What the “class =” line in a node means
The most common class in that node — the simple majority — with ties broken by taking the class with lowest index. It is the label the tree would output if it had to stop right there, which is why every node carries one, not just the leaves.

The Gini index

What it measures
How ‘impure’ the set of points in a node is, with respect to the classes. The left node of the second row in Figure 7.5 has Gini 0: every point in it is Low, so there is no impurity at all.

That is the motivation in one line — we want to branch so that the children are as pure as possible.

The root of Figure 7.5, by hand — how do you get to 0.658?
For each class, multiply the chance of sampling it by the chance of not sampling it, then add over the classes:
(6/15)(9/15) + (5/15)(10/15) + (4/15)(11/15) ≈ 0.658   (7.8)

Exactly, that is (54 + 50 + 44)/225 = 148/225 = 0.6578…. The notes invite you to do the same for the right-hand node of the second row and get 0.494: (5/9)(4/9) + (4/9)(5/9) = 40/81 = 0.4938…

Definition 7.4 — Gini Index
Let v = (v₁, …, vk) ∈ ℕk be a k-dimensional vector of non-negative integers, and let n = Σᵢ vᵢ. Then
Gini(v) = Σi=1..k pᵢ(1 − pᵢ)   where  pᵢ = vᵢ/n   (7.9)

Note what the argument is: a vector of counts, not a set of points. Gini does not care which points are in the node, only how many of each class.

Three properties worth carrying into the exam
  • Gini = 0 exactly when the node is pure — one class has everything.
  • Maximum is 1 − 1/k, reached when all k classes are equally represented. For k = 2 that is ½ (Exercise 4); for k = 3 it is ⅔; for k = 4, ¾.
  • Equivalently Gini(v) = 1 − Σ pᵢ², since Σpᵢ = 1. Faster to compute under time pressure, and identical in value.

Tool · Gini index calculator

Interactive

Every pᵢ(1 − pᵢ) term, and where you sit on the curve

Type a count vector, or nudge any count with the + / − buttons and watch the total move. The curve underneath is the k = 2 case, Gini = 2p(1 − p) — the shape that makes “maximum ½ at p = ½” obvious rather than memorised.

A caution about Figure 7.5

Figure 7.5, drawn with the labels the vectors imply

Class order is alphabetical — [High, Low, Medium] — which the root fixes: [6, 5, 4] with class High can only be that order, and Table 7.3 has High 6, Low 5, Medium 4.

Read every label off the vector. [0, 5, 4] is Low (5 beats 4). [0, 0, 4] is Medium. [0, 5, 0] is Low. The printed figure has Low and Medium swapped in these three nodes; Figures 7.4 and 7.6 are both correct.

Three class labels in Figure 7.5 are swapped — the Gini numbers are all correct

Figure 7.5 is meant to be Figure 7.4 with the extra bookkeeping added. Its gini, samples and value lines all check out against Table 7.3. But three of its class = lines disagree with both Figure 7.4 and Figure 7.6, and the value vectors themselves say which is right.

nodevalueFigure 7.5 saysthe vector implies
HasJob = Yes (n = 9)[0, 5, 4]class = Mediumclass = Low — Low has 5, Medium has 4
… & OwnsHome = No (n = 4)[0, 0, 4]class = Lowclass = Medium — the only non-zero entry is Medium
… & OwnsHome = Yes (n = 5)[0, 5, 0]class = Mediumclass = Low

The ordering is fixed by the root itself: [6, 5, 4] with class = High can only be [High, Low, Medium], because Table 7.3 has High 6, Low 5, Medium 4. Under that ordering Figure 7.4 and Figure 7.6 are both entirely correct, and Figure 7.5 has Low and Medium interchanged in its three lower nodes.

What to do in an exam: read the labels off the vector, not off a remembered picture. Cross-check against Figure 7.4, which says plainly that HasJob = Yes and OwnsHome = No gives Medium — and Table 7.3 rows 2, 6, 10 and 13 confirm it.

Gini-Split — choosing what to ask

Where 0.444, 0.494 and 0 come from

Each one is the Gini of one child group, from Definition 7.4 applied to that group's class counts. Nothing else.

splitgroupcounts [High, Low, Medium]Gini = Σ pᵢ(1 − pᵢ)
OwnsHome= No, 6 people[2, 0, 4] (2/6)(4/6) + 0 + (4/6)(2/6) = 16/36 = 0.444
= Yes, 9 people[4, 5, 0] (4/9)(5/9) + (5/9)(4/9) + 0 = 40/81 = 0.494
HasJob= No, 6 people[6, 0, 0] (6/6)(0/6) + 0 + 0 = 0 — pure
= Yes, 9 people[0, 5, 4] 0 + (5/9)(4/9) + (4/9)(5/9) = 40/81 = 0.494

And the 6/15 and 9/15 are simply what fraction of the 15 rows landed in each group. So:

OwnsHome: (6/15)(0.444) + (9/15)(0.494) = 0.178 + 0.296 = 0.474
HasJob:   (6/15)(0)      + (9/15)(0.494) = 0      + 0.296 = 0.296

That zero is the whole reason HasJob wins. Splitting on it hands you one group with nothing left to decide — all six are High.

Figure 7.6 — the same data split the other way
Splitting Table 7.3 by OwnsHome instead gives a tree that looks worse. Why?

Because splitting by ‘OwnsHome’ generates children with worse Gini values on average — well, weighted average. Weighting matters: a very impure child holding two points should not count as much as a slightly impure one holding nine.

The two calculations, side by side
Gini-Split(OwnsHome) = (6/15)·0.444 + (9/15)·0.494 ≈ 0.474
                         ↑ OwnsHome = False, Gini(2,0,4)    ↑ OwnsHome = True, Gini(4,5,0)

Gini-Split(HasJob)   = (6/15)·0     + (9/15)·0.494 ≈ 0.296
                         ↑ HasJob = False, Gini(6,0,0)      ↑ HasJob = True, Gini(0,5,4)

HasJob is less impure, so we split by it. Exactly: 64/135 ≈ 0.4741 against 8/27 ≈ 0.2963.

Definition 7.5 — Gini-Split Index
Assume categorical features only. Let S be a set of n data points with features A₁, …, Ak, and let Ai be an attribute with a possible values. Then
Gini-Split(Ai) = Σj=1..a (nj/n) · Gini(vj)   (7.10)

where vj counts the classes in the child node where Ai = j, and nj is the sum of its entries. To choose the attribute:

arg minA₁,…,Ak { Gini-Split(Ai) }   (7.11)

arg min, not min — the answer is which attribute, not the number. Write the attribute name.

Two extensions the definition already covers
  • More than two features: compute Gini-Split for all of them and pick the lowest.
  • More than two values: the sum simply runs over all the children. Nothing in (7.10) assumes a is 2.

Building the rest of the tree

The recursion, and the question people get wrong
Formula (7.11) applies at every node, not just the root. So: at each node, score every remaining attribute against the points that reached that node, take the arg min, split, and recurse. Stop when the node is pure — or when you run out of attributes.

Look at Figure 7.6: both children of the root are split by the same feature, HasJob, but only because there were only two features to choose from. In general, should we force different branches to split the same way?

No. Nothing stops us, but it makes more sense to allow different splits in different branches: when a new point arrives, its feature values are no secret to us, so we can simply traverse the tree taking the current best option at each node. Allowing branches to differ is what scikit-learn does.

Why re-splitting on a used feature is pointless, not just inelegant
Everything reaching a node below HasJob = Yes has HasJob = Yes. That feature now has one value across the whole node, so the split has a single child containing everything, and its Gini-Split equals the node's own Gini — no improvement, ever. The tool below marks such features useless here rather than scoring them.
What happens when you run out of features before you run out of impurity
Two rows with identical features but different classes can never be separated. The node becomes a leaf labelled with the majority class — impure, and accepting some training error. Table 7.4 in Exercise 5 does this on purpose: with 3 binary features there are only 8 possible feature vectors but 20 rows and 4 classes, so no tree on those features can be perfect.

A note on neural networks

Explicitly out of scope
Neural networks are beyond the scope of this course — they are not examinable here, and several later modules cover them properly. The chapter closes by listing resources for anyone who wants to start early:
  • Neural Networks — 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson), a five-part video series, recommended for its animations and simple examples.
  • Understanding Deep Learning — Simon J. D. Prince (MIT Press, 2023), with free PDF and Jupyter notebooks.
  • Deep Learning — Goodfellow, Bengio and Courville, the classical reference.

For the examinable material, the chapter again points at Chapter 19 of Russell & Norvig, Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach (4th edition), with the caveat that it is not very complete on some machine learning parts.

The footnote worth reading twice
The notes raise, in passing, whether it is fair that machine learning “seems to have absorbed all these statistical methods known for a long time” — it sounds fancier to put linear regression in the ML pot, though statisticians have been calling it regression for a century. Worth having an opinion on; it is the kind of thing that makes a good sentence in a discussion answer.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • Gini(v) = Σ pᵢ(1 − pᵢ), pᵢ = vᵢ/n. Zero ⟺ pure. Maximum 1 − 1/k at equal classes; ½ when k = 2.
  • Gini-Split(A) = Σⱼ (nⱼ/n)·Gini(vⱼ) — a weighted average over the children, and you pick the arg min.
  • Show the weights. Marks in these questions sit on the (nⱼ/n) factors as much as on the Gini values.
  • Node label = majority class, ties to the lowest index, and index order is the alphabetical class order.
  • Apply (7.11) at every node, on that node's points only, and let different branches split on different features.
  • Left = True in a binary tree; label the arrows in a non-binary one.
  • Decision Tree Regression is out of scope; continuous features are not.
  • Neural networks are out of scope.
