Class order is alphabetical, [High, Low, Medium]. Read every label off the vector: [0,5,4] is Low, [0,0,4] is Medium, [0,5,0] is Low. The printed figure has Low and Medium swapped in those three nodes.

The Five Exercises, Worked

every solution box in the PDF is blank — these are filled in and checked
Why this section exists
Chapter 7 poses five exercises and prints an empty Solution to Exercise n box after each one. Every answer below has been worked from the definitions and independently re-computed in exact arithmetic, so the fractions are exact rather than rounded. Attempt each one before reading on — these are close to the shape of an exam question.
Exercise 1

Estimate the value of x = 5 using the regression line from the values in Table 7.1.

The line was found in §7.2.2 to be ŷ = −(4/7)x + 6/7. Prediction is one substitution:

ŷ(5) = −(4/7)·5 + 6/7 = −20/7 + 6/7 = −14/7
answerŷ(5) = −2, exactly. Table 7.1's missing entry is −2.
Worth noticing
x = 5 is well outside the range of the data, which runs from −1 to 2. The arithmetic is trivial; the honest caveat is that this is extrapolation, and a linear model has nothing to say about whether the straight-line relationship survives out there. If a question asks you to comment, that is the comment.
Exercise 2

Find the best fit line for the dataset that is the same as this one but changing the last point to (2, 1), instead of (2, 0).

Data: (−1, 2), (0, 0), (2, 1). Doing it the notes' way — residuals first:

ε₁² = (2 − β₀ + β₁)²   ε₂² = (0 − β₀)²   ε₃² = (1 − β₀ − 2β₁)²

Expanding and collecting:

SSE = 3β₀² + 5β₁² + 2β₀β₁ − 6β₀ + 0·β₁ + 5

The β₁ term has vanished, because Σxᵢyᵢ = (−1)(2) + 0 + (2)(1) = 0. Reading the two vertices at −b/2a:

β̂₀ = (6 − 2β₁)/6     β̂₁ = −2β₀/10 = −β₀/5
30β₀ = 30 + 2β₀  ⟹  28β₀ = 30

Or straight from Theorem 7.3 with n = 3, Σx = 1, Σy = 3, Σx² = 5, Σxy = 0, denominator 3·5 − 1² = 14:

β̂₁ = (3·0 − 1·3)/14 = −3/14    β̂₀ = (5·3 − 1·0)/14 = 15/14
answer β̂₀ = 15/14 ≈ 1.0714 and β̂₁ = −3/14 ≈ −0.2143, so
ŷ = −(3/14)x + 15/14

SSE at the optimum is 25/14 ≈ 1.7857.

What moving one point by one unit did
The slope went from −4/7 = −8/14 to −3/14 — flattened to just over a third of its former steepness — and the intercept rose from 6/7 to 15/14. With only three points, every one of them is high leverage. That is the whole reason Week 5 spent time on outliers and MSE.
Exercise 3

Using your favourite method (formula or ‘by hand’), find values for β₀ and β₁ from the dataset in Table 7.2: (−1, 2), (0, 0), (2, 1), (3, −7).

Four points, so the formula route is the sane one. The five numbers:

xᵢyᵢxᵢ²xᵢyᵢ
−121−2
0000
2142
3−79−21
Σ = 4Σ = −4Σ = 14Σ = −21

n = 4, so the shared denominator is n·Σx² − (Σx)² = 4·14 − 4² = 40.

β̂₁ = (4·(−21) − 4·(−4)) / 40 = (−84 + 16)/40 = −68/40 = −17/10
β̂₀ = (14·(−4) − 4·(−21)) / 40 = (−56 + 84)/40 = 28/40 = 7/10
answer β̂₀ = 0.7 and β̂₁ = −1.7, so ŷ = −1.7x + 0.7. SSE at the optimum is 21.1.
Check it before you move on
Predictions are 2.4, 0.7, −2.7, −4.4; residuals are −0.4, −0.7, 3.7, −2.6. They sum to 0. Any answer whose residuals do not cancel is arithmetically wrong, and this check costs one line.

Also note how much worse the fit is than in Exercises 1–2: SSE 21.1 against 1.79. And look where the error ends up. The squared residuals are 0.16, 0.49, 13.69 and 6.76 — the biggest by far belongs to (2, 1), not to the obviously odd (3, −7). Squared error pulls the line so hard towards the extreme point that a perfectly ordinary point becomes the worst-fitted one, contributing 65% of the total. That is outlier sensitivity doing real damage, and it is the argument for Least Absolute Deviations in a sentence.

Exercise 4

For a vector with two dimensions (k = 2), what is the maximum possible Gini(v)?

With k = 2, write p₁ = p, so p₂ = 1 − p. Definition 7.4 gives

Gini(v) = p(1 − p) + (1 − p)p = 2p(1 − p) = 2p − 2p²

A downward parabola in p. Its vertex is at p = −b/2a = −2/(2·(−2)) = ½, and there

Gini = 2·(½)·(½) = ½
answer The maximum is ½, reached when the two classes are exactly balanced — v = (m, m) for any m. The minimum is 0, at p = 0 or p = 1, i.e. a pure node.
The general result, which is what a follow-up would ask
For k classes, Gini = 1 − Σpᵢ², and Σpᵢ² is minimised subject to Σpᵢ = 1 when every pᵢ = 1/k. So
max Gini = 1 − k·(1/k)² = 1 − 1/k
k = 2 → ½, k = 3 → ⅔ ≈ 0.667, k = 4 → ¾. Note that the root of Figure 7.5 sits at 0.658 against a ceiling of 0.667 — that node is very nearly as impure as three classes can be, which is why any split at all looks like an improvement.
Exercise 5

Refer to the toy dataset in Table 7.4 — 20 data points, 3 binary features, 4 classes. Which of the 3 attributes should we start splitting the tree by, and what are the three Gini-Split values involved?

Classes in alphabetical order A, B, C, D. The 20 rows give A 6, B 5, C 5, D 4, so the root is [6, 5, 5, 4] and

Gini(root) = (6·14 + 5·15 + 5·15 + 4·16)/20² = 298/400 = 0.745

Now split by each feature in turn. Every feature is binary and — conveniently — splits 10/10, 9/11 and 10/10, so the weights are easy.

splitrowsvalue [A,B,C,D]Gini of that child
Feature1 = 010[4, 2, 4, 0]0.24 + 0.16 + 0.24 + 0 = 0.64
Feature1 = 110[2, 3, 1, 4]0.16 + 0.21 + 0.09 + 0.24 = 0.70
Feature2 = 09[3, 2, 3, 1]58/81 ≈ 0.7160
Feature2 = 111[3, 3, 2, 3]90/121 ≈ 0.7438
Feature3 = 010[2, 3, 3, 2]0.16 + 0.21 + 0.21 + 0.16 = 0.74
Feature3 = 110[4, 2, 2, 2]0.24 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.16 = 0.72

Weighted averages, by Definition 7.5:

Gini-Split(Feature1) = (10/20)(0.64) + (10/20)(0.70) = 0.67
Gini-Split(Feature2) = (9/20)(58/81) + (11/20)(90/121) = 362/495 ≈ 0.7313
Gini-Split(Feature3) = (10/20)(0.74) + (10/20)(0.72) = 0.73
answer Split by Feature1, the arg min. The three values are 0.67, 0.7313… and 0.73 for Features 1, 2 and 3 respectively.
Two things this exercise is really testing
  • Feature2 is the one that does not split 10/10. If you average its two child Ginis unweighted you get 0.7299, which would beat Feature3 and change nothing — but on a differently shaped dataset the unweighted average flips the answer outright. Write the (nⱼ/n) factors down.
  • Every split is barely an improvement. The root sits at 0.745 and the best split only reaches 0.67 — against a theoretical maximum of 1 − ¼ = 0.75 for four classes. These features carry almost no information about the class, which is exactly why the tree that eventually gets built cannot classify the training set perfectly.

Build it in the tree tool with the Table 7.4 preset: three binary features give at most 8 distinct feature vectors for 20 rows across 4 classes, so several leaves stay impure and training accuracy tops out well below 100%.

End of Week 7.

Week 08 · Part 1 · Reinforcement Learning

Bandits & Action Values

two numbers per machine, and that is the whole algorithm

What reinforcement learning is

In one line
Learn by doing. You try things, you see what you get, and you get better at choosing.

That is the lecture's own phrasing: by repeatedly attempting to solve a problem, the agent learns about it and about the result of each of their actions.

How it differs from Week 4
In Week 4 you were told the rewards. You could sit down and compute the answer before moving.

Here nobody tells you anything. The only way to find out what an action is worth is to do it and see. That is the entire difference, and everything in Week 8 follows from it.

The setup: a row of slot machines

The k-armed bandit

You are in front of k slot machines. Each one pays out a different amount on average, but you do not know which is which. You pull one machine per turn.

Your goal: collect as much as possible in total.

Each pull gives a random amount. Even the best machine sometimes pays badly, and the worst one sometimes pays well. That is what makes this hard.

Example 8.1 — two machines

Two machines, A and B. You press one and get whatever it pays. You can do this as often as you like.

Should you keep pressing the one that has done well so far, or try the other? That question is the whole week.

The notes suggest A ∼ N(10, 1) and B ∼ N(11, 4) for experimenting. Careful: N(11, 4) means variance 4, so σ = 2. B is better on average but twice as noisy, which is exactly why it takes a while to tell them apart.

The figure

The two arms from Example 8.1. B has the higher mean (11 vs 10), so B is the better arm — but it is twice as spread out, which is exactly what makes it hard to tell them apart from a few pulls. Remember N(11, 4) means variance 4, so σ = 2.

Tool · Play a bandit

Interactive

Pull the arms yourself, then let a policy try

Click an arm to pull it. Every reward it has paid appears as a dot, and the orange bar is your current Qt(a). The true distributions stay hidden until you tick reveal the true q⋆ — so do what the notes ask: pull a few times, commit to a guess about which arm is better, and only then look. Then hand the controls to greedy, random, ε-greedy or UCB and watch how each one spends its pulls.

The number you can never see: q⋆(a)

Definition 8.2
q⋆(a) is what machine a really pays on average. Written formally:
q⋆(a) = E[Rt | At = a]

Read it as: the average reward you get, given that you pulled machine a. That is all E[…] means — "the average of".

For A ∼ N(10, 1), q⋆(A) is just 10. The mean of the distribution.

The important part
You never get to see q⋆. It is a fact about the machine, not about you. The agent playing Example 8.1 has no way of learning that A's true mean is exactly 10.

In an exam you are handed q⋆ only so the question can be marked. The star means "the real one" — the thing you are trying to guess.

Why the definition has a t in it
The full version is q⋆(a, t), because in principle a machine could change over time. This course assumes it does not — the machines are stationary — so the t is pointless and we drop it.

The number you actually keep: Qt(a)

Q is a running average. That is genuinely all it is.

For each machine you write down two things:

N(a)  — how many times you have pulled it
Q(a)  — the average of what it has paid you

Those two numbers per machine are the entire state of the algorithm. Nothing else is remembered.

Watch it update — this is Exercise 2

Suppose the pulls go: A pays 0.5, A pays −0.3, B pays 0.4, A pays 1.0, B pays 1.5.

Here is what you know each time you are about to choose:

about to choose…what has happened so farQ(A)Q(B)
step 1nothing00
step 2A paid 0.50.5/1 = 0.50
step 3A paid 0.5, −0.30.2/2 = 0.10
step 4… and B paid 0.40.10.4/1 = 0.4
step 5… and A paid 1.01.2/3 = 0.40.4

Read the Q columns straight down and that is the answer to Exercise 2.

The three things that catch people
  • Qt uses everything before step t, not including it. When you are deciding what to pull at step 5, you have seen steps 1 to 4. So the 1.5 that B pays at step 5 does not appear anywhere in the table above.
  • A machine you have never pulled has Q = 0. Not "unknown", not "blank" — the convention is zero. So Q₁(a) = 0 for everything.
  • Only that machine's own rewards count. Money from B never touches Q(A).
The formula, now that you know what it says
Qt(a) = total paid by a before step t / number of times a was pulled before t

Written with symbols it becomes equation (8.4), and the 1Aᵢ=a in it is just a switch: 1 on the steps where a was chosen, 0 everywhere else. It is there to pick out the right rewards. Nothing more.

Tool · Qt(a) from a history

Interactive

Every step, every average, and what greedy would do next

Type a sequence of action reward lines and step through it. The table is exactly the one Exercise 2 asks for, and the panel underneath spells out which rewards went into each average — including the ones that are still 0 because the arm has never been touched. Loaded with Table 8.1 by default.

The dilemma

The whole problem in two sentences

One machine currently has the best average. Do you keep playing it, or try another one?

ExploitExplore
You doplay the machine with the best average so farplay a different one
Becauseit is the best thing you know aboutyour averages might be wrong
Riskyou never discover a better machineyou waste pulls on bad machines
Why your averages might be wrong
You may have been unlucky. Pull the best machine twice and get two poor payouts, and its average now looks terrible — so you stop playing it and never find out.

The notes make this point early with A and B: your very first result from a machine could just be an outlier. One sample tells you almost nothing.

Do not look for a threshold
There is no number that says how much exploring is enough. The lecture says so outright: what counts as too much exploration in one situation is too little in another.

What is examinable is the trade-off itself and the named methods that manage it — which is Part 2.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • RL = learn by doing. The rewards are unknown; you find out by acting.
  • k-armed bandit: k machines, one pull per turn, each pays randomly, maximise the total.
  • q⋆(a) = E[Rt | At = a] — the machine's true average. Unknown to the agent. Constant, because we assume stationary.
  • Qt(a) — your running average, from the pulls strictly before step t. Q₁(a) = 0, and 0 for anything never pulled.
  • N(a) — how many times you pulled it. Q and N are the only things you store.
  • 1predicate is a switch: 1 when true, 0 when false. It selects the right rewards in (8.4).
  • N(µ, σ²) carries the variance. N(11, 4) means σ = 2.
  • Exploit = play the current best. Explore = try something else in case you were unlucky. No fixed definition of "too much".

Part 2 turns the dilemma into three rules.

Week 08 · Part 2 · Reinforcement Learning

Random, Greedy & ε-Greedy

three ways to pick an arm, and only one is a compromise

The 10-armed testbed

The figure

Ten arms. Each shape is one arm's reward distribution — the wider it is at a height, the more likely that reward. The horizontal bar is the arm's true mean q⋆(a). One arm is genuinely best; the agent has to find it by pulling.

What Figure 8.3 shows

Ten arms. Each one pays out with a normal distribution. Two separate random things are going on:

  • How good each arm is. Its true mean was drawn once from N(0, 1).
  • What it pays on a given pull. That varies around its mean, with standard deviation 1.

So one arm really is the best. In the figure it looks like a₅. And it is unique — two arms cannot tie, because drawing the same value twice from a continuous distribution has probability zero.

Two numbers that make Figure 8.4 readable

The arm values came from N(0, 1). So:

  • The average arm is worth 0. A method that hovers at zero has learned nothing.
  • The best arm is worth about 1.54 — that is the expected largest of ten standard normal draws.

Every curve in Figure 8.4 lives between those two numbers. Knowing them turns Exercise 7 from a guess into arithmetic.

The random method

Definition 8.4
Pick an arm uniformly at random, every time:
Pr(At = ai) = 1/k

It does not look at Q at all.

What is wrong with it
It collects information perfectly and then ignores it. Its estimates converge nicely — it just never acts on them.

Its chance of taking the best arm is 1/k on every step, forever. After a million pulls it is still 1/k. For the 50-armed case in Exercise 4 that is 2%.

The greedy method

Definition 8.5
Start with Q₁(a) = 0 for every arm. Then always take the arm with the highest current estimate:
At = arg maxa Qt(a)

If several arms tie for the highest estimate, pick randomly among them.

arg max means "the arm that achieves the maximum" — the arm, not the number.

Three consequences of starting at zero
  • Greedy is not deterministic. At t = 1 every arm sits at 0, so they all tie, and the first pull is a uniform random choice.
  • If rewards are usually positive, greedy gets stuck. The first arm to pay anything above zero beats every untried arm forever. The other k − 1 arms are never pulled once.
  • If rewards are usually negative, the opposite happens. A zero estimate beats any arm you have actually sampled, so greedy keeps switching to untried arms until it has tried them all.

So zero is an optimistic start for negative rewards and a pessimistic one for positive rewards. The notes flag this as a choice, and mention you could instead pull each arm once at the start — “although this is not how we will define it in the context of this lecture”.

The ε-greedy method (epsilon-greedy)

Definition 8.6
Flip a weighted coin before every pull:
  • with probability ε — act at random;
  • with probability 1 − ε — act greedily.

That is the whole method. It is a dial between the two extremes above.

The mistake that costs marks

The random branch picks from all k arms — including the greedy one.

So the chance of taking the greedy arm is not 1 − ε. It is:

(1 − ε) + ε·(1/k)

And the chance of taking any one specific non-greedy arm is ε/k — not zero.

That extra ε/k is exactly what Exercise 5 tests.

The general formula

Let G be the set of arms currently tied for the highest estimate. Then for any arm a:

Pr(At = a) = ε/k  +  (1 − ε)/|G|  if a is in G

Read it as: everyone gets ε/k. The tied leaders split the remaining 1 − ε between them.

So a two-way tie gives each leader (1 − ε)/2, not the full 1 − ε. Ties matter.

Both extremes are already in there
εyou getbecause
0the greedy methodthe random branch never fires
1the random methodthe greedy branch never fires

That is Exercise 6. It is why ε-greedy is presented as the compromise rather than a third option — it contains both of the others.

Reading Figure 8.4

The figure

Recomputed here over 400 simulations. Random sits at 0. Greedy climbs then stalls. ε = 0.1 leads at 500 steps; ε = 0.01 is still catching up and would overtake it much later.

What is plotted
Average reward at each step, up to 500 steps, for ε ∈ {0, 0.01, 0.1, 1}. Averaged over 5000 simulations, and each simulation built a fresh set of 10 arms. So the curves describe the methods, not one lucky testbed.
The four readings
curvewhat it doeswhy
ε = 1 (random)flat, around 0the average arm is worth 0
ε = 0 (greedy)climbs, then stallsit gets stuck on the first arm that paid something positive
ε = 0.1highest at 500 stepsexplores fast enough to find the good arm early
ε = 0.01below 0.1 here, but wins eventuallysee below
Why the smaller ε wins in the long run

The law of large numbers. For any ε > 0, every arm gets sampled infinitely often, so every estimate eventually converges to the truth.

Once that has happened, both methods know which arm is best. The learning is over. What is left is the standing cost of still exploring — and ε = 0.1 randomises ten times as often as ε = 0.01, so it keeps paying more.

Put numerically, once things have settled:

average reward ≈ (1 − ε)·q⋆(best) + ε·(average arm)

On this testbed the average arm is 0, so it is just (1 − ε) × 1.54. Decreasing in ε. That one expression also settles Exercise 7.

Answer the horizon the question asks about
  • “At 500 steps, which is best?” → ε = 0.1.
  • “In the long run, which is best?” → the smallest positive ε.

The crossover happens well past the right edge of the plot. And ε = 0 is excluded from the long-run claim entirely — with no exploration there is no convergence guarantee, because an arm you never pull is an arm you never learn about.

Tool · The testbed, recomputed

Interactive

Figure 8.4, live — and Exercise 7 in one click

Toggle any ε on or off and the curves recompute. Turn on ε = 0.75 to answer Exercise 7 by looking. Switch to % optimal action for the reading Figure 8.4 does not show you: the ceiling 1 − ε + ε/k that each ε imposes on itself, which is why ε = 0.1 flattens out near 91% and never reaches 100%.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • Random: Pr = 1/k, forever. Greedy: arg max Q, ties randomised, Q₁ = 0.
  • ε-greedy: random with probability ε, greedy otherwise. ε = 0 → greedy, ε = 1 → random.
  • Pr(greedy arm) = 1 − ε + ε/k. Pr(a specific other arm) = ε/k. The ε/k is where the marks are.
  • Ties split the greedy share: |G| leaders each get (1 − ε)/|G| plus ε/k.
  • Figure 8.4: random ≈ 0, greedy stalls, ε = 0.1 leads at 500, ε = 0.01 wins asymptotically — by the law of large numbers.
  • Asymptote ≈ (1 − ε)·q⋆(best), which is (1 − ε) × 1.54 here.
  • ε-greedy's flaw: when it explores it treats every arm equally, including ones it already knows are terrible. That is what UCB fixes.

Part 3 fixes exactly that flaw.

Week 08 · Part 3 · Reinforcement Learning

Upper Confidence Bound

explore on purpose, not at random

What is wrong with ε-greedy

It explores stupidly

When ε-greedy decides to explore, it picks completely at random. Suppose you have three machines:

Q(a₁) = 1    Q(a₂) = 10    Q(a₃) = 100

You have pulled a₁ fifty times. You are certain it is bad. But when ε-greedy explores, a₁ is just as likely to be picked as anything else. That pull is wasted.

The fix, in one sentence
Explore the machines you are unsure about, not random ones.

To do that you need to track not just what you think a machine is worth, but how confident you are about it. And confidence has a simple proxy: how many times you have pulled it.

The figure

a₁ has the better estimate (Q = 6 against 4) but a narrow interval — we have pulled it a lot and we are confident. a₂ has been pulled barely at all, so its interval is wide and its upper end reaches 9. UCB picks a₂, because it might be much better than it currently looks.

Reading that picture

Each bar is a machine. The dot is its current average; the bar is how uncertain you are — wide means "barely tried it".

  • a₁ has the better average (6 vs 4), and a narrow bar. You have pulled it a lot and you trust the 6.
  • a₂ has a worse average but a very wide bar. You have barely tried it, so it could be much better than 4.

UCB judges by the right-hand end of the bar. a₂'s reaches 9, a₁'s only reaches 7 — so it takes a₂. Not because a₂ looks good, but because it might be good and you do not yet know.

And this cannot go on forever. Every time you pull a₂ its bar shrinks. Eventually it either proves itself, or its bar drops below a₁'s and you go back to a₁.

The rule

In words first
For each machine, add a bonus to its average. The bonus is big when you have not pulled it much. Then pull whichever total is highest.

That is the entire method. The formula just says how big the bonus is.

Definition 8.7
At = arg maxa [ Qt(a) + c √( ln t / Nt(a) ) ]
pieceis
Atthe machine you pull at step t. It is arg max, so the answer is a machine, not a number.
Qt(a)its average so far — the same running average from Part 1
Nt(a)how many times you pulled it before now
twhich step you are on overall
ca dial you set in advance — bigger c means more exploring

Because N is on the bottom of the fraction, a machine you have barely pulled gets a big bonus. Pull it more and the bonus shrinks.

Remark 8.8 — two rules you need before you can compute anything
  • If you have never pulled a machine, N = 0, and dividing by zero gives ∞. An infinite score always wins, so every machine gets tried once before any machine gets tried twice. A UCB trace therefore always starts a₁, a₂, a₃, … in order.
  • If two machines tie, take the lower-numbered one. a₁ beats a₂.

Careful: the greedy method breaks ties by randomising. UCB breaks them by lowest index. Two different rules in the same week, and swapping them wrecks a whole trace.

One nice consequence: because N = 0 forces a pull, UCB needs no starting value for Q, unlike greedy.

The two halves

Computing ln t without a calculator

Most papers give you these or allow a calculator — but t is always small, so four numbers cover everything:

ln 2 = 0.693    ln 3 = 1.099    ln 5 = 1.609    ln 7 = 1.946

Everything else is those added together, because multiplying inside a log means adding outside it:

ln 1ln 4ln 6ln 8ln 9ln 10
—2·ln2ln2+ln33·ln22·ln3ln2+ln5
01.3861.7922.0792.1972.303

For the square root, bracket it. √1.386 sits between 1.1 (1.21) and 1.2 (1.44); try 1.18, whose square is 1.392. Two decimals is plenty.

And a shortcut that often saves the whole calculation: when every arm has the same N, the bonus is identical for all of them, so it cannot change the ranking — just compare the Q values. That is exactly what happens at t = 4 in Exercise 8.

One half is what you know, the other is what you don't
partnamewhat it is doing
Qt(a)exploitation termuse what you have learned
c √(ln t / Nt(a))exploration termreward machines you are unsure about
cexploration parameterhow much you care about being unsure

c is called a parameter because you choose it before you start and it never changes. Everything else in the formula is produced by playing.

c = 0 kills the bonus entirely, and UCB becomes the greedy method. A common choice is √2; Exercise 8 uses c = 2.

Why ln t is up there

The bonus has t on top and N on the bottom, so:

  • Pull a machine → N grows → its bonus shrinks. You are getting surer about it.
  • Ignore a machine → t keeps growing while its N stays fixed → its bonus slowly creeps up. Time passing makes old information less trustworthy.

That second point is why UCB can never abandon a machine forever. And because it is ln t rather than t, the creep is slow — otherwise UCB would just cycle through every machine in turn and never settle.

The notes also ask you to see that √(ln t / t) → 0: keep pulling the same machine and its bonus vanishes. A-level calculus is enough; no proof required.

Tool · UCB, step by step

Interactive

Every arg max, with the intervals drawn

Loaded with Exercise 8. The picture is Figure 8.5 redrawn at whatever step you are on: one interval per arm, centred on Qt(a) with half-width equal to the exploration term, and the method takes the one whose right-hand end reaches furthest right. Step through with ▶ and the table below shows the full arithmetic — ln t, each √(ln t / N), each UCB. Drag c to 0 and watch UCB become the greedy method.

How this relates to Week 4

Two differences, and the lecture names both
Week 4 · MDPsWeek 8 · Bandits
Rewardsgiven to you — you can compute the answer up frontunknown — you must estimate them by playing
Statesmany; where you are mattersonly one — after every pull you face the same choice again
You estimateU(s), a value per squareq⋆(a), a value per machine

Because there is only one state, some researchers hesitate to call bandits reinforcement learning at all. In a richer problem you would need q⋆(s, a) — a value for every state-and-action pair, not just every action. That single change is the bridge to everything beyond this course.

The chapter's own summary — each line is a complaint about the one before
  1. We have k actions and get rewards from our choices.
  2. Stick with whichever looks best.  → greedy
  3. But what if we were just unlucky with the others?  → ε-greedy
  4. But now we explore even the obviously bad ones.  → UCB
  5. And all of this has only one state.  → MDPs and beyond

Learn those five lines and you can rebuild the whole chapter.

Sources
The notation follows Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, Chapter 2. For UCB specifically, Auer, Cesa-Bianchi & Fischer (2002) — flagged in the notes as heavy maths, and not examinable.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • Why UCB exists: ε-greedy explores at random, wasting pulls on machines it already knows are bad.
  • The rule: score = average + bonus; bonus is big when N is small; pull the highest score.
  • UCBt(a) = Qt(a) + c√(ln t / Nt(a)), and At is the arg max of it.
  • N = 0 gives ∞, so the first k steps are a₁ … ak in order, and no starting Q is needed.
  • Ties → lowest index. (Greedy randomises. Different rule.)
  • N counts pulls before now; ln t uses the current step. Mixing these up shifts every number.
  • c = 0 gives greedy. Bigger c explores more. Common value √2; Exercise 8 uses 2.
  • ln t on top means a neglected machine slowly becomes attractive again — UCB never abandons anything permanently.
  • vs MDPs: rewards unknown, and only one state, so we estimate q⋆(a) not q⋆(s, a).
  • Show a table — t, N, Q, bonus, total, arg max. Exercise 8 is marked on the working.

The Eight Exercises, Worked

every solution box in the PDF is blank — these are filled in and checked
Why this section exists
Chapter 8 poses eight exercises and prints an empty Solution to Exercise n box after each. Every answer below is worked from the definitions and independently re-computed — Exercise 8's trace was reproduced twice, once by hand and once in code, and the UCB tool reproduces it a third time so you can step through it yourself.
Exercise 1

Using the example given before with A and B, what is q⋆(A) and q⋆(B)?

The suggested set-up was A ∼ N(10, 1) and B ∼ N(11, 4). By Definition 8.2, q⋆(a) = E[Rt | At = a] — the expected value of the reward distribution, and the expected value of N(µ, σ²) is µ.

answer q⋆(A) = 10 and q⋆(B) = 11. The optimal action is B.
The three things this one-line question is checking
  • q⋆ is the mean, not the maximum and not any observed reward. B can and will pay less than A on plenty of individual pulls.
  • The variance is irrelevant to q⋆. B's σ² = 4 makes it noisier, not better or worse. It affects how hard B is to identify, not what it is worth.
  • This is exactly the number the agent never sees. You can answer it only because you were handed the distributions; an agent playing Example 8.1 has to approach 10 and 11 through Qt.
Exercise 2

Consider the sequence of actions and rewards in Table 8.1. Assuming Qt(a) = 0 if a has not been taken before t, evaluate Qt(A) and Qt(B) for each t, 1 ≤ t ≤ 5.

t12345
AtAABAB
Rt0.5−0.30.41.01.5

The whole exercise turns on “before t”: Qt averages steps 1 … t − 1 only.

trewards from A so farQt(A)rewards from B so farQt(B)
1none0none0
20.50.5/1 = 0.5none0
30.5, −0.30.2/2 = 0.1none0
40.5, −0.30.2/2 = 0.10.40.4/1 = 0.4
50.5, −0.3, 1.01.2/3 = 0.40.40.4/1 = 0.4
answer
Qt(A):  0,  0.5,  0.1,  0.1,  0.4
Qt(B):  0,  0  ,  0  ,  0.4,  0.4
Four traps in five columns
  • Q₁ is 0 for both, not undefined. Nothing has happened yet.
  • R₅ = 1.5 never appears anywhere, because the table stops at t = 5 and Q₅ only sees steps 1–4. If the question had asked for Q₆ you would get Q₆(B) = (0.4 + 1.5)/2 = 0.95.
  • Q₃(A) = 0.1, not 0.5. The −0.3 at t = 2 has already landed.
  • At t = 5 the two estimates tie at 0.4. Definition 8.5 then says a greedy player randomises between them — a 50/50 choice, not "keep doing what you were doing". The tool's verdict line makes this call at every step.
Exercise 3

For each of the two strategies, discuss whether they could be considered doing too much exploration or exploitation, and why. (a) A greedy algorithm — the next action is determined by the highest average reward given so far. (b) A random algorithm — it just picks the next action at random.

answer Greedy does far too much exploitation; random does far too much exploration. Neither uses the other mode at all.

(a) The greedy algorithm — pure exploitation.

  • It acts on its current estimates and nothing else. Every step is spent on the arm that currently looks best.
  • The failure mode is the one the notes name in §8.5: it gets ‘stuck’ in any action with a positive value and misses ones possibly much better. With Q₁(a) = 0 and positive rewards, an arm that pays well once may be the only arm ever tried.
  • A single lucky sample is never corrected, because correcting it would require sampling a rival — which greedy will not do. Equally, a single unlucky sample of the truly best arm is fatal: it will never get a second chance.
  • Its one saving grace: ties are randomised, so at t = 1 it does pick uniformly. After that it can narrow to one arm forever.

(b) The random algorithm — pure exploration.

  • It gathers information beautifully — every arm is sampled 1/k of the time, so all its estimates converge to the true q⋆.
  • And then it throws that information away. Nothing it learns ever changes what it does. It is not really a learning algorithm at all.
  • Its expected reward per step is the average over all arms, forever — 0 on the N(0, 1) testbed of Figure 8.4, which is why the random curve is flat at zero.
The point the exercise is setting up
Both are extreme, and in opposite directions — which is what makes them the two endpoints of a single dial. “A balance between greedy and random could be a possible way forward”, and ε-greedy is exactly that dial: a weighted coin between (a) and (b), with ε as the weight.

If a question asks you to argue rather than classify, the strongest line is about information: greedy never buys any, random never spends any, and the useful algorithms do both.

Exercise 4

Consider a 50-armed bandit problem. What is the probability, at each time t, that a random method selects the optimal action?

By Definition 8.4 the random method takes each action with probability 1/k, independently of everything that has happened. There is exactly one optimal action — the notes justify uniqueness in §8.4: the probability of drawing two exactly equal values from a normal distribution is null. With k = 50:

Pr(At = optimal) = 1/50 = 0.02
answer 1/50 = 0.02 = 2%, at every t, forever — it never improves.
The follow-up worth pre-empting
“At each time t” is doing real work in the question. The answer is constant in t, which is the whole indictment of the random method: after a million steps it is still 2%. Contrast ε-greedy, whose probability of the optimal action rises towards its ceiling of 1 − ε + ε/k as the estimates converge.

For k = 50 and ε = 0.1 that ceiling is 0.9 + 0.002 = 90.2%. Same problem, forty-five times better, from one weighted coin.

Exercise 5

A 2-armed bandit at t = 10, with q⋆(a₁) = 2 and q⋆(a₂) = 2.3. Using ε-greedy with ε = 0.5, what is the probability that the optimal action is selected at step t = 10, when (i) Q₁₀(a₁) = 2.4, Q₁₀(a₂) = 2.1; (ii) Q₁₀(a₁) = 2.1, Q₁₀(a₂) = 2.4; (iii) Q₁₀(a₁) = 2.4, Q₁₀(a₂) = 2.4?

First: the optimal action is a₂, because q⋆(a₂) = 2.3 > 2 = q⋆(a₁). The q⋆ values are used only for that — the agent's choice depends on the Q's alone. With k = 2 and ε = 0.5, the random branch gives each arm ε/k = 0.25.

Pr(a₂) = ε·(1/k)  +  (1 − ε)·Pr(greedy picks a₂) = 0.25 + 0.5·Pr(greedy picks a₂)
caseQ₁₀(a₁), Q₁₀(a₂)greedy takesPr(greedy → a₂)Pr(optimal a₂)
(i)2.4, 2.1a₁00.25 + 0.5·0 = 0.25
(ii)2.1, 2.4a₂10.25 + 0.5·1 = 0.75
(iii)2.4, 2.4tie → randomise½0.25 + 0.5·0.5 = 0.5
answer (i) 0.25  ·  (ii) 0.75  ·  (iii) 0.5
Three ways to lose the marks here
  • Answering 0 for case (i). Even when greedy points the wrong way, the random branch still reaches a₂ with probability ε/k = 0.25. The greedy branch is not the only route.
  • Answering 1 − ε = 0.5 for case (ii). The greedy action also collects its share of the random branch: 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75.
  • Forgetting the tie rule in case (iii). Definition 8.5 randomises among the maxima, so the greedy branch itself is a coin flip. Answering 0.75 (treating a₂ as “the” greedy choice) or 0.25 (treating a₁ as it) both miss it.

Sanity check on the whole answer set: the three cases are 0.25 < 0.5 < 0.75, in the order estimates point away → estimates tie → estimates point at it. The middle case must sit exactly halfway, and it does.

Exercise 6

Both random and greedy methods are particular cases of the ε-greedy method. What should you set ε to in order to obtain, respectively, the greedy and random methods?

answer ε = 0 gives the greedy method. ε = 1 gives the random method.

Straight from Definition 8.6, which says: with probability ε act randomly, with probability 1 − ε act greedily.

  • ε = 0 — the random branch fires with probability 0, so every step is arg maxa Qt(a). That is Definition 8.5 exactly, ties and all.
  • ε = 1 — the greedy branch fires with probability 0, so every step is uniform over the k arms. That is Definition 8.4 exactly.
Why the question is asked at all
It fixes the shape of ε as a dial between two named extremes, not a free parameter with arbitrary meaning. Every claim in §8.5 then reads as a statement about position on that dial — and it is worth noticing that Figure 8.4 plots both endpoints and two interior points of the same one-parameter family.

A likely follow-up: does some ε strictly dominate? No. Larger ε learns faster but pays more forever; smaller ε learns slower but pays less. The best ε depends on how long you intend to play — which is precisely why §8.5 is careful to say ε = 0.1 wins at 500 steps while ε = 0.01 wins in the long run.

Exercise 7

Assume the ε = 0.1 line in Figure 8.4 is close to stabilising, and will stabilise before an average reward of 2. If we add the line for ε = 0.75, at 500 steps do you expect its average reward to be: (1) lower than random, (2) between random and greedy, (3) between greedy and ε = 0.01, (4) between ε = 0.01 and ε = 0.1, or (5) higher than ε = 0.1?

answer (2) — between random and greedy.

The argument. Once the estimates have roughly converged, an ε-greedy agent spends a fraction (1 − ε) of its steps on the best arm and a fraction ε on a uniformly random arm, so its average reward is about

(1 − ε)·q⋆(best)  +  ε·(mean arm value)

On this testbed the arm values come from N(0, 1), so the mean arm is worth 0 and the second term vanishes. The reward is therefore roughly proportional to (1 − ε):

ε≈ (1 − ε) × q⋆(best)simulated at 500 steps
1 (random)0≈ 0.00
0.750.25 × 1.54 ≈ 0.39≈ 0.38
0 (greedy)— stalls early, does not reach q⋆(best)≈ 1.04
0.010.99 × 1.54 ≈ 1.52 eventually≈ 1.22
0.10.90 × 1.54 ≈ 1.39≈ 1.36

So ε = 0.75 lands near 0.39 — clearly above random's 0, and clearly below greedy's ≈ 1.0. Option 2. Turn ε = 0.75 on in the testbed tool and the curve appears exactly there.

Where the 1.54 comes from, if you want the number rather than the shape
It is the expected maximum of 10 independent standard normals ≈ 1.54 — the value of the best arm on an average testbed. You are not expected to know it; the hint in the question (“ε = 0.1 stabilises before 2”) exists so you can work backwards: if ε = 0.1 stabilises at 0.9·q⋆(best) and that is under 2, then q⋆(best) is a bit over 1.5, and 0.25 of it is around 0.4.

The qualitative argument alone earns the answer: ε = 0.75 spends three quarters of its steps choosing uniformly at random — which is worth 0 — so it cannot do much better than a quarter of the best arm's value, and that is well below what even greedy manages. The only genuinely tempting wrong answer is (1), on the thought that "more randomness is worse than random"; but ε = 0.75 still exploits a quarter of the time, so it must strictly beat pure random.

Exercise 8

Determine A₁, …, A₈ in the 3-armed bandit whose arms pay, in order, a₁: 5, 4, 7, 3, 7 · a₂: 3.5, 7, 1, 1, 1 · a₃: 6, 0, 4, 4, 3. Also give UCB₈(a) for the three actions — the values used to determine A₈. Use c = 2.

Apply (8.5) with c = 2, using Remark 8.8: N = 0 counts as +∞, and ties go to the lowest index. Nt(a) counts pulls strictly before t.

tln tUCBt(a₁)UCBt(a₂)UCBt(a₃)AtRt
10+∞+∞+∞a₁ tie → lowest5
20.69316.6651+∞+∞a₂ tie → lowest3.5
31.09867.09635.5963+∞a₃6
41.38637.35485.85488.3548a₃0
51.60947.53736.03734.7941a₁4
61.79186.39306.17714.8930a₁7
71.94596.94416.28994.9728a₁3
82.07946.19206.38415.0393a₂7
answer
A₁ … A₈  =  a₁, a₂, a₃, a₃, a₁, a₁, a₁, a₂

UCB₈(a₁) = 4.75 + 2√(2.0794/4) = 6.1920
UCB₈(a₂) = 3.5   + 2√(2.0794/1) = 6.3841
UCB₈(a₃) = 3     + 2√(2.0794/2) = 5.0393

Two steps written out in full, since that is what earns the marks:

t = 5:  N₅ = (1, 1, 2),  Q₅ = (5, 3.5, 3),  ln 5 = 1.6094
    a₁: 5 + 2√(1.6094/1) = 5 + 2(1.2686) = 7.5373  ←  max
    a₂: 3.5 + 2(1.2686) = 6.0373
    a₃: 3 + 2√(1.6094/2) = 3 + 2(0.8971) = 4.7941

t = 8:  N₈ = (4, 1, 2),  Q₈ = (4.75, 3.5, 3),  ln 8 = 2.0794
    a₁: 4.75 + 2√(2.0794/4) = 4.75 + 2(0.7210) = 6.1920
    a₂: 3.5 + 2√(2.0794/1) = 3.5 + 2(1.4420) = 6.3841  ←  max
    a₃: 3 + 2√(2.0794/2) = 3 + 2(1.0198) = 5.0393
What the trace is actually demonstrating
  • The first three steps are forced. Every arm has N = 0 and therefore +∞, so a₁, a₂, a₃ come out in index order. This is always how a UCB trace starts, for any rewards.
  • a₃ is picked twice in a row and then dropped. Its 6 at t = 3 made it the leader; the 0 at t = 4 halved its average to 3 and it is never seen again in these eight steps. UCB reacts fast to a bad sample because the estimate moves and the interval shrinks at the same time.
  • a₁ is exploited three times running (t = 5, 6, 7) — UCB is not obliged to alternate. It only moves on when the exploitation term stops covering the shrinking exploration term.
  • A₈ = a₂ is the whole point of the chapter. At t = 8, a₂ has the worst estimate of the three (Q = 3.5 against a₁'s 4.75) but it has been pulled once, so its interval is by far the widest — 2√(2.0794/1) = 2.884 against a₁'s 1.442. It wins on uncertainty, not on merit. That is Figure 8.5, arrived at by arithmetic.
  • And it was right. a₂'s second reward is 7, lifting Q(a₂) to 5.25 — the best of the three. An ε-greedy agent would have reached that only by luck; a purely greedy one, never.
Three arithmetic slips that derail the whole table
  • Using log₁₀ instead of ln. ln 8 = 2.0794, log₁₀ 8 = 0.9031. Everything downstream changes.
  • Counting the current pull in Nt. N is pulls prior to t. At t = 8, a₁ has been pulled 4 times (t = 1, 5, 6, 7), not 5.
  • Putting c inside the square root. It is c·√(ln t / N), not √(c·ln t / N). With c = 2 that is a factor of √2 wrong on every exploration term.

Keep a running (N, Q) pair per arm in the margin and update it after each pick — that alone prevents all three.

End of Week 8.

Week 09 · Part 1 · AI Ethics

Application & Access

what AI is used for, and who gets to use it

Where this week comes from

The opening slide, and why it is the whole module in one box
AlgorithmsSearch, Constraint Satisfaction, Planning · Regression, Classification, Reinforcement
PromisesEfficiency, accuracy
ApplicationsMap navigation · Scheduling · Logistics planning · Robotics · Computer games · Visual classification · Recommendation · Decision-making in finance and government
Risks?→ AI ethics

That first row is Weeks 1–8, exactly. The lecture's move is to point out that every one of those techniques has now been deployed on people, and to ask what follows.

The five key questions — the spine of the whole lecture
  1. How is AI applied in practice? Who has access? Who benefits?
  2. What are the harms and ethical considerations of AI? Who is harmed?
  3. How does bias manifest in AI? Why does it arise?
  4. Who is responsible for the harms of AI?
  5. How do we minimise these harms?

The final slide answers all five in one line each. If you learn one structure from this week, learn this one — it turns any open-ended ethics question into five headings you can write under.

How this week is examined differently
There is nothing to compute here and no worked exercises. Questions are “name and explain”, “classify this case” and “discuss”. What earns marks is using the lecture's own vocabulary — allocative vs representational, direct vs indirect discrimination, the five named causes of bias — rather than general concern. The tools in this week's sections drill exactly those distinctions.

How is AI applied?

Two columns, and two different questions
Well-intentioned applicationsFundamentally problematic applications
Map navigation, music recommendation, phone assistants, computer games, home robots, face detection in photos Military drones, deepfake pornography, criminality prediction from faces, crowd surveillance, phrenology-style facial analysis, oil & gas exploration
“What could be the hidden problems/risks?” “Should we even build this?”

The two questions are not interchangeable, and that is the point of the slide. For the left column, ethics is a matter of mitigation — find the hidden harm and design it out. For the right column, no amount of mitigation is the answer; the question is whether the system should exist. An answer that responds to a right-column case with “use a more balanced dataset” has missed what is being asked.

Applied to policing

Three consequences the lecture names
  • Increased breadth of surveillance.
  • Worse facial recognition performance on minorities due to lack of data → wrongful arrests / stop-and-search.
  • Lack of accountability of AI systems.

Note the causal chain in the middle bullet, because it is the one the exam can ask you to unpack: lack of data → representation bias → worse performance on a group → a real-world allocative harm. Four of this module's concepts in one sentence.

Applied to the military

Two uses, and what follows from each
Search for specific (human) targetsAutomated defense
  • Propagation of bias into war
  • More deaths
  • Dehumanization of war
  • Loss of moral engagement
  • Simplification of complex moral choices
  • Easier escalation
  • Arms races

The automated-defense column is worth reading closely: none of those five harms requires the system to malfunction. They follow from it working exactly as designed. That is a distinction worth making explicitly in an essay answer — most harms in this lecture are failure modes, and these are not.

Applied to political control

Two mechanisms
  • State surveillance of opposition, ethnic and religious minorities → strengthening authoritarian states; human rights losses: privacy, freedom of speech, religious freedom.
  • Increased censorship and disinformation → loss of freedom of speech; less informed citizens; political polarisation and control.
The Week 1 callback
Week 1 introduced the value alignment problem — the difficulty of exactly specifying what “good” means for a system. Weeks 4 and 8 made it numeric: a reward function is the specification. This slide is the same problem at the scale of a state: a system aligned to its operator's values is not thereby aligned to anyone else's. Value alignment appears again as a mitigation method in Part 4, and it is worth being able to connect all three appearances.

The revival of phrenology

The definition to be able to give
Phrenology: a disproved pseudoscience that assumes predictions of gender, intelligence, criminality and internal states can be made from facial analysis.

The lecture's charge is that current AI applications revive it: prediction of gender, sexuality, race, emotion, criminality from images.

Why this is a category error, not just an accuracy problem
These are social constructs, or unobservable — only the subjects can say.

That sentence is the crux, and it is what separates this slide from the rest of the lecture. Everywhere else the complaint is that the system gets the answer wrong for some people. Here there is no ground truth to get right. You cannot fix a sexuality classifier by collecting a more representative dataset, because the label was never a property of the face. This is measurement bias in its purest form — wrong categorization of people — and it is unfixable by construction.

The consequences listed

Such systems allow the oppression of already marginalized communities — the lecture names LGBT and Black communities — through:

  • Reinforcing harmful stereotypes
  • Mis-identification and micro-aggressive ad-targeting
  • The policing case: “our AI system tells us you are feeling guilty, why?!”

That last example is doing real work. It shows the harm arriving even when nobody believes the output is reliable — the mere existence of the claim shifts the burden of proof onto the person. A false accusation you must disprove is a harm regardless of the system's accuracy.

Who has access to AI?

AI is expensive
  • Lots of computation power
  • Expensive hardware (e.g. GPUs)
  • Money to train, money to house
  • Big Tech monopoly (Google, Amazon…)

The result:

  • Universities can't compete, and their resources end up used for Big Tech's priority problems.
  • Poorer labs and countries can't afford it at all.
Why "who has access" is an ethics question and not an economics one
Because access determines which problems get solved. If the only actors who can train large models are a handful of companies, then the research agenda is set by their priorities — and the problems of people those companies do not sell to simply do not get worked on. That is a harm without a villain and without a bug, which is why it needs its own slide.

It also links forward to Part 4: team diversity and participatory design are mitigations aimed at exactly this, an agenda set by too narrow a group.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • The five key questions — application/access, harms, bias, responsibility, minimisation. Use them as headings.
  • Two kinds of application: well-intentioned (“what are the hidden risks?”) and fundamentally problematic (“should we even build this?”). Answer the right question for the case.
  • Policing: breadth of surveillance · worse performance on minorities from lack of data → wrongful arrests · lack of accountability.
  • Military: targeting (bias into war, more deaths); automated defense (dehumanization, loss of moral engagement, simplification of moral choices, easier escalation, arms races).
  • Political control: surveillance of opposition and minorities; censorship and disinformation → polarisation, less informed citizens.
  • Phrenology: define it, then say why prediction of gender/sexuality/race/emotion/criminality from faces revives it — social constructs or unobservable, only the subjects can say.
  • Access: compute, hardware, money, Big Tech monopoly → universities can't compete, poorer labs and countries excluded.

Part 2 sets out the seven categories of harm.

Week 09 · Part 2 · AI Ethics

The Seven Harms

a taxonomy worth knowing in order

The seven categories

The list, in the lecture's order
  1. Human agency harms
  2. Accountability harms
  3. Safety and wellbeing harms
  4. Privacy harms
  5. Fairness and dignity harms
  6. Societal harms
  7. Environmental harms

A question that says “discuss the harms of this system” is asking you to walk this list. Most systems touch four or five of them, and naming the categories you rule out is worth as much as developing the ones you keep.

1 · Human agency

Four items
  • Loss of human control over algorithms
  • Loss of the human right to contest decisions
  • Over-delegation
  • Loss of critical thinking

All four can occur while the system is working perfectly. That is what distinguishes agency harms: they are about what happens to the human in the loop, not about errors.

2 · Accountability

Two items, pointing in opposite directions
  • Loss of human accountability for harm — nobody is answerable.
  • Incorrect blaming of humans for AI failures — the wrong person is answerable. The lecture's example: warehouse workers blamed for robot mistakes.

Worth stating as a pair in an answer. Accountability can fail by evaporating or by landing on the wrong person, and the second is easy to forget.

3 · Safety and wellbeing

Four items
  • Physical safety
  • Abuse and tech-facilitated violence
  • Health
  • Wellbeing

The lecture gives physical safety its own slide first and then adds the other three, which is a hint about how easily the non-physical ones get overlooked. Abuse and tech-facilitated violence sits here rather than under privacy, because the harm is the abuse the tool enables, not the information it exposes.

4 · Privacy invasion

Split by setting, not by mechanism
  • Privacy in intimate spaces
  • Privacy at work & school
  • Privacy in public spaces

Name the setting in an answer. “Privacy in public spaces” is the least intuitive of the three and the one that covers city-scale camera networks — the expectation of privacy does not vanish because you are outdoors.

5 · Fairness and dignity

The one distinction most likely to be examined
Allocative / distributionalRepresentational
Aboutwho gets thingshow people are portrayed
Sub-types
  • Distribution of opportunities
  • Distribution of resources
  • Distribution of quality-of-service
  • Stereotyping
  • Demeaning — cast as less deserving of respect
  • Erasing
  • Alienating — cast as not belonging
  • Loss of the opportunity to self-identify
  • Essentialist social categories
Examplea hiring model shortlisting fewer women; speech recognition working worse on some accentsan image generator returning only men for “CEO”; a form with two gender boxes
Why the split matters practically
Allocative harms are measurable and representational harms often are not. You can count how many loans went to each group; you cannot straightforwardly count how demeaned a depiction is. That asymmetry is why the anticipation slide pairs quantitative methods with qualitative methods and critique — some harms are only reachable through interviews, ethnography and argument.

Quality-of-service is the sub-type students most often miss. Nobody is refused the service; it simply works worse for them. Gender Shades and the pedestrian-detection results in Part 3 are both this.

6 · Societal

Five items
  • Information
  • Cultural
  • Civic and political
  • Social relationships
  • Deskilling

Societal harms have no identifiable individual victim — that is the test for putting something here. A polarised electorate and a deskilled profession are harms to a public, which is also why they are the hardest to litigate and the easiest to ignore.

Deskilling vs over-delegation — a distinction worth making
Over-delegation (human agency) is about this decision, now being handed to a system. Deskilling (societal) is about the capability being lost across a profession, so that nobody could take the decision back even if they wanted to. One is a choice; the other is the accumulated consequence of everyone making it.

7 · Environmental

Three items
  • Energy consumption and pollution
  • Mineral mining for datacentres
  • AI and robots for the oil & gas industry

The third is the one people forget, and it is different in kind from the other two: the harm is not the model's own footprint but what the model is used to accelerate. A perfectly efficient model that helps locate new oil reserves is an environmental harm by this taxonomy.

Tool · The harm map

Interactive

Browse the seven, then classify cases against them

The seven harms tab is the full taxonomy with every sub-item, collapsed so you can test yourself before opening a card. ★ classify a case gives you a short scenario and asks which category the lecture would file it under — including the cases that plausibly span two, where the explanation says which is primary and why.

What happens after harm — reparation

Ten types of harm reparation
  1. Public outcry — protests, petitions, online backlash
  2. Perpetrator communication — denials, justifications, apologies
  3. Investigation of harm — audits, journalism
  4. Initiation of legal actions
  5. Legal repercussions — fines, criminal charges, dismissals
  6. Compensation — refunds, settlements
  7. Removal — data removal, product recall
  8. Product discontinuation
  9. Design changes
  10. Law/policy change
Reading the list as a sequence
It is roughly ordered from immediate and informal to slow and structural. Outcry costs nothing and changes nothing on its own; law change is the only item that affects anyone other than the perpetrator. Note that “perpetrator communication” includes denials and justifications — the list is descriptive of what does happen, not prescriptive of what should.

All ten are after the harm. That is precisely why the next slide exists.

Anticipating and evaluating harm — before it happens

Four families of method
FamilyMethods
Quantitative measurement
of model/data statistics
  • Performance differences between social groups (e.g. accuracy)
  • Output differences between social groups
  • Incidence of bad data (e.g. explicit content)
Ablation studies
  • Removing/changing data and observing results
  • Changing algorithm parameters and observing results
Qualitative methods Interviews · Surveys · Workshops · Literature reviews · Ethnography
Critique Speculation · Logical or philosophical argument
Why all four families are needed
Quantitative methods can only find harms you already thought to measure. A performance gap between groups shows up in a table only once you have decided which groups to break the data down by — and deciding that is not itself a quantitative act.

That is what qualitative methods and critique are for, and it is also why “who is discovering these issues” gets its own slide in Part 3. A question asking how you would evaluate a system for harm should name methods from more than one family.

Note too that “performance differences between social groups” is precisely the disaggregated evaluation that the fairness tool computes — the first row of this table is a thing you now know how to do.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • The seven harms in order: human agency · accountability · safety and wellbeing · privacy · fairness and dignity · societal · environmental.
  • Allocative vs representational is the key sub-distinction. Allocative = opportunities, resources, quality-of-service. Representational = stereotyping, demeaning, erasing, alienating, loss of self-identification, essentialist categories.
  • Accountability fails two ways: it evaporates, or it lands on the wrong person.
  • Privacy is split by setting: intimate spaces, work & school, public spaces.
  • Societal harms have no identifiable individual victim — that is the test.
  • Environmental includes AI for oil & gas, not just the model's own footprint.
  • Reparation happens after the harm — ten types, from public outcry to law change. Anticipation happens before — quantitative, ablation, qualitative, critique.
  • Deskilling (societal) ≠ over-delegation (agency); abuse (safety) ≠ privacy invasion.

Part 3 asks where the bias comes from.

Week 09 · Part 3 · AI Ethics

Discrimination & Bias

three definitions, four examples, five causes

The three definitions

Direct and indirect discrimination — learn both names for each
Direct discrimination
“disparate treatment”		Indirect discrimination
“disparate impact”
Definition when somebody is disadvantaged because of a personal attribute (e.g. age, gender, race) when people with a certain personal attribute are disadvantaged even though the attribute is not explicitly considered in decisions
Is the attribute an input?YesNo — and this is the point
Examplea model that takes race as a feature and scores accordinglya model that takes postcode, which correlates with race

The exam-relevant consequence: deleting the protected attribute from your feature set does not make a system fair. It rules out direct discrimination and leaves indirect discrimination completely untouched — and indirect is the kind almost every real AI case turns out to be.

Bias, in the context of AI ethics
The lecture gives it two senses, and you should be able to say which you mean:
  • Imbalance or tendency in data — the input sense.
  • Direct or indirect discrimination — the output sense.

These are connected but not the same, and conflating them is a common source of muddle: imbalanced data does not automatically produce discrimination, and discrimination can arise from perfectly balanced data (via the label, the objective, or the metric). The five causes on the next slide are precisely the routes from one to the other.

Four documented examples

1 · Recidivism prediction — ProPublica, “Machine Bias”
The algorithm was more likely to mistakenly predict high-risk on Black than on White defendants.

Read the sentence carefully, because the precision matters: the claim is about mistaken high-risk predictions — a difference in the false positive rate between groups, not simply a difference in scores. Two groups can receive different score distributions for entirely legitimate reasons; being wrongly flagged at different rates is harder to defend.

In the taxonomy: an allocative harm (distribution of opportunities — liberty, bail), arising from measurement bias if the label is re-arrest, and it is indirect discrimination since race is not an input.

2 · Generative models — GPT-3 and DALL·E
The slide shows outputs from both, with the caption “All white male.”

This is a representational harm rather than an allocative one — nobody is denied a resource. Stereotyping and erasing are the relevant sub-types. It is worth noticing that this failure has no victim who can point to a decision made about them, which is exactly why the reparation list in Part 2 works so poorly for it.

3 · Pedestrian detection — Brandao (2019)
“Age and gender bias in pedestrian detection algorithms.” The slide shows miss rates differing by age and gender group.

A quality-of-service allocative harm with an obvious physical safety consequence — a detector that misses children more often is a safety harm, not merely an accuracy footnote. This is the clearest case in the lecture of one harm category producing another.

4 · Gender classification — Buolamwini & Gebru, “Gender Shades” (2018)

The slide reproduces the error-rate table across Fitzpatrick skin types I–VI for three commercial systems:

systemType IType IIType IIIType IVType VType VI
Microsoft1.7%1.1%3.3%0%23.2%25.0%
Face++11.9%9.7%8.2%13.9%32.4%46.5%
IBM5.1%7.4%8.2%8.3%33.3%46.8%

What to take from the numbers. Two of the three systems are close to a coin flip on the darkest skin type — 46.5% and 46.8% error on a binary classification. And the best system goes from 0% error on Type IV to 25% on Type VI. No single overall accuracy figure would have shown any of this, which is the whole argument for disaggregated evaluation.

Why "intersectional" is in the paper's title
The disparity is far larger for combinations of attributes than for either attribute alone. A system can look nearly even across gender overall and nearly even across skin type overall, and still fail catastrophically for the group at the intersection of both. Checking one attribute at a time is not enough — and this is a good, specific point to make in an answer about evaluation.

Feed these numbers into the fairness-function tool to see what different objectives do with them.

The five causes of discrimination by AI

Branch 1 — the risk was not anticipated, tested, or alleviated
causethe lecture's descriptiondeveloper's fault?
World biasworld distribution problemno
Representation biasdata collection problem★ yes
Measurement biaswrong categorization of people, or wrong measurements★ yes
Algorithm biaswrong choice of algorithm★ yes
Evaluation biaswrong choice of evaluation metric or test set★ yes

Four of the five carry the developer's-fault marker. Only world bias does not — because the data is an accurate record of an unequal world, so no amount of better collection fixes it. That single exception is an easy thing to be asked about, and the answer is not “so it's nobody's fault”: deploying a system that reproduces world bias is still a decision somebody made.

Branch 2 — the risk is obvious, the task is problematic
failuredeveloper's fault?
Ethics board does not flag a problem—
Developer doesn't oppose building it, doesn't report, doesn't blow the whistle★ yes
Management makes the decision to deploy—

This is the branch for the right-hand column of Part 1 — cases where the question was “should we even build this?” and the answer was no. The developer's fault here is not a technical failure but a failure to object, which is why whistleblowing appears in the mitigation list in Part 4.

Tool · Where bias enters

Interactive

The pipeline, and a diagnosis drill

The pipeline tab lays the five causes out along the stages they arise in — the world, data collection, measurement, the algorithm, evaluation — with each one's fault marker, an example and its usual mitigation. ★ diagnose a case gives you something that went wrong and asks which cause the lecture would name. The pairs that are easy to confuse — representation vs evaluation, algorithm vs evaluation — are deliberately both in the bank.

Who is discovering these issues

The slide, in full
  • Women
  • Black scholars
  • LGBTQ
  • …

→ Importance of lived experience & diversity.

Why this slide sits here rather than in the mitigation section
Because it is an empirical claim about how these findings actually got made, not a recommendation. Gender Shades was authored by Buolamwini and Gebru; the disparities had been sitting in deployed commercial products, measurable by anyone, for years before someone thought to break the numbers down that way.

The argument it supports is a practical one: you cannot test for a harm you have not imagined, and what you imagine is bounded by who is in the room. That is why team diversity and participatory design appear as mitigations in Part 4 — they are not gestures at fairness, they are proposed as error-detection mechanisms. Making that argument explicitly is worth more than asserting that diversity is good.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • Direct discrimination = disparate treatment — disadvantaged because of a personal attribute. Indirect = disparate impact — disadvantaged even though the attribute is not explicitly considered.
  • Removing the protected attribute does not prevent indirect discrimination, and most real cases are indirect.
  • Bias has an input sense (imbalance or tendency in data) and an output sense (direct or indirect discrimination).
  • The five causes: world · representation · measurement · algorithm · evaluation. All but world bias are marked the developer's fault.
  • Second branch: obvious risk, problematic task — ethics board, developer not objecting/whistleblowing (★), management deploying.
  • The examples: ProPublica recidivism (mistaken high-risk more often for Black defendants) · GPT-3 / DALL·E (“all white male”) · Brandao 2019 pedestrian miss rates · Buolamwini & Gebru 2018 Gender Shades (up to 46.8% error on the darkest skin type against near-zero on the lightest).
  • Lived experience and diversity — the people finding these problems are disproportionately from the groups affected, which is an argument for diversity as error detection.

Part 4 is what to do about all of it.

Week 09 · Part 4 · AI Ethics

Mitigation & Responsibility

principles, governance, named methods — and who is answerable

Designing with ethical principles

Who publishes these
Many institutions are adopting guidelines for the ethical development and deployment of AI — governmental (UK EPSRC, NHS, EU…) and professional (IEEE, ACM…).
The seven principles table — reproduced in full
PrincipleDescription
Human oversight and agencyUpholding fundamental rights, informed decisions, correct trust, human-in-the-loop
Safety and robustnessMinimization of errors, functioning for a range of settings, resilience to attack
PrivacyConsent, anonymity, access, de-anonymization
TransparencyDocumentation and logging of data/decisions, explainability, informing when AI is used
FairnessNon-discrimination, accessibility, stakeholder participation
Societal & environmental wellbeingEnvironmental impact, impact to social relationships, democracy, politics
AccountabilityAuditability, documenting how dilemmas and trade-offs were resolved, responsibility for harms
The structure that makes this table memorable
The principles are the harms, restated as requirements. Line them up: agency ↔ human agency harms, safety ↔ safety and wellbeing, privacy ↔ privacy, fairness ↔ fairness and dignity, societal & environmental ↔ the last two harm categories, accountability ↔ accountability harms.

The one principle with no matching harm category is transparency — and the one harm category with no matching principle name is none, since societal and environmental are merged into one principle. So the mapping is nearly one-to-one, with transparency as the extra. If you can recall the seven harms you can reconstruct this table.

Note also what sits under accountability: documenting how dilemmas and trade-offs were resolved. Not avoiding trade-offs — recording how you made them. That is a realistic standard, and worth quoting.

Governance methods

Three items
  • Strengthening regulations, standards, codes of conduct — to safeguard current deployments and to guide/constrain the trajectory of future development.
  • Implementing processes of internal and external auditing, verification and validation.
  • “Trustworthy AI”: design AND governance that leads to AI we can trust — designing AI with ethical principles, and governing development and deployment.

The capitalised AND is the lecture's own emphasis, and it is the examinable point: “trustworthy AI” is not a design property alone. A perfectly principled system inside an ungoverned organisation is not trustworthy, and vice versa.

Two timescales in one bullet
Regulation is doing two different jobs: safeguarding what is already deployed (a present-tense job, backward-looking) and constraining the trajectory of future development (a forward-looking one). Most public argument about AI regulation conflates them, and separating them is a good move in a discussion answer.

Note too that auditing is specified as internal and external. Internal audit alone has an obvious conflict of interest, and external audit alone lacks access — the pairing is the point.

Value alignment methods

What it is
Aligning AI behaviour with human values.
  • Used extensively in chatbots.
  • For example, a machine learning model trained to predict how aligned a given output is to human values (e.g. honesty, clarity) based on many examples.
Both a technical and a social problem
  • How to encode behaviour rules into a system — the technical half.
  • Finding out what values we (and society) want for a system — the social half.

Important in Game AI, credit scoring, Gen AI — most systems.

The split is the thing to remember. Solving the technical half perfectly gets you a system that faithfully implements whatever values were specified — which, if the second half was skipped, is exactly the political-control slide from Part 1.

The third appearance of this idea
Value alignment was introduced in Week 1 as the difficulty of exactly specifying “good”. Weeks 4 and 8 made it concrete: the reward function is the specification, and an agent optimises precisely what you wrote, not what you meant. Here it returns as a named mitigation method. Being able to trace it through all three is the kind of cross-week connection that reads well in an exam.

Bias mitigation methods

Four named methods — and they are genuinely different
MethodWhat it changesThe lecture's description
Dataset curationthe data itselfImprove the curation process, to appropriately represent minority and marginalized groups, to remove harmful content, etc. Includes participatory design.
Reweightingthe weight of each exampleDuring training, weight data from minority groups more highly.
Resamplinghow often each example is drawnDuring training, sample data from minority groups more often.
Fairness functionsthe objectiveInstead of maximizing average accuracy → maximize minimum accuracy; maximize accuracy and minimize performance differences, etc.

Reweighting and resampling are not the same method described twice. One changes each example's contribution to the loss; the other changes the composition of the batches. They often have similar effects, and an answer that treats them as synonyms is losing an easy mark.

Which method for which cause
The four map onto the five causes from Part 3 rather neatly, and pairing them is a strong way to answer a “how would you mitigate this” question:
causemethod that addresses it
Representation biasdataset curation · resampling · reweighting
Measurement biasnone of the four — you must change the label, or abandon the task
Algorithm biasfairness functions
Evaluation biasdisaggregated metrics — the “performance differences between social groups” row of the anticipation table
World biasfairness functions, or reconsidering the label — no data fix exists

Measurement bias is the one with no technical remedy on the list, which is why the phrenology slide ends the way it does.

Tool · What a fairness function actually changes

Interactive

Average accuracy vs minimum accuracy vs smallest gap

The fourth bias-mitigation bullet says to maximise the minimum accuracy rather than the average. This computes both, plus the gap, for any table of per-group accuracies — and tells you when the three objectives pick different models. Group sizes go in the header as name (n=…), which is what makes the overall figure diverge from the macro average. Presets: the Gender Shades table from the lecture's own slide, a case built so the objectives disagree, and Week 5's accuracy trap.

Privacy mitigation methods

Two named methods
  • Anonymization algorithms — face blurring; text anonymization techniques.
  • Differential privacy — releasing information about a dataset in a way that does not allow you to know if a person is part of that dataset, usually by adding noise to computations in a smart way.
The distinction the definition is making
Anonymization removes identifying content. Differential privacy protects something stronger and less obvious: membership. Even a fully anonymised aggregate can leak the fact that a particular person was in the dataset — and if the dataset is “patients treated for X”, membership is the sensitive fact. That is why noise is added to the computation rather than to the records.

“In a smart way” is doing real work: the noise has to be calibrated so the aggregate stays useful while any single person's presence stays undetectable.

Environmental mitigation methods

Two named methods
  • Code emission estimation methods — many libraries exist, e.g. CodeCarbon.
  • Solving problems with smaller models.

Note the order: measure first, then reduce. It is the same shape as the anticipation table in Part 2 — you cannot manage what you have not instrumented.

Tool · Principles & mitigation reference

Interactive

The two tables, plus a drill on the principles

Both reference tables in one place — the seven principles with their descriptions, and every mitigation method the lecture names, grouped by the area it addresses. ★ name the principle shows you a description and asks which principle it belongs to, which is the form these come up in.

Who is responsible for the harms of AI?

Three answers, and the lecture gives all three
WhoFor what
The institution that designs the systemFor allowing any of the harms to take place
The ethics boardFor passing an unethical product/application
The developers
  • Many harms are best anticipated by developers
  • Many harms can only be tested or minimized by developers
  • Responsible for algorithm transparency, inefficiency, power consumption…

The argument for developer responsibility is an argument from position, not from blame. It is not that developers are the worst actors — it is that they are frequently the only people who can see the problem coming and the only ones who can test for it. Responsibility follows capability. That is the reasoning to reproduce, and it is why four of the five bias causes carry the ★.

Minimising the harms of AI

The nine-item list
  1. Awareness of ethical issues; staying informed; being critical
  2. Participatory design
  3. Team diversity — marginalized communities have different lived experience, and it is important to anticipate issues
  4. Balanced datasets
  5. Testing with diverse groups
  6. Documenting datasets, models, algorithms, design choices
  7. Logging, explainable methods
  8. Ethics boards
  9. Whistleblowing
The list has a shape worth pointing out
It runs roughly through the lifecycle: before building (awareness, participatory design, team diversity) → while building (balanced datasets, testing with diverse groups) → documenting what you built (documentation, logging, explainability) → institutional checks (ethics boards) → and, when all of that fails, whistleblowing.

Whistleblowing being last is not an accident. It is the remedy for the second branch of the causes slide — the case where the risk was obvious, the task was problematic, and the organisation decided to proceed anyway. Every other item on the list assumes good faith; that one does not.

A “how would you minimise these harms” answer that names items from several stages will beat one that lists three technical fixes.

The conclusion slide — all five questions answered

Worth learning close to verbatim
QuestionThe lecture's answer
How is AI applied in practice? Who has access? Who benefits? Well-meaning and bad applications; unequal access; unequal benefits
What are the harms and ethical considerations of AI? Who is harmed? Human agency, safety, privacy, transparency, fairness, societal, environmental, accountability; more harm often to already marginalized groups
How does bias manifest in AI? Why does it arise? Different impact on different social groups; because of world / representation / measurement / algorithm / evaluation bias, and lack of anticipation, testing and action
Who is responsible for the harms of AI? Institutions designing algorithms, managers, ethics boards, and developers too
How do we minimise these harms? Awareness, anticipation, participation, diversity, testing, documentation, reporting, whistleblowing

Two things to notice. The harms line in the conclusion says “transparency” where the harms slide said fairness and dignity — the conclusion is loosely blending the harm list with the principles list, so quote whichever the question asks for. And “more harm often to already marginalized groups” is the single sentence that ties the entire lecture together: it is the answer to “who is harmed?” in every section.

Exam takeaways

What to have ready
  • The seven principles: human oversight and agency · safety and robustness · privacy · transparency · fairness · societal & environmental wellbeing · accountability. They mirror the seven harms, with transparency as the extra.
  • Governance: regulations/standards/codes (safeguard present, constrain future) · internal and external auditing, verification, validation · “Trustworthy AI” = design AND governance.
  • Value alignment is technical (encode the rules) and social (decide what the values are).
  • Bias mitigation: dataset curation (incl. participatory design) · reweighting · resampling · fairness functions. Know that reweighting ≠ resampling, and that fairness functions maximise the minimum accuracy.
  • Privacy mitigation: anonymization (face blurring, text) · differential privacy (hides membership, by adding noise to computations).
  • Environmental mitigation: emission estimation (e.g. CodeCarbon) · smaller models.
  • Responsibility: the institution, the ethics board, and developers — the last because they are best placed to anticipate and the only ones able to test.
  • Minimising: awareness · participatory design · team diversity · balanced datasets · testing with diverse groups · documentation · logging and explainability · ethics boards · whistleblowing.
  • The conclusion slide answers all five key questions in one line each — the safest possible structure for an open-ended question.

End of Week 9.
