★ Revision · One-Page Quick Reference

Exam Cram Sheet

every core concept, condensed

A distilled summary of the whole module. Use Ctrl/Cmd+P to print it — the sidebar and tools are hidden in print. One card per week, added as the content goes in.

W1 · What AI is

  • Two senses: a kind of intelligence (a property — no such thing as "an AI"), and a field of research.
  • McCarthy 1956: science and engineering of making intelligent machines — need not confine itself to biologically observable methods.
  • Four approaches: think / act × like humans / rationally. "Like humans" = cognitive models; "rationally" = laws of logic and probability.
  • Turing test 1950, Q&A. Total Turing test = a robot, physical behaviour too.

W1 · Agents

  • Agent: makes an intelligent decision when given the opportunity, using the knowledge and actions available at that time.
  • Autonomous agent: decides without human input.
  • Rational agent: always takes the best action.
  • The loop: Sensors → what the world is like now → what it'll be like if I do A → what action to do now → Effectors. Knowledge = how the world evolves, effects of my actions, goals.
  • Value alignment: aligning system goals with human ones; exactly specifying "good" is the hard part.

W1 · Model-based vs data-driven

  • Model-based = explicit knowledge = Symbolic / Classical AI: encode the world, encode how it changes, search for strategies. "Pretends to think."
  • Data-driven = tacit knowledge = ML: read coarse data, be told the problem, adjust the model. "Pretends to learn."
  • Dimensions: knowledge explicit/tacit, model-based/data-driven; perception perfect/imperfect; environment fully/partially observable, static/dynamic; actions instantaneous/durative, deterministic/stochastic.
  • Search assumes the easy end of every axis.

W1 · Search problems

  • Search = computing a sequence of actions that form a path to a goal.
  • Five parts: state space; initial state + goal test; actions; transition model; action costs.
  • Search tree: node = state, edge = action. Redundant paths ⇒ infinite tree.
  • Two fixes: check the path back to the root, or track visited states.
  • Notation: b branching factor, d depth of shallowest solution, m max depth.

W1 · The five algorithms

  • One algorithm, five f's. Best-first = priority queue on f(n).
  • BFS f = depth. Queue + reached. Complete ✓. Optimal ✓ only if equal costs. Time & space b + b² + … + b^d.
  • DFS f = −depth. Complete ✓ if redundant paths prevented. Optimal ✗ (left-most solution). Time b^m, space b·m.
  • UCS f = g. Complete ✓, optimal ✓. Time & space ∝ nodes cheaper than the goal. Minimum-cost, not minimum-action.
  • Greedy f = h. Fast, not optimal.
  • A* f = g + h. Optimal if h admissible.

W1 · Numbers to remember

  • BFS vs UCS from D: 2 actions cost 310 vs 3 actions cost 278.
  • Greedy ARAD → D → F → BUCHAREST = 140 + 99 + 211 = 450.
  • A* ARAD → D → E → G → BUCHAREST = 140 + 80 + 97 + 101 = 418.
  • First f-values from ARAD: A 447, B 449, D 393. Then C 671, E 413, F 415. Then G 417, H 526.
  • Goal offered via F at 450, via G at 418.

W1 · Heuristics

  • Heuristic = rule of thumb estimating cost from n to the goal. UCS looks backwards (g); h looks forwards.
  • Admissible = never over-estimates: actual cost ≥ h(n). Straight-line distance is admissible.
  • A* + admissible ⇒ optimal.
  • h ≡ 0 is admissible but turns A* into UCS.
  • Challenge: admissible and informative — obtained by relaxing problem constraints.
  • A* stops on expanding the goal, not on generating it.

W2 · Minimax

  • Game tree: nodes = states, edges = moves; Max, Min and Terminal nodes; only terminals have no children.
  • MINIMAX(n) = utility for MAX, assuming both play optimally.
  • MIN nodes take the min of their children; MAX nodes the max. Bottom-up.
  • Complexity: time O(bd), space O(b·d) — it's a DFS.
  • Complete if the tree is finite; optimal if the opponent is optimal.
  • Worked tree: 3,12,8 | 2,4,6 | 14,5,2 → B=3, C=2, D=2, A=3 via a₁.

W2 · Alpha-beta

  • α = minimum score the MAX player could get (a floor, only rises).
  • β = maximum score the MIN player could get (a ceiling, only falls).
  • Cut rule: skip the rest of the children when β ≤ α — same condition at MAX and MIN nodes.
  • Same value as minimax, always. Only the node count changes.
  • Worked tree: B=3 sets α=3; C's first leaf 2 gives β=2 ≤ 3 → prune C's other two. 7 of 9 leaves.
  • Ordering: worst case O(bd), best case O(bd/2) — twice the depth for the same effort.

W2 · CSPs

  • Three parts: variables X, domains D, constraints C. Each constraint = scope + relation.
  • Solution = instantiation of all of X from D satisfying all of C. Solvers search incomplete but consistent partial assignments.
  • Australia: X = {WA, NT, Q, NSW, V, SA, T}; D = {red, green, blue}; 9 constraints; SA degree 5, T degree 0.
  • n-Queens: X = {xij}, D = {0,1}, Σxij = N plus "not both 1" on rows, columns, both diagonals.
  • Tree depth n, but n! × mn paths; commutativity cuts it to mn.

W2 · Solving CSPs

  • Backtracking = DFS, one variable per level, backtrack on failure.
  • MRV — fewest legal values. Degree — most constraining. LCV — rules out fewest values elsewhere.
  • Forward checking — track legal values, stop when one empties; propagates assigned → unassigned only.
  • Arc consistency — X→Y consistent iff every value of X has a support in Y; deletes from X; if X shrinks, re-queue all Z→X.
  • AC detects failure earlier: AC fails after WA=red, Q=green; FC needs V=blue too.
  • {SA=blue}: 3⁵ = 243 → 2⁵ = 32, an 87% reduction.

W3 · Classical planning

  • Given I, G and A (actions with preconditions and effects); find a plan — a sequence taking I to G.
  • Planning is more powerful than CSP — CSPs can be modelled as planning problems.
  • An action has: parameters, preconditions (relations that must hold), effects (relations added or deleted).
  • Closed-world assumption — what is not listed in the initial state is assumed false.
  • Logistics: Move (at t from / connected → +at t to, −at t from) · Load (at t l, at c l → +on c t, −at c l) · Unload (mirror of Load).

W3 · PDDL

  • Language + algorithm — write any problem in PDDL, any planner solves it.
  • Versions: PDDL propositional · 2.1 numbers + time · 3 preferences · + continuous change, processes, events.
  • One domain file (predicates, actions) + many problem files (objects, init, goal).
  • Action syntax: :parameters, :precondition, :effect; (and …); deletes as (not (…)).
  • Fluents (2.1): :functions, comparisons in preconditions, increase/decrease in effects, (:metric minimize …).
  • Durative: :duration; conditions at start / over all / at end; effects at start / at end.

W3 · Forward chaining & RPG

  • Forward chaining: S′ = S − {deletes} + {adds}; a goal state contains the goal conditions.
  • Put X on Y from Z — pre: clear X, on X Z, clear Y; add: clear Z, on X Y; del: on X Z, clear Y.
  • RPG — plan from S to G ignoring delete effects; its length is h(S). FF, Hoffmann & Nebel 2001.
  • Build: f(0) = initial state; a(n+1) = actions with preconditions in f(n); f(n+1) = f(n) + adds. Layers only grow.
  • Extract: backwards from g(m) = goals; fact in f(n−1) drops down, else pick an action from a(n) and add its preconditions.
  • h(s) := Σ |Oi| — actions, not layers. Demo: m = 2 but h = 3.
  • Used as h in A*, rebuilt for every node added to the open list.

W4 · Uncertainty & MDPs

  • Search assumed the state is known (fully observable) and actions execute as intended (deterministic).
  • MDP = sequential decision making for a fully observable but stochastic environment.
  • Two principles: Markov property holds for action transitions; probability distributions are stationary.
  • Markov property: next state depends only on the current state, not the history.
  • Transition model T(s,a,s′) = P(s′|s,a). Grid: 0.8 intended, 0.1 each side, blocked ⇒ stay.
  • Plan → policy. A sequence breaks when an action slips; a policy covers every state.

W4 · Rewards & policies

  • Utility = sum of rewards of all states visited. Up,Up,Right,Right,Right ⇒ (5×−0.04)+1 = 0.8; that plan executes with probability 0.8⁵ ≈ 33%.
  • Negative reward incentivises optimality.
  • π must be complete · optimal · stationary · proper (guaranteed to reach a terminal).
  • Uπ(s) = E[Σ γtR(St)]; γ values current over future rewards.
  • Four regimes: R=−1.65 rush for any exit · −0.04 balanced · −0.01 take no risks (stall against the wall) · R>0 never terminate.
  • At (4,1) with R=−0.04 the policy points away from the goal — a 10% slip would hit the −1.

W4 · Expected utility

  • E[U] = Σc∈C P(c)U(c). Coin: 0.5×0 + 0.5×5 = 2.5.
  • P(a,b) joint — both true at once. P(a|b) conditional — a true given b known. P(a|b) ≥ P(a,b).
  • Bayes: P(a|b) = P(a,b) / P(b).
  • E[U|s,a] = Σs′∈nei(s) P(s′|s,a)U(s′) — sum over every state the action could reach.
  • It's an expectation because the action may not do what you asked; all you know is the probability of each outcome.

W4 · Value iteration

  • Bellman update: Ui+1(s) = R(s) + γ maxa Σs′ P(s′|s,a)Ui(s′).
  • Max over your actions, average over the world's outcomes.
  • Init: U = 0 everywhere except end states, where U(s) = R(s).
  • Stop when Ui+1 = Ui; formally δ < ε(1−γ)/γ.
  • One sweep by hand (R=−0.04, γ=1): all −0.04 except (3,3) = −0.04 + 0.8 = 0.76.
  • Converged U: 0.812 0.868 0.918 / 0.762 ▪ 0.660 / 0.705 0.655 0.611 0.388.
  • Policy: π(s) = arg maxa Σ P(s′|s,a)U(s′) — R and γ drop out.
  • Iterations blow up as γ → 1; distant states dip negative before climbing.

W5 · ML overview

  • Samuel 1959: "gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed".
  • Mohri et al. 2018 experience → performance · R&N 2022 observes data, builds a model that is both hypothesis and software · Murphy 2012 detect patterns, predict future data.
  • Supervised = trained on labelled examples. Unsupervised = unlabelled, discover patterns. Reinforcement = learns from reward/punishment, exploitation vs exploration.
  • Supervised problems: classification (labels), regression (numbers).
  • Unsupervised problems: clustering (discovers groups), dimensionality reduction (high-dim → low-dim, preserving desired properties).
  • Many ML algorithms have no proof they work — hence measurement replaces proof.

W5 · Classification metrics

  • Training set = used for learning, with labels. Test set = untouched, labels hidden, used after training.
  • Accuracy = correct / all = (TP+TN)/total.
  • The 99% trap: 1% prevalence, always answer "no" → 99% accuracy, catches nothing.
  • Precision = TP/(TP+FP) — of what I flagged, how much was real. Punishes false alarms.
  • Recall / sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) — of what was real, how much I caught. Punishes misses.
  • F1 = 2/(recall⁻¹+precision⁻¹) = 2PR/(P+R), the harmonic mean — high only if both are high.
  • Recall exposes the always-"no" model; precision is 0/0 or a perfect 1.00. Neither uses TN.

W5 · Regression metrics

  • MAE = (1/n) Σ |ŷᵢ − yᵢ| — every unit of error equal.
  • MSE = (1/n) Σ (ŷᵢ − yᵢ)² — squares, so very sensitive to outliers.
  • RMSE = √MSE — same as MSE but back in the original units.
  • RMSE ≥ MAE always; equal only when all errors have the same size.

W5 · Under- and overfitting

  • Generalisation error = error on unseen data. Can't compute it, so minimise the empirical error — the one we control.
  • Underfitting = fails to capture the complexity of the training data. Too simple.
  • Overfitting = fits too much to the training data, fails to generalise. Too complex — it memorises the noise.
  • Training error only ever falls with complexity; validation error is U-shaped. Pick the bottom of the U.
  • The three fits: deg 1 → 1.89e−01 / 3.79e−01 · deg 4 → 6.91e−03 / 1.20e−02 · deg 29 → 3.22e−03 / 1.76e+15.
  • Diagnose from the gap: both high & close = under · both low & close = right · train ≈ 0 with validation climbing = over.
  • Validation not test: choosing with a set means fitting to it. Train / choose / report, on three sets.

W6 · K-means

  • Unsupervised = patterns without labels; clustering finds groups but cannot name them.
  • V(Ck) = (1/|Ck|) Σi,i′∈Ck d(pi,pi′)². Each pair once; divide by the number of points.
  • Better clustering = lower total within-cluster variance.
  • Algorithm: pick K data points as centres → assign each point to the nearest centre (ties to lowest index) → recompute centres as means → repeat until clusters stop changing.
  • Why not brute force: n = 20, K = 2 gives 2²⁰ − 1 = 1,048,575 assignments; exponential in n.
  • Local minima: initialisation decides. Fixes = many restarts (n_init) + smart seeding (k-means++).
  • Prop 6.3 (non-examinable): V(C) = 2 Σ d(p,µ)² — justifies "assign to nearest centre", and only for Euclidean.

W6 · Hierarchical

  • Start: n singleton clusters. Step: merge the closest pair. Stop: one cluster.
  • Two independent choices: linkage (cluster–cluster) and metric (point–point). Any combination.
  • L₁ = Σ|p₁ᵢ − p₂ᵢ| · L₂ = (Σ(p₁ᵢ − p₂ᵢ)²)½. L₂ ≤ L₁.
  • Single = min · Complete = max · Average = mean (divide by mn).
  • Single chains (straggly clusters); complete stays compact (bounds the diameter).
  • Ties: merge all clusters at the threshold — two pairs → two merges, a chain → one big cluster. Cost: some K unreachable.
  • Max steps = n − 1. Dendogram: join height = merge threshold; a long vertical gap = good place to cut.
  • Worked run (single, L₁): thresholds 4, 5, 7, 8, 12 — {1,5}, {2,3}, {2,3,6}, {2,3,4,6}, all.

W6 · The exercise answers

  • Ex 1: V(C̃₁)=13.75, V(C̃₂)=1, V(Ĉ₁)=6.67, V(Ĉ₂)=9.33 → totals 14.75 vs 16.00, so {p₁p₂p₃p₄}/{p₅p₆} wins.
  • Ex 2: C₁={p₁..p₄}, C₂={p₅,p₆}; µ₁=(2.5, 2.25), µ₂=(6.5, 6.5); converges at t = 2.
  • Ex 3: swap the centres → C₁={p₄,p₅,p₆}, C₂={p₁,p₂,p₃}; µ₁≈(5.67,5.67), µ₂≈(2,1.67). Total 16.00 — a local minimum that is not global.
  • Ex 4: 6 + 0 + 1 + 6 = 13.
  • Ex 5: n − 1 (a maximum, because ties can merge several at once).
  • Ex 6: single and complete first differ at K = 3 — {1,5}{2,3,6}{4} vs {1,5}{2,3}{4,6}.
  • Ex 7: complete-linkage — it bounds the worst pair, so every city in a cluster is within 100 miles.

W7 · Linear regression

  • Supervised = labelled data. Regression → a number; classification → a class.
  • Model: y = β₀ + β₁x + ε, ε ∼ N(0, σ²). Prediction ŷ = β₀ + β₁x; residual ε = y − ŷ.
  • N(µ, σ²) carries the variance. σ = 0.3 ⟹ N(µ, 0.09). µ ± σ ≈ 68%, ±2σ ≈ 95%, ±3σ ≈ 99.7%. P(one exact value) = 0.
  • Objective: minimise SSE = Σεᵢ². (Least Absolute Deviations minimises Σ|εᵢ| instead.)
  • By hand: collect SSE = nβ₀² + (Σx²)β₁² + (2Σx)β₀β₁ − (2Σy)β₀ − (2Σxy)β₁ + Σy², freeze one β, take the vertex at −b/2a, solve the pair.
  • Theorem 7.3: β̂₁ = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy)/(nΣx² − (Σx)²); β̂₀ = (Σx²Σy − ΣxΣxy)/(same denominator).
  • Notes' example (−1,2),(0,0),(2,0): β̂₀ = 6/7, β̂₁ = −4/7, SSE = 8/7. Ex 1: ŷ(5) = −2.
  • "Linear" is about the βs — polynomial regression is a special case of linear regression.
  • Normality is not used in the proof of Theorem 7.3, only for further properties like unbiasedness.
  • Free check: residuals sum to zero at the optimum; the line passes through (x̄, ȳ).

W7 · Decision trees

  • Gini(v) = Σ pᵢ(1 − pᵢ), pᵢ = vᵢ/n. Equivalently 1 − Σpᵢ².
  • 0 ⟺ pure. Maximum 1 − 1/k at equal classes: ½ (k=2), ⅔ (k=3), ¾ (k=4).
  • Gini-Split(A) = Σⱼ (nⱼ/n)·Gini(vⱼ) — a weighted average. Choose by arg min (7.11), at every node, not just the root.
  • Table 7.3: Gini(root) = 148/225 ≈ 0.658. Gini-Split(HasJob) = 8/27 ≈ 0.296 beats Gini-Split(OwnsHome) = 64/135 ≈ 0.474.
  • Node label = majority class, ties → lowest index; ordering is alphabetical.
  • ⚠ Figure 7.5 mislabels three nodes — [0,5,4] is Low not Medium, [0,0,4] is Medium, [0,5,0] is Low. Figures 7.4 and 7.6 are correct. Read labels off the vector.
  • Branches may split differently — that is what scikit-learn does, and re-using a feature on the same path is pointless (one child, no gain).
  • Left = True for binary nodes; label each arrow for non-binary ones.
  • Ex 4: max Gini for k=2 is ½. Ex 5: split by Feature1 — 0.67 vs 0.7313 vs 0.73.
  • Out of scope: Decision Tree Regression, neural networks. In scope: continuous features in a classification tree.

W8 · Bandits & action values

  • RL = learn by doing. k-armed bandit = k arms, each with its own reward distribution, maximise long-run average.
  • q⋆(a) = E[Rt | At = a] (8.2) — the true value, unknown. Stationary ⟹ drop the t (8.3).
  • Qt(a) (8.4) = average of rewards a paid on steps strictly before t. Q₁(a) = 0; 0 whenever N = 0.
  • 1predicate = 1 if true, 0 otherwise — it selects a's own steps in (8.4).
  • Incremental form: Q ← Q + (1/N)(R − Q). Same average, constant memory.
  • N(µ, σ²) is the variance. B ∼ N(11, 4) ⟹ σ = 2.
  • Exploit = take the current best. Explore = try something else in case an early sample was an outlier. No fixed definition of "too much".
  • Ex 1: q⋆(A)=10, q⋆(B)=11. Ex 2: Qt(A) = 0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4; Qt(B) = 0, 0, 0, 0.4, 0.4 (tie at t=5).

W8 · Selection methods

  • Random (8.4): Pr(At=ai) = 1/k, forever. Ex 4: k=50 → 0.02.
  • Greedy (8.5): At = arg maxa Qt(a), Q₁=0, ties randomised.
  • ε-greedy (8.6): random w.p. ε, greedy w.p. 1−ε. Ex 6: ε=0 → greedy, ε=1 → random.
  • Pr(greedy action) = 1 − ε + ε/k; Pr(specific other) = ε/k. Ties split the 1−ε.
  • Ex 5 (ε=0.5, k=2, optimal a₂): estimates point away 0.25 · tie 0.5 · point at it 0.75.
  • Fig 8.4: random ≈ 0 (arm values ~ N(0,1)); greedy stalls, stuck on the first positive arm; ε=0.1 leads at 500; ε=0.01 wins asymptotically by the law of large numbers — every arm sampled infinitely often for any ε>0, then the bigger ε just pays more to randomise.
  • Asymptote ≈ (1−ε)·q⋆(best) + ε·(mean arm); testbed q⋆(best) ≈ 1.54. Ex 7: ε=0.75 → ≈0.39 → between random and greedy.
  • % optimal ceiling for ε-greedy = 1 − ε + ε/k.

W8 · UCB

  • Why: ε-greedy explores uniformly — it wastes pulls on arms it already knows are bad.
  • (8.5)/(8.6): At = arg maxa [ Qt(a) + c√(ln t / Nt(a)) ].
  • Remark 8.8: N=0 ⟹ +∞ ⟹ maximising, so no Q₁ needed and the first k steps are a₁…ak in order. Ties → lowest index (greedy randomises — different rule!).
  • Terms: Q = exploitation · c = exploration parameter (a priori, data-independent) · c√(ln t/N) = exploration term ≈ uncertainty.
  • c ↑ ⟹ explore more. c = 0 ⟹ greedy. Common value √2; Ex 8 uses c = 2.
  • (8.7): √(ln t / t) → 0 — intervals shrink under repeated sampling. But ln t grows while N stays fixed, so a neglected arm's bound creeps back up.
  • Ex 8 (c=2): A₁…A₈ = a₁ a₂ a₃ a₃ a₁ a₁ a₁ a₂; UCB₈ = 6.1920 / 6.3841 / 5.0393. A₈ picks the worst Q because its interval is widest — Figure 8.5.
  • vs MDPs: the reward function is unknown (must be estimated), and there is only one state — richer RL needs q⋆(s, a).

W9 · Application & access

  • Five key questions: how applied / who has access / who benefits · what harms, who is harmed · how bias manifests and why · who is responsible · how to minimise. Use as headings.
  • Two columns: well-intentioned → “what are the hidden risks?”; fundamentally problematic → “should we even build this?”
  • Policing: breadth of surveillance · worse face recognition on minorities due to lack of data → wrongful arrests / stop-and-search · lack of accountability.
  • Military: targeting → bias into war, more deaths. Automated defense → dehumanization, loss of moral engagement, simplification of moral choices, easier escalation, arms races.
  • Political control: surveillance of opposition & minorities → authoritarianism, loss of privacy/speech/religious freedom · censorship & disinformation → polarisation, less informed citizens.
  • Phrenology: disproved pseudoscience predicting gender, intelligence, criminality, internal states from facial analysis. Revived by predicting gender/sexuality/race/emotion/criminality — but these are social constructs or unobservable; only the subjects can say.
  • Access: compute · GPUs · money to train and house · Big Tech monopoly → universities can't compete, poorer labs/countries excluded.

W9 · The seven harms

  • Order: human agency · accountability · safety and wellbeing · privacy · fairness and dignity · societal · environmental.
  • Agency: loss of control · loss of right to contest · over-delegation · loss of critical thinking.
  • Accountability: loss of accountability, or incorrect blaming of humans (warehouse workers blamed for robot mistakes).
  • Safety: physical safety · abuse & tech-facilitated violence · health · wellbeing.
  • Privacy by setting: intimate spaces · work & school · public spaces.
  • Fairness — allocative: opportunities · resources · quality-of-service. Representational: stereotyping · demeaning · erasing · alienating · loss of self-identification · essentialist categories.
  • Societal: information · cultural · civic and political · social relationships · deskilling. No identifiable individual victim — that's the test.
  • Environmental: energy & pollution · mineral mining for datacentres · AI for oil & gas.
  • Reparation (after): outcry · perpetrator communication (incl. denials) · investigation · legal action · legal repercussions · compensation · removal · discontinuation · design changes · law change.
  • Anticipation (before): quantitative measurement · ablation studies · qualitative (interviews, surveys, workshops, lit reviews, ethnography) · critique (speculation, argument).

W9 · Discrimination & bias

  • Direct = disparate treatment — disadvantaged because of a personal attribute.
  • Indirect = disparate impact — disadvantaged even though the attribute is not explicitly considered. Removing the attribute does not prevent it.
  • Bias, two senses: imbalance/tendency in data (input) · direct or indirect discrimination (output).
  • Five causes: world (world distribution) · representation (data collection) · measurement (wrong categorization/measurements) · algorithm (wrong algorithm) · evaluation (wrong metric or test set).
  • ★ Developer's fault: all except world bias.
  • Second branch (obvious risk, problematic task): ethics board doesn't flag · ★ developer doesn't oppose/report/whistleblow · management deploys.
  • ProPublica: more likely to mistakenly predict high-risk for Black than White defendants.
  • GPT-3 / DALL·E: “All white male” — representational (stereotyping, erasing).
  • Brandao 2019: age & gender bias in pedestrian detection miss rates.
  • Gender Shades (Buolamwini & Gebru 2018): Type VI error 46.5% (Face++), 46.8% (IBM), vs ~1–5% on Type I. Microsoft 0% (IV) → 25% (VI). Intersectional — one attribute at a time hides it.
  • Who finds these: women, Black scholars, LGBTQ → lived experience & diversity.

W9 · Mitigation & responsibility

  • Seven principles: human oversight & agency · safety & robustness · privacy · transparency · fairness · societal & environmental wellbeing · accountability. (Mirror the harms; transparency is the extra.)
  • Transparency = documentation/logging, explainability, informing when AI is used. Accountability = auditability, documenting how trade-offs were resolved, responsibility for harms.
  • Governance: regulations/standards/codes (safeguard present + constrain future) · internal AND external audit/verification/validation · “Trustworthy AI” = design AND governance.
  • Value alignment: technical (encode rules) and social (decide the values). Used in chatbots; important in game AI, credit scoring, Gen AI.
  • Bias mitigation: dataset curation (+ participatory design) · reweighting (weight more) · resampling (sample more often) · fairness functions (maximise minimum accuracy).
  • Privacy mitigation: anonymization (face blurring, text) · differential privacy — hides whether a person is in the dataset, by adding noise to computations.
  • Environmental: emission estimation (CodeCarbon) · smaller models.
  • Responsible: institution (allowing harms) · ethics board (passing it) · developers (best placed to anticipate, only ones able to test; also transparency, inefficiency, power).
  • Minimising: awareness · participatory design · team diversity · balanced datasets · testing with diverse groups · documentation · logging & explainability · ethics boards · whistleblowing (last — every other item assumes good faith).

Cross-cutting threads

  • "Search for good strategies" in the model-based bullet list is Parts 2–3. Classical AI = encode + search.
  • Optimal is always relative to something — fewest actions (BFS) vs cheapest (UCS) vs looks-closest (greedy).
  • Every trade is memory vs quality vs information — DFS buys memory with quality; A* buys expansions with a heuristic.
  • Relaxation is the general recipe for building heuristics: make the problem easier, use its cost as the estimate. Straight-line distance (W1) and the RPG's "ignore deletes" (W3) are the same trick twice.
  • Everything is still search. Minimax is a DFS. Backtracking is a DFS. Forward chaining is A*. Only the state and the successor rule change.
  • Fail first, cheaply. Alpha-beta's β ≤ α, forward checking's empty domain and the RPG's fixpoint are all the same move: prove a branch is dead before paying to explore it.
  • Heuristics cost something. W1's h was a lookup; W3's h is an entire sub-problem solved per node — worth it because the node saving is larger.
  • The reward function is the specification. Week 1's value alignment problem, made numeric: R(s) = −1.65 quietly means "please die quickly".
  • When the world stops cooperating, the answer changes shape. Deterministic ⇒ a plan. Stochastic ⇒ a policy. Adversarial (W2) ⇒ a strategy that assumes the worst.
  • W1–4 are the model-based half; W5 is the data-driven half. Weeks 1–4 all need you to write the world down first — that's what "without being explicitly programmed" rules out.
  • Guarantees give way to measurement. A*, alpha-beta, AC-3 and value iteration all come with proofs. Machine learning largely doesn't, so it substitutes held-out evaluation — which is why metrics and the train/validation/test split get two thirds of Week 5.
  • Reinforcement learning is Week 4 with the model taken away. Same rewards and policies; you're no longer given P(s′|s,a), so you must explore to find out.
★ Final Revision · Weeks 1–9

The Theory, Condensed

every definition, acronym and distinction, in one place
How to use this page
This is the state-it-back material — the things an exam asks you to define, name, or tell apart, with no working required. The cram sheet is per-week facts; this page is organised by the kind of question instead, because that is how it comes at you under time.

Cover the right column of any table and see whether you can produce it. If you can do that for every table here, the definition marks are safe.

Agents and the four approaches

Three neighbours that are easy to confuse
TermDefinition
Agentmakes an intelligent decision when given the opportunity, using the knowledge and actions available at that time
Autonomous agentdecides without human input — about who supplies the decision
Rational agentalways takes the best action — about how good the decision is

Four approaches = think / act × like humans / rationally. “Like humans” gives cognitive models and the Turing test; “rationally” gives the laws of logic and probability.

Turing test (1950) judges behaviour only, by question and answer — so it tests acting like humans. The total Turing test adds a robot and physical behaviour.

Model-based vs data-driven
Model-basedData-driven
Also calledSymbolic AI, Classical AIMachine learning
Knowledgeexplicit — you encode the worldtacit — it comes out of the data
Methodencode the world, encode how it changes, then searchread coarse data, be told the problem, adjust the model
Slogan“pretends to think”“pretends to learn”
Weeks1–45–8
Problem dimensions — six words, three pairs
PairWhat it is about
instantaneous vs durativean action takes time
deterministic vs stochastican action's effect varies
fully vs partially observablehow much the agent can see
static vs dynamicthe environment changes on its own

The trap: stochastic is about the action, dynamic is about the world.

Search: one engine, five values of f

Every algorithm is “expand the frontier node with smallest f”
Algorithmf(n)Complete?Optimal?Memory
Breadth-firstdepth(n)yesonly if all step costs equalexponential
Depth-first−depth(n)no (infinite depth)nolinear
Uniform-costg(n)yesyesexponential
Greedy best-firsth(n)nonoexponential
A*g(n) + h(n)yesyes, if h admissibleexponential
g, h, f — and where h comes from
g(n)h(n)
Meanscost of the path already travelledestimated cost still to go
Exact?exact — you went that wayan estimate, from outside the search
Sourcesumming edges as you searchstraight-line distance, or a relaxation of the problem

Admissible = never overestimates the true remaining cost, i.e. h(n) ≤ h*(n) for every n. A straight line can never be longer than a road, which is why the ruler heuristic is admissible by construction. Admissibility is what makes A* optimal — lose it and A* can return a worse path.

h = 0 everywhere is admissible (and turns A* into UCS). A more informed heuristic is one that is larger while still admissible — it expands fewer nodes.

Adversarial search

Definitions
  • Minimax value — the value of a node assuming both players play optimally: MAX takes the max of its children, MIN the min.
  • Ply — one move by one player. A “two-ply” lookahead is one move each.
  • Evaluation function — a heuristic estimate of a state's value, used when you cut off before a terminal state.
  • α — the best value MAX can already guarantee on the path so far. Only ever increases.
  • β — the best value MIN can already guarantee. Only ever decreases.
  • The cut rule — prune when β ≤ α.

Alpha-beta returns exactly the same value as minimax — it is a pruning optimisation, never an approximation. With perfect move ordering it can search roughly twice as deep in the same time.

Constraint satisfaction

The definitions
  • CSP — a set of variables, a domain of values for each, and constraints.
  • A constraint = a scope (which variables it involves) + a relation (which combinations are legal).
  • Solution — a complete and consistent assignment.
  • Constraint graph — variables are nodes, constraints are edges.
  • Arc consistency — X→Y is consistent when every value in X's domain has some legal partner in Y's.

Unlike Week 1 search, the path is irrelevant — only the final assignment is the answer.

The pair of names one letter apart
Most constrained variableMost constraining variable
NameMRVdegree heuristic
Looks atits own domain — fewest values leftits neighbours — most constraints on unassigned variables
Rolethe primary rulethe tie-breaker for MRV

On Australia every region starts with 3 colours, so MRV ties seven ways and degree picks SA, which touches 5 others.

Forward checking vs AC-3
Forward checkingAC-3
How far it looksone step — the assigned variable's immediate neighboursthe whole graph, propagating repeatedly to a fixpoint
Detects failurewhen a neighbour's domain emptiesearlier — catches dead ends forward checking misses
Costcheapmore work per step

Neither changes the set of solutions. All the CSP heuristics are pure accelerators — turn them all off and backtracking still finds the same answers, only slower.

Planning

The vocabulary
  • Closed-world assumption — anything not stated in the state is false. This is why you only list what is true.
  • Action schema — parameters, precondition, effect (add list and delete list).
  • Fluent — a numeric quantity that actions change, as opposed to a boolean predicate.
  • Durative action — has a duration, with conditions at start, over all, at end.
  • Forward chaining — search forward from the initial state, applying applicable actions. It is A* with a planning heuristic.
  • Relaxation — solve an easier problem and use its cost as h. The RPG's relaxation is ignore all delete effects.

The RPG heuristic is h = Σ|Oi|, the total number of actions in the extracted relaxed plan. Because deletes are ignored, fact layers only ever grow, so the graph reaches a fixpoint.

MDPs and value iteration

The pieces
  • Transition model P(s′ | s, a) — where you actually end up. Markov = it depends only on the current state, not the history.
  • Policy π(s) — an action for every state. Stochastic worlds need a policy, not a plan.
  • Discount factor γ — how much a future reward is worth now. γ < 1 keeps infinite sums finite.
  • Bellman update — U(s) ← R(s) + γ·maxa Σs′ P(s′|s,a)·U(s′).
  • Value iteration — apply the Bellman update to every state, repeatedly, until it stops changing.
  • Policy extraction — once U has converged, π(s) = the arg max of that same expression.

Stopping rule: iterate until the largest change δ satisfies δ < ε(1 − γ)/γ.

The reward function is the specification. Week 1's value alignment problem, in numbers — set R too negative and the optimal policy is to die quickly.

Machine learning: the setting and the metrics

Supervised vs unsupervised vs reinforcement
SupervisedUnsupervisedReinforcement
Givendata with labelsdata, no labelsno data — you act and collect rewards
Goalpredict labels for new pointsfind structuremaximise long-run reward
Weeks5, 768
Train / validation / test — and why validation exists
  • Training set — fits the parameters.
  • Validation set — chooses between models (degree, K, hyperparameters).
  • Test set — used once, to report performance.

Selecting on the test set makes it a training set, and the number you report stops meaning anything. That is the whole reason there are three.

Classification metrics
MetricFormulaAnswers
Accuracy(TP + TN) / allhow often am I right? — useless on imbalanced data
PrecisionTP / (TP + FP)when I say yes, how often am I right?
RecallTP / (TP + FN)of the real yeses, how many did I catch?
F12·P·R / (P + R)harmonic mean — punishes a bad one of the pair

The accuracy trap: a disease affecting 1 in 1000, always predicting “no”, scores 99.9% accuracy with recall 0.

Under- and overfitting
UnderfittingOverfitting
Training errorhighlow
Validation errorhighhigh
Causemodel too simplemodel too complex, memorising noise

The tell for overfitting is the gap, not the level.

Clustering

K-means and hierarchical
  • K-means — pick K initial centres; assign each point to the nearest centre (ties to the lowest index); recompute each centre as the mean of its points; repeat until the clusters stop changing.
  • Within-cluster variance — the quality measure; lower total is better.
  • K-means finds a local optimum only — a different initialisation can give a different, worse answer.
  • Hierarchical — start with every point its own cluster, repeatedly merge the two closest, until one remains.
  • Dendogram — the merge tree; cut it at a height to choose K. A tall vertical gap is a good place to cut.
Linkage — the distinction that gets examined
LinkageDistance between clustersGuarantees
Singlethe closest pairconnectivity — chains of short hops; prone to chaining
Completethe furthest pairbounds the cluster's diameter — every pair is within the threshold
Averagethe mean over all cross pairscompromise; guarantees nothing about the worst pair

L1 (Manhattan) = Σ|differences|; L2 (Euclidean) = √(Σ differences²). L2 ≤ L1 always — a free sanity check.

Regression and decision trees

Linear regression
  • ŷ = β₀ + β₁x; the residual is ε = y − ŷ; we minimise SSE = Σε².
  • “Linear” refers to the parameters β, not the variables x — so polynomial regression is a special case of linear regression.
  • Theorem 7.3 gives a closed form from five numbers: n, Σx, Σy, Σx², Σxy. Rare in ML — most methods cannot be proved optimal.
  • Normality of the errors is not used in that proof, only for further properties of the estimators.
  • At the optimum the residuals sum to zero — the cheapest possible check on an answer.
Decision trees
  • Gini(v) = Σ pᵢ(1 − pᵢ), equivalently 1 − Σpᵢ². Zero ⟺ pure; maximum 1 − 1/k when all classes are equal.
  • Gini-Split(A) = Σⱼ (nⱼ/n)·Gini(vⱼ) — a weighted average over the children.
  • Choose by arg min, at every node, not just the root. Different branches may split on different features.
  • Node label = majority class, ties to the lowest index; class order is alphabetical.
  • Left branch = True in a binary tree; label the arrows in a non-binary one.

Reinforcement learning

The two quantities
q⋆(a)Qt(a)
Isthe true expected reward, E[Rt | At = a]your estimate of it
Known to the agent?neveryes — it is built from experience
Changes over time?no (stationary assumption)yes, that is the point

Qt(a) averages the rewards a paid on steps strictly before t. Q₁(a) = 0, and 0 whenever the action has never been taken.

The three selection methods
MethodRuleTie-break
RandomPr(At = aᵢ) = 1/k—
Greedyarg maxa Qt(a), with Q₁ = 0randomise among the maxima
ε-greedyrandom with probability ε, greedy with probability 1 − εas greedy
UCBarg maxa [ Qt(a) + c√(ln t / Nt(a)) ]lowest index

The two tie rules are different — greedy randomises, UCB takes the lowest index. And Pr(greedy action) = 1 − ε + ε/k, not 1 − ε, because the random branch can reach it too.

ε = 0 gives greedy; ε = 1 gives random. In UCB, N = 0 counts as +∞, so the first k steps are forced, and c = 0 collapses UCB into greedy.

Bandits vs MDPs — the two differences
  • The reward function is unknown and must be estimated.
  • There is only one state — whichever action you take you return to the same choice. Richer RL estimates q⋆(s, a) per state-action pair.

Ethics: the lists that get asked

The five key questions — use them as headings
  1. How is AI applied? Who has access? Who benefits?
  2. What are the harms? Who is harmed?
  3. How does bias manifest, and why does it arise?
  4. Who is responsible?
  5. How do we minimise the harms?
The two taxonomies to have by heart
Seven harmsFive causes of bias
human agency · accountability · safety and wellbeing · privacy · fairness and dignity · societal · environmental world (not the developer's fault) · representation ★ · measurement ★ · algorithm ★ · evaluation ★

Allocative harms are about who gets things (opportunities, resources, quality-of-service); representational harms are about how people are portrayed (stereotyping, demeaning, erasing, alienating, loss of self-identification, essentialist categories).

Direct discrimination = disparate treatment (because of an attribute); indirect = disparate impact (despite the attribute not being used). Removing the attribute stops the first and not the second.

The distinctions most likely to be tested

Pairs that look alike and are not
ThisNot thisThe difference
most constrained (MRV)most constraining (degree)own domain vs effect on neighbours
stochasticdynamicthe action's effect vs the environment changing
greedy tie → randomiseUCB tie → lowest indextwo different rules, one module
over-delegation (agency)deskilling (societal)this decision now vs the profession's capability
precisionrecallof my yeses vs of the real yeses
reweightingresamplingweight in the loss vs how often it is drawn
single linkagecomplete linkageclosest pair vs furthest pair
allocative harmrepresentational harmwho gets things vs how people are shown
anonymizationdifferential privacyhides content vs hides membership
h in Week 1heuristics in Week 2an estimate that can change the answer vs an ordering rule that cannot
Threads that run through the whole module
  • Everything is search. Minimax is a DFS. Backtracking is a DFS. Forward chaining is A*. Only the state and the successor rule change.
  • Relaxation is the general recipe for a heuristic. Straight-line distance (W1) and “ignore delete effects” (W3) are the same trick.
  • Fail first, cheaply. Alpha-beta's β ≤ α, forward checking's empty domain and MRV are all the same move.
  • When the world stops cooperating the answer changes shape. Deterministic ⇒ a plan. Stochastic ⇒ a policy. Adversarial ⇒ a strategy assuming the worst. Unknown rewards ⇒ exploration.
  • Guarantees give way to measurement. A*, alpha-beta, AC-3 and value iteration come with proofs; machine learning substitutes held-out evaluation.
  • The objective is the specification. The MDP reward function, the regression loss, the fairness function — each one is somebody deciding what “good” means.

Now go and be tested on it.

★ Final Revision · The Recipes

How To Compute It

every calculation in the module, as steps you can follow
How to use this page
The theory page tells you what things mean. This page tells you what to actually write down, in order, when a question says "compute", "find" or "apply".

Each recipe is: what you are given → the steps → a tiny worked example → the check and the trap. If you can run all of these, the calculation marks are safe.

Run a search algorithm

BFS · DFS · UCS · Greedy · A*

Given: a graph with edge costs, a start, a goal, and (for greedy/A*) a table of h values.

  1. Put the start in the frontier.
  2. Pick the frontier node with the smallest f, where f is:
    BFS → depth  ·  DFS → deepest first  ·  UCS → g
    Greedy → h  ·  A* → g + h
  3. If it is the goal, stop. Otherwise move it to the explored set.
  4. Add its neighbours to the frontier with their g values (cost so far).
  5. Repeat from 2.

Worked: from ARAD, children are A (g 118, h 329), B (g 75, h 374), D (g 140, h 253). A* takes f = 118+329 = 447, 75+374 = 449, 140+253 = 393 → expand D.

⚠ Trap: g is the cost from the start to that node, not the cost of the last edge. Add it up along the path.

✓ Check: A* and UCS must return the same total cost if h is admissible.

Check a heuristic is admissible
  1. For each node, work out the true cheapest cost to the goal (h*).
  2. Compare: admissible means h(n) ≤ h*(n) for every n.
  3. One violation anywhere and it is not admissible.

Worked: h(D) = 253; true road D→E→G→BUC = 80+97+101 = 278. 253 ≤ 278 ✓

⚠ Trap: h must never overestimate. Under is fine, and h = 0 is always admissible.

Minimax and alpha-beta

Minimax value of a tree
  1. Start at the leaves — their values are given.
  2. Work upward. At a MAX node take the largest child; at a MIN node the smallest.
  3. The root's value is the answer; the move is the child that produced it.

⚠ Trap: the root is usually MAX and the layers alternate. Count the layers before you start.

Alpha-beta pruning
  1. Walk the tree left to right, depth first.
  2. Carry two numbers down: α (best MAX can guarantee, only ever rises) and β (best MIN can guarantee, only ever falls). Start α = −∞, β = +∞.
  3. At a MAX node update α; at a MIN node update β.
  4. Prune the remaining children as soon as β ≤ α.

✓ Check: the value at the root must be identical to plain minimax. Pruning never changes the answer, only the work.

Solve a CSP by hand

Backtracking with the heuristics
  1. Pick the variable: fewest legal values left (MRV). If tied, most unassigned neighbours (degree).
  2. Pick the value: the one ruling out fewest options for neighbours (LCV).
  3. Assign it, then forward check: delete that value from every unassigned neighbour's domain.
  4. If any domain becomes empty, undo and try the next value.
  5. Repeat until every variable is assigned.

Worked: Australia, all regions start with 3 colours, so MRV ties 7 ways → degree picks SA (touches 5 others).

⚠ Trap: degree counts only unassigned neighbours, and it recounts as you go.

AC-3
  1. Put every arc (both directions of every constraint) in a queue.
  2. Take an arc X→Y. For each value in X's domain, is there some legal partner in Y? If not, delete it from X.
  3. If you deleted anything, put every arc pointing back into X onto the queue again.
  4. Repeat until the queue is empty. An empty domain means failure.

⚠ Trap: arcs are directional. X→Y and Y→X are two separate checks.

Planning

Apply an action
  1. Check every precondition is true in the current state. If not, the action is not applicable.
  2. Take the current state, remove the delete list, add the add list.
  3. Anything not mentioned stays as it was (and anything not listed is false — closed-world).
Build the RPG and read off h
  1. Fact layer f(0) = the initial state.
  2. Action layer a(i) = every action whose preconditions are all in f(i).
  3. Fact layer f(i+1) = f(i) plus every add effect of a(i). Ignore all delete effects.
  4. Stop when the goal is in a fact layer, or nothing new appears.
  5. Extract a relaxed plan backwards, then h = Σ |Oᵢ|, the number of actions in it.

⚠ Trap: fact layers only ever grow, because deletes are ignored. If a layer shrank, you used a delete effect.

One Bellman update

The core Week 4 calculation

Given: the grid, R, γ, the slip probabilities, and last sweep's U values.

  1. Pick a square. For each of the four actions:
    • list the three outcomes: intended (0.8) and the two perpendicular slips (0.1 each)
    • a blocked move leaves you on your own square — use your own value
    • multiply each probability by that square's previous U and add them up
  2. Take the largest of the four totals.
  3. Unew = R + γ × that largest total.

Worked — (3,3) at sweep 2, R = −0.04, γ = 1:

Right: 0.8×1 + 0.1×0.76 (slip up bounces off the edge) + 0.1×(−0.04) = 0.872
U = −0.04 + 1×0.872 = 0.832

⚠ Traps: use last sweep's numbers for every square, not ones you just recomputed. Terminals always contribute their raw ±1. A blocked slip still happens — it just leaves you where you were.

✓ Check: 0.8 + 0.1 + 0.1 = 1. If your outcomes do not sum to 1 you have missed one.

Extract the policy
  1. Wait until U has stopped changing.
  2. At each square do the same expected-value sum for all four actions.
  3. Write down the action that scored highest, not the number. That is π(s).

⚠ Trap: R and γ drop out here — they are the same for every action, so they cannot change which one wins.

Classification and regression metrics

From a confusion matrix
  1. Label the four cells: TP, FP, FN, TN.
  2. Then:
    accuracy  = (TP + TN) / everything
    precision = TP / (TP + FP)   ← of my yeses
    recall    = TP / (TP + FN)   ← of the real yeses
    F1        = 2PR / (P + R)

⚠ Trap: precision and recall share TP on top — the difference is what is on the bottom. Higher is better for all four.

MAE, MSE, RMSE
  1. Column of errors: e = ŷ − y for each point.
  2. Column of |e|, and column of e².
  3. MAE = sum of |e| ÷ n  ·  MSE = sum of e² ÷ n  ·  RMSE = √MSE.

✓ Check: RMSE ≥ MAE always. Lower is better for all three.

⚠ Trap: divide by n before the square root.

Diagnose under- or overfitting
  1. Is the training error high? → underfitting. Stop.
  2. Training low but validation much higher? → overfitting.
  3. Both low and close → fine.

⚠ Trap: with accuracy the direction flips — overfitting is high train, low validation.

Clustering

Distances

Subtract coordinate by coordinate first, once. Then:

L₁ = add the absolute values
d² = add the squares
L₂ = √ of that

Worked: (4,4) to (6,7) → differences −2, −3 → L₁ = 5, d² = 13, L₂ = 3.61.

✓ Check: L₂ ≤ L₁ always.

Within-cluster variance V(C)
  1. List every unordered pair in the cluster — n points give n(n−1)/2 pairs.
  2. For each pair compute d² (no square root).
  3. Add them all up.
  4. Divide by |C|, the number of points — not the number of pairs.

Worked: {(4,4),(6,7),(7,6)} → 13 + 13 + 2 = 28, then 28/3 = 9.33.

One K-means iteration
  1. Assign: each point goes to the nearest centre. Ties → lowest cluster index.
  2. Update: each centre becomes the mean of its points.
  3. Repeat. Stop when the assignments stop changing (not when the centres barely move).

⚠ Trap: you can compare d² instead of d when assigning — same winner, no square roots needed.

One hierarchical merge
  1. For every pair of clusters, list all cross distances (every point of one against every point of the other).
  2. Reduce each list to one number: single = min, complete = max, average = mean.
  3. Merge the two clusters with the smallest such number, and record that number as the merge height.
  4. Repeat until one cluster remains.

To read a dendogram: find the tallest vertical gap and cut just below it. The number of lines you cross is K.

Fit a line

Theorem 7.3 — five numbers
  1. Build columns: x, y, x², xy. Add each up.
  2. You now have n, Σx, Σy, Σx², Σxy.
  3. Denominator (same for both): nΣx² − (Σx)².
  4. β̂₁ = (nΣxy − ΣxΣy) / denominator
  5. β̂₀ = (Σx²Σy − ΣxΣxy) / denominator
  6. Predict with ŷ = β̂₀ + β̂₁x.

Worked: (−1,2), (0,0), (2,0) → n=3, Σx=1, Σy=2, Σx²=5, Σxy=−2, denom=14 → β₁ = −8/14 = −4/7, β₀ = 12/14 = 6/7.

✓ Check: the residuals must sum to zero. Ten seconds, catches almost everything.

Decision trees

Gini of one node
  1. Count the classes: a vector like [2, 0, 4], total n = 6.
  2. For each class, pᵢ = count / n.
  3. Gini = Σ pᵢ(1 − pᵢ).

Worked: [2,0,4], n=6 → (2/6)(4/6) + 0 + (4/6)(2/6) = 16/36 = 0.444.

✓ Check: 0 means pure; the biggest it can be is 1 − 1/k.

Gini-Split, and choosing the feature
  1. Split the rows by the feature — one group per value.
  2. Compute Gini for each group.
  3. Weight each by group size / total rows.
  4. Add them up — that is Gini-Split for that feature.
  5. Repeat for every feature and take the arg min.

Worked: HasJob → (6/15)(0) + (9/15)(0.494) = 0.296; OwnsHome → (6/15)(0.444) + (9/15)(0.494) = 0.474. HasJob wins.

⚠ Traps: the weights are where the marks are. And the answer is a feature name, not a number.

Reinforcement learning

Qt(a) from a history
  1. Look only at steps strictly before t.
  2. Pick out the ones where that arm was chosen.
  3. Average their rewards. No pulls at all → Q = 0.

Worked: A paid 0.5, then −0.3, then (B), then 1.0. At t = 5: Q(A) = (0.5 − 0.3 + 1.0)/3 = 0.4.

ε-greedy probability of an action
  1. Everyone gets ε/k from the random branch.
  2. Find the arm(s) with the highest Q. They share the remaining 1 − ε equally.
  3. Add the two parts for the arm you were asked about.

Worked: k = 2, ε = 0.5, and a₂ is greedy → 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75. If a₂ is not greedy → just 0.25.

⚠ Trap: a non-greedy arm is never probability 0 — the random branch still reaches it.

One UCB step
  1. Note t, compute ln t.
  2. For each arm read off N (pulls before now) and Q.
  3. Bonus = c × √(ln t / N), or ∞ if N = 0.
  4. Total = Q + bonus. Pull the biggest; ties → lowest index.
  5. Take that arm's next reward, update its N and Q, move to t+1.

Worked — t = 8, c = 2, ln 8 = 2.079:

a₁: N=4, Q=4.75 → 4.75 + 2√(2.079/4) = 4.75 + 1.442 = 6.192
a₂: N=1, Q=3.5  → 3.50 + 2√(2.079/1) = 3.50 + 2.884 = 6.384 ← wins

⚠ Traps: it is ln, not log₁₀. c sits outside the root. N counts pulls before t.

Shortcut: if every arm has the same N, the bonus is identical, so just compare Q.

The direction check, before anything else

Half the marks are picking min vs max correctly
minimise / take the smallestmaximise / take the largest
path cost g, and f in A*
Gini and Gini-Split (arg min)
within-cluster variance
SSE, MAE, MSE, RMSE
δ in value iteration		 utility U(s) (arg max)
expected reward, Q(a), UCB
accuracy, precision, recall, F1
minimax value at a MAX node

Rule: anything called error, loss, cost, impurity or variance you minimise. Anything called accuracy, utility, reward, value or score you maximise.

★ Test Yourself

Mock Exam

pick your weeks, pick your length, get marked
What this is
A full paper drawn from every question generator in the file — tick the weeks you want, choose a length, optionally put a clock on it. Nothing is marked until you press finish, so you can move back and forth like a real paper.

At the end you get a per-week breakdown, every question you got wrong with its full explanation, and a retry-the-wrong-ones button. Numbers are randomised on every draw, so re-sitting the same selection is a genuinely new paper.

Exam mode

Sit a paper

How to use it in the last week
  1. All weeks, 40 questions, untimed. This is a diagnostic, not a test — you are looking for which rows come back red.
  2. Re-sit with only the red weeks ticked, 20 questions, until they are green. Read the explanation on every wrong answer before moving on.
  3. Then all weeks again, 60 questions, on a 90-minute clock. The point of the clock is to find out which topics you can do but cannot do quickly — those are the ones that cost you marks under pressure.

A score below 50% on a week means go back to that week's section. Between 50% and 70% usually means the theory page rather than the worked examples — it is normally a definition or a distinction that is missing, not the method.

Good luck.
